items.title: Films for artists, galleries and creative studios
items.excerpt: What video artists, galleries and creative businesses need, the film types that suit them, six ideas, permissions for filming art and performance, and cost.
items.coverAlt: An artist beside her portrait at an exhibition
items.body:
For artists, galleries, makers and creative studios, the most useful video shows the person and the process behind the work, because the finished piece can already be seen in a photograph. Film adds what a photo can't: how it's made, why it's made that way and who someone would be buying from or commissioning. That helps sell work, fill exhibitions, win commissions and support funding applications.

This is the arts and creative businesses edition of our series on video by sector. We've already written about filming craft and making the invisible process visible, so this one sticks to what creative businesses need from video and how to plan it.

What do buyers and audiences want to see from a creative business?

The maker, first. Someone choosing between two painters, two jewellers or two studios at a similar price is really choosing a person. Then the process, at the speed it actually happens, because that's what explains the price. Then the work in context: on a wall, worn, in the room it was made for. And the thinking behind it, in the maker's own words rather than an artist statement. That last one matters more than people expect. Written statements tend to drift into abstract language, and the same person talking about their work at the bench is almost always clearer and warmer.

Which video types suit arts and creative businesses?

  • Exhibition films, made in the room where the work hangs.
  • Artist or maker profiles. Who they are and why they work the way they do.
  • Process films. One piece, start to finish, cut short.
  • Commission stories, told by the client.
  • Openings and events.
  • Performance capture, which is its own skill, usually multi-camera and planned around the performance.

If what you need is a catalogue of a whole collection, good photography beats film. A film is for the story. The pictures do the inventory. Most creative businesses need both, and it's cheaper to shoot the stills on the same days as the film than to book them separately.

For Aliyah Art we made an exhibition film in the gallery, built around the artist and the people in her portraits. Filming art is harder than it looks. Galleries are lit for paintings rather than faces, reflections are everywhere, and a film that only pans across canvases tells you nothing about who made them or why. The lighting had to let the work read on camera without flare, and the edit was made for the artist's own promotion.

Catherine Marche is a French bespoke jeweller and goldsmith who's been in London around twenty five years. She works only in recycled metal, holds her packaging to the same rule, and teaches as well as makes. Her film is about why she works that way, told at the bench and in the shop, and filmed in a glass fronted shop where reflections and mixed lighting fight you the whole way. It's a film she can use as her own introduction.

Six film ideas for artists, galleries and creative studios

  1. The exhibition film, made in the room, with the artist talking about the work on the walls.
  2. A commission from sketch to handover, told partly by the client.
  3. One piece made start to finish, cut to a couple of minutes.
  4. Why you work the way you do. Materials, methods, the rules you've set yourself.
  5. The teaching side. A class or workshop, for makers who teach.
  6. Opening night, cut the next morning while people are still talking about it.
A photograph shows the work. A film shows why anyone would make it that way.

What permissions does filming art need?

General guidance, not legal advice.

  • Other people's work. Artworks are protected by copyright. In a group show, get permission from the other artists before their work features in your film.
  • Venues and loans. Galleries often have filming policies, and loaned works can come with conditions. Ask the venue before the shoot, not on the day.
  • Performances. Performers have their own rights in recordings of their performances, so filming a performance needs the performers' consent.
  • Visitors. At openings, put up signs saying filming's taking place and get releases from anyone featured.
  • Music. Music playing in the space ends up in your film. How licensing works covers what that means.

Galleries light paintings beautifully and people terribly. Somebody has to bring a light that doesn't bounce off the varnish.

What does it cost to film a creative business?

Typical UK market ranges, not our quotes: under £2,000 for a freelancer filming a short profile in a day, £2,000 to £8,000 for a small production company with one or two shoot days and some cut-downs, and £8,000 to £30,000 for documentary-style films with research, multi-day shoots, a specialist grade and mix and a full set of cuts.

The drivers in this sector are lighting and reflections, access to a venue out of hours, how long the process takes to film properly, and the number of pieces and people. If you're applying for funding for an exhibition or project, it's worth building documentation into the application budget from the start rather than squeezing it in afterwards. How to set a video budget covers how to work out a sensible number.

Where should an artist use the film?

At the top of the website, in gallery and commission enquiries, in funding applications, and cut into short pieces for social between shows. A film that explains how and why you work saves a lot of first conversations, because people arrive already knowing whether they're a fit. Where to put your brand film goes channel by channel.

If you make something worth watching being made, tell us about the work.
items.author: Earl Duncan

faqs.q: Can I film my own exhibition on a phone?
faqs.a: For quick social clips, yes. Short walk-throughs, a piece being hung, a few words from you at the opening. For a film that represents your practice for years, it's worth getting help, because galleries are difficult to light and reflections on glass and varnish are hard to control. Sound in a busy opening is the other thing phones struggle with.

faqs.q: How long should an artist profile film be?
faqs.a: Usually two to four minutes for the main film, with a sixty to ninety second version and a few short verticals. Process-heavy work can justify longer if the making is genuinely absorbing to watch. The test is whether a viewer who's never heard of you would still be watching at the end, and if not, cut the weakest section.

faqs.q: Do I need permission to film in a public gallery?
faqs.a: Usually, yes, for anything beyond personal snaps. Galleries and museums tend to have filming policies, often with fees for commercial work, and some works on loan can't be filmed at all. Contact the venue's press or events team well before the shoot, explain what the film is for and get permission in writing.

faqs.q: Should a creative business show prices in its videos?
faqs.a: Generally no. Prices change, and a film should last years. What a film can do is explain why the work costs what it does, by showing the time, skill and materials that go into it. That makes the price conversation easier when it happens, without dating the film or putting off people at the first glance.

stat.title: Adults in England who engaged with the arts in the last 12 months
stat.takeaway: Most people still meet the arts in person, so a film's main job is usually getting them through the door or into the studio, not replacing the visit.

source.name: DCMS, Participation Survey 2024-25 annual publication (April 2024 to March 2025)

items.title: Video for gyms, fitness brands and sports clubs
items.excerpt: Why gyms, clubs and fitness brands should film real sessions, the video types that suit sport, six film ideas, consent and safeguarding, and what drives cost.
items.coverAlt: Two jiu-jitsu competitors grappling on the mat
items.body:
Gyms, clubs and fitness brands should film sessions as they really happen: real members, real coaches, the noise and the effort. That's what someone nervous about walking in for the first time needs to see, and it's what makes a coach or a piece of kit credible to people who already train. Staged fitness content is everywhere, and most of it looks like nobody's sweating.

This is the sport and fitness edition of our series on video by sector.

What do people want to see before they join a gym or club?

It depends who's watching. A beginner wants to know whether they'll fit in, who trains there, what the first session is actually like and whether the coach is kind or terrifying. Someone who already trains wants to see the standard of coaching, the training partners and whether the place takes the sport seriously. A fitness brand's buyer wants to see the kit used hard by someone who knows what they're doing.

The same thing answers all three: the real session, filmed properly. Not a model doing one rep in perfect light.

Which video types suit sport and fitness businesses?

  • A club or gym story film. Who started it, who coaches, and why people keep coming back.
  • Coach profiles. Short pieces on the people doing the teaching.
  • First-class films for beginners, from their side of the door.
  • Event and competition coverage, with photographs and short edits competitors will share.
  • Seminar highlights that sell the next one.
  • Brand content for kit, filmed in real training.

One exception. If you're building a library of exercise demos for an app or a members' area, you need consistent, clean studio-style filming, the same angle and light every time. That's a different job from documentary, and a simpler setup usually does it best.

What does that look like in practice?

Most of our sport work is in combat sports. For Boxraw we filmed professional cruiserweight Isaac Chamberlain training: bag work, pads and the kit in use, shot around the session rather than staged, and cut for the brand's social channels. A boxer mid-session isn't a model. You get the round you get, in the light the gym has.

At London Fight Factory we filmed a seminar with Rafael Lovato Jr and Demian Maia, a packed room in a single afternoon, cut into a highlight edit the gym can use to sell the next one. The moments that matter at a seminar are small: a grip, a correction, a face when something finally clicks.

For competitions, we covered two London grappling events, All Stars BJJ and Mat Masters, and delivered 343 edited photographs across two athlete galleries, an overview video in 16:9 and 9:16, and vertical shorts. Those events have two audiences at once: the organiser wants next year's entries, and every competitor wants a photo and a clip they're proud to repost. We're also making Manxinha, a long form documentary with London Fight Factory, which is currently in production.

Six film ideas for gyms, clubs and fitness brands

  1. The first class, from the beginner's side, with someone who's genuinely new and happy to be filmed.
  2. The coach, on why they still teach.
  3. Competition day, cut fast enough that competitors can share it while it still feels current.
  4. A seminar or guest coach highlight, built to sell the next event.
  5. Kit in a real session, close on the wear and the effort.
  6. A long-term member's story, told about the club and the people rather than a before and after.
If nobody in the video is out of breath, nobody watching it will believe it.

What should gyms and clubs be careful about?

General guidance, not legal advice.

  • Members' consent. Tell people in advance when filming's happening, give anyone who'd rather not be filmed a space out of shot, and get releases from anyone featured. Changing rooms are never filmed.
  • Children. Follow your safeguarding policy and your sport's governing body guidance on photography, and get written parental consent for anyone under 18.
  • Health and results claims. The CAP Code has rules on weight control and health claims. Be careful with before and after results and anything promising a figure.
  • Safety. Never interrupt a live round or a heavy lift for a shot. The camera works around the session.
  • Music. The licence that lets you play music in the gym doesn't cover putting it in a video. Music licensing for brand videos explains the difference.

A fighter mid-round doesn't do take two. Neither should the person filming them.

What does sport and fitness video cost?

Typical UK market ranges, not our quotes: under £2,000 for a freelancer filming a session and a short edit, £2,000 to £8,000 for a small production company with one or two shoot days and several cut-downs, and £8,000 to £30,000 for documentary-style club or brand films with research and a full set of cuts. Our own Spotlight shoot, for gyms and coaches who'll post it themselves, is £795 + VAT: up to four hours on location, 30 edited photographs and three short-form videos.

The drivers here are event length, how many mats or areas are running at once, whether you need photographs as well as video, the number of edits and galleries, and how quickly it has to turn round. Competition content loses value fast, so turnaround is worth paying for. Turning one shoot into a year of content shows how to get the most from a single day.

If you run a gym, a club or an event and want it filmed the way it actually feels, get in touch.
items.author: Earl Duncan

faqs.q: Can we film during normal classes?
faqs.a: Yes, and it usually gives the best footage, because nobody's performing. Tell members beforehand, give anyone who'd rather not appear a place to train out of shot, and get releases from anyone featured prominently. A small crew working around the session rather than through it barely changes the class, which is what you want on screen.

faqs.q: How quickly should competition content be delivered?
faqs.a: As fast as you can manage. Competitors share their clips and photographs while the event's still fresh, and enthusiasm drops within days. A few short reels within a day or two, followed by the full gallery and an overview video, keeps the event in people's feeds. Agree turnaround times before the day so everyone knows when to expect them.

faqs.q: Should a gym use music in its videos?
faqs.a: Only music you're licensed to use in video. The licence that covers playing music in the gym doesn't extend to syncing it to a film, and platforms will flag or mute unlicensed tracks. Some of the best training content uses no music at all, just the sound of the session, which also avoids the problem entirely.

faqs.q: Do sports clubs need parental consent to film juniors?
faqs.a: Yes. Get written consent from a parent or guardian for anyone under 18 who'll be identifiable, follow your club's safeguarding policy and check your governing body's guidance on photography. Many clubs keep a list of juniors who mustn't be filmed, and the person filming needs to know it before the session starts.

stat.title: How active adults in England are
stat.takeaway: A quarter of adults do less than 30 minutes of activity a week, and they're exactly the people a gym's video has to reassure.

source.name: Sport England, Active Lives Adult Survey November 2024-25 (published 23 April 2026)

items.title: How accountants, consultants and architects use video
items.excerpt: What clients of accountants, consultants and architects want from video, the types that suit professional firms, six ideas, confidentiality rules and cost.
items.coverAlt: People at work in an office
items.body:
For accountants, consultants, architects and other professional firms, video's main job is to let a prospective client meet the people before they meet them. You sell expertise and judgement, which can't be seen, and clients buy it from people they trust. A short film of the team explaining how they think, and a client describing what working together was actually like, does more than any list of services on a website.

This is the professional services edition of our series on video by sector.

Why do professional firms find video hard?

Three reasons come up again and again. The work is invisible, because a tax plan or a strategy review doesn't look like anything on camera. A lot of it is confidential, so the best stories are the ones you can't tell without permission. And every firm describes itself in the same words. Approachable. Trusted. Bespoke. A prospective client reading five websites in a row can't tell them apart.

Video gets round the first and third problems because it films people rather than the work. The second needs some care, which I'll come to.

What do clients of professional firms want to see?

  • The person they'll actually deal with, not just the founding partner.
  • How you explain things. Whether you make a complicated subject simple, or hide behind jargon.
  • Evidence from someone like them. A client in the same position, explaining what changed.
  • For architects, the buildings and the people who live or work in them, which is where the judgement finally becomes visible.

We've written about why a documentary approach lands differently from corporate video. In professional services that gap is wide, because clients have seen every version of the polished partner reading a script.

Which video types suit professional services?

  • A practice film. Who you are, how you work and why, in two to four minutes.
  • Client stories. The strongest thing you can publish, if a client's willing.
  • Short expert answers. One partner, one question clients always ask, one to two minutes. Easy to make in batches.
  • Project films for architects. The finished building, and the client and users talking about it.
  • Trainee and graduate films for recruitment.
  • Talks and seminars, recorded and cut down.

Where you need to explain a process with numbers in it, say how a particular calculation works, on-screen graphics or animation will usually do it better than a person talking. We don't make animation. We'd film the partner explaining why it matters and leave the diagram to someone who draws.

This is a contractor's film rather than a practice's, but the format transfers directly, especially to architects. For the Barry Road renovation the homeowner gives their own account of the job: what they wanted, what it was like to live through and what they ended up with. Before and after floorplans are cut in so the scale of the work reads on screen. The builder never makes a claim about themselves, which is exactly why it's something they can send to a prospective client deciding whether to trust them.

Six film ideas for accountants, consultants and architects

  1. The first meeting, answered. A partner going through the five questions clients always ask at the start.
  2. A client's problem, solved. Told by the client, with their permission and sign-off.
  3. A building a year on. The people using it, talking about how it works for them.
  4. One idea on a whiteboard. A consultant explaining a single way of thinking about a problem.
  5. A deadline explained. A short piece ahead of a filing date or rule change, recorded in plain English.
  6. The trainee intake. Who joins, what they learn and who teaches them.
You can't film judgement. You can film someone explaining how they use it.

What should professional firms watch out for?

General guidance, not legal or regulatory advice. Check your own professional body's rules.

  • Client confidentiality. Written permission for any client story, agreement on what can and can't be said, and approval of the edit. Check screens, desks and files in shot.
  • Professional conduct rules. Most professional bodies, including those for accountants and architects, have codes covering how members promote themselves, usually requiring it to be honest and not misleading. Some have specific points on testimonials. Read yours before publishing a client story.
  • Claims. "Leading", "best" and "guaranteed savings" need evidence under the CAP Code.
  • General versus personal advice. An expert answer video should be clearly general, and say so. Nobody should mistake it for advice on their own situation.

Every firm's website says they're approachable. A two minute film is the only place anyone can check.

What does professional services video cost?

Typical UK market ranges, not our quotes: under £2,000 for a freelancer and a simple interview piece in a day, £2,000 to £8,000 for a small production company with one or two shoot days and a few cut-downs, which is where most corporate video sits, and £8,000 to £30,000 for documentary-style work with proper research, several voices and a full set of cuts.

The drivers in this sector are the number of people on camera, the number of offices or sites, how available your clients are to be filmed, and approvals. Compliance review and partner sign-off add time, so build them into the schedule rather than discovering them at the end. How to set a video budget covers working the number out from what the film needs to do.

What if the partners hate being on camera?

Most people do, at first. A conversation with an interviewer goes far better than reading to a lens, and nobody needs to memorise anything. How to speak on camera when you're not a presenter is worth sending round before the shoot. And it's fine if the senior partner isn't the face of the film. Clients would often rather meet the person they'll actually be working with.

If your firm sounds the same as every other one on paper, tell us who's behind it.
items.author: Earl Duncan

faqs.q: Will clients agree to appear in a case study film?
faqs.a: More often than firms expect, if you ask well. Pick a client with a good result and a good relationship, explain exactly how the film will be used, give them approval of the edit and keep the filming short and at their convenience. Some will say no for confidentiality reasons, which is fine. One willing client is enough to start.

faqs.q: Should every partner have their own video?
faqs.a: Not necessarily. A short introduction for each client-facing person is useful on a team page, and they're cheap to make in one sitting. But a film built around how the firm works, with several voices, usually does more than a row of separate talking heads. Start with the main film and add individual pieces from the same shoot.

faqs.q: Is LinkedIn the right place for professional services video?
faqs.a: It's usually the most useful channel, because that's where clients and referrers already look at people in your field. Short expert answers and clips from a practice film suit it well. The full film still belongs on your website, where people go when they're seriously considering you, and in emails after a first meeting.

faqs.q: How do architects film projects without the original clients?
faqs.a: With the current owners' or occupiers' permission, you can film the finished building and the people using it, which is often more persuasive than the original client anyway. If the original client is happy to take part, even better. Get written permission to film the property, and agree whether its location can be identified.

items.title: Video for car dealerships and automotive brands
items.excerpt: What car buyers want to see before they visit, the video types that suit dealerships and automotive brands, six film ideas, driving and finance rules, and cost.
items.coverAlt: A man working on a forecourt fitting
items.body:
For dealerships, garages and automotive brands, video does two jobs. It gets a specific car or service in front of someone researching from their sofa, and it shows them who they'll be dealing with when they turn up. Most dealers only do the first job. Stock walkarounds are everywhere, and they're useful, but the people, the workshop and what happens after the sale are what make someone choose one forecourt over the one down the road.

This is the automotive edition of our series on video by sector.

What do car buyers want to see before they visit?

More than the car's best side. People now do most of their research before they set foot on a forecourt, and they're looking for reasons to trust or rule out a seller. That means:

  • The actual car, including the marks and the tyres, not just the angles that flatter it.
  • The people they'll deal with, sales and service both.
  • The workshop and the prep, because that's what tells a used car buyer whether the car was looked after before it went on sale.
  • The handover, and what happens if something goes wrong a month later.
  • Honest opinions on the cars themselves, from someone who isn't reading the brochure.

Which video types suit automotive businesses?

  • Vehicle walkarounds. Consistent, quick and frequent. These are fine on a phone if the light and sound are decent, and phone video for business covers how.
  • Presenter-led reviews by your own staff. They don't need to be slick. They need to be honest.
  • A dealer or brand story film. The family business, the founder, the reputation. Two to four minutes, for the website and YouTube.
  • Customer stories. A buyer explaining why they came back, told in their words.
  • Workshop and technician films. The skill behind the service department.
  • Finance and warranty explainers. In fairness, clear on-screen graphics or animation often explain a finance product better than live action. That's not something we make, and I'd say so if it were the right tool for you.

Six film ideas for dealerships and automotive brands

  1. The handover, a month later. A customer telling you how it's gone, not how excited they were on the day.
  2. The longest-serving technician. What they've seen change, and what they still check on every car.
  3. Prep, start to finish. What happens to a used car between arriving and going on sale.
  4. Staff-presented reviews. We've made honest car reviews for a client, presented by their own team rather than a hired face, because buyers believe someone who works with the cars every day.
  5. The family business story. Why the dealership exists and who's behind it.
  6. A launch night or open day, cut for social the next morning.

The Car Planet film shows the conditions most automotive shoots run in. Car Planet went from thirty cars to around two and a half thousand in four years. We filmed a customer story there for an installer on a working day, with cars moving and staff on the floor, and nothing stopped for the camera. The client didn't want the site itself on display, so most setups were framed tight, and the edit was filled out with b-roll from previous installs and Car Planet's own image bank. The interviews with the Car Planet team were recorded between jobs, and the day produced a YouTube film and two vertical cuts. Different subject from selling cars, same problem every dealer has: a trading business that can't shut for a film.

We've also filmed at a car showroom in Poole and made a dealership case study with Eden Motor Group, following a customer from the forecourt through to a charger being fitted at home. The common thread is that customers and staff carry the film, and the business doesn't make claims about itself.

Stock walkarounds show the car. They don't show anyone why they should buy it from you.

What rules apply to automotive video?

General guidance, not legal advice, and worth running past whoever handles compliance for you.

  • Driving on screen. The CAP Code has a section on motoring. Marketing mustn't show or encourage speeding, dangerous or irresponsible driving, so no dramatic road shots that look like a chase.
  • Finance offers. If a video mentions a monthly price or a finance deal, consumer credit advertising rules may require a representative example. Check with your finance provider before publishing.
  • Accuracy. Mileage, condition, spec and price must match the car. A walkaround is an advert, and the same rules on misleading claims apply.
  • People and plates. Customers need to consent to being filmed. Blur number plates on other people's cars.
  • Road filming. Nobody presents while they're actually driving at speed. Some councils need notice or a permit for filming on public roads and pavements, so check with the local film office.

Every dealership has someone who's brilliant on camera and doesn't know it yet. It's rarely the one who volunteers.

What does automotive video cost?

Walkarounds can be done in-house for the cost of your staff's time and a decent microphone. For anything commissioned, typical UK market ranges, not our quotes, run from under £2,000 for a freelancer filming a simple piece in a day, through £2,000 to £8,000 for a small production company with one or two shoot days, to £8,000 to £30,000 for documentary-style brand films with research, a crew and a full set of cuts. Agency campaigns with tracking vehicles and closed roads go well beyond that.

What moves the number in this sector: car-to-car tracking shots, closed locations, drone work (which needs a properly licensed operator), the number of vehicles and people, and how many versions you need for the website, YouTube and social. The film budget calculator is a quick way to rough it out, and brand documentary vs corporate video explains why a customer-led film reads so differently from a showroom advert.

How often should a dealership publish video?

Walkarounds as often as stock changes. Bigger films, like a brand story or a customer story, once or twice a year, then cut into shorter pieces to run between them. Consistency matters more than polish for the everyday stuff, and polish matters more than frequency for the films that carry your name.

If there's a story behind your business that the walkarounds aren't telling, tell us about it.
items.author: Earl Duncan

faqs.q: Do car walkaround videos actually sell cars?
faqs.a: They help buyers shortlist, which is what they're for. A clear, honest walkaround saves a wasted trip, answers questions before a call and makes a listing feel more trustworthy. They rarely close a sale on their own. That's the job of the people, the test drive and the price, which is why it's worth also filming who buyers will deal with.

faqs.q: Can our sales staff present reviews themselves?
faqs.a: Yes, and buyers often prefer it. Someone who works with the cars every day knows what owners actually ask about. Keep it honest, mention the downsides as well, and avoid scripts that sound like the brochure. A short brief, a decent microphone and a couple of practice takes usually do more than an expensive hired presenter.

faqs.q: Do we need permission to film customers at handover?
faqs.a: Yes. Anyone identifiable needs to agree, and a simple signed release recording how the footage will be used is the sensible way to do it. Ask before the handover rather than in the middle of it, make it easy to say no, and blur number plates if the customer would rather not have their car identifiable online.

faqs.q: Is drone footage worth paying for at a dealership?
faqs.a: Occasionally. A drone shot shows the size of a site or a forecourt well and can open a brand film nicely. It doesn't tell anyone why to buy from you, and the operator needs the right registration and permissions, so it adds cost. For most dealers, the money is better spent on people and customer stories.

stat.title: UK new car registrations
stat.takeaway: More cars are being sold, but buyers have more choice of where to buy them, so being the dealer they feel they already know counts.

source.name: SMMT, full-year 2025 new car registrations (published 6 January 2026)

items.title: Recruitment video: what candidates want to see
items.excerpt: What candidates want from a recruitment video, how agencies and HR teams use film differently, six ideas, consent and equality points, and what it costs.
items.coverAlt: Two people laughing together at a trade show
items.body:
Recruitment video works when it shows candidates the actual job and the actual people: the place, the team, a manager talking straight and an honest sense of a normal day. For in-house HR teams that means careers pages, job adverts and onboarding. For recruitment agencies there's a second job as well, winning hiring clients, which needs its own kind of film. In both cases real staff on camera beat actors, stock footage and slogans by a long way.

This is the recruitment and HR edition of our series on video by sector.

What do candidates actually want to see?

The things a job advert can't tell them. Who they'd sit next to. What the manager's like when they're not interviewing. Whether the place is calm or chaos at ten on a Tuesday. Whether people get promoted, or just say they do.

So the strongest recruitment films are built on a few specific things:

  • The people already doing the job, talking about it in their own words.
  • The manager, answering the questions candidates actually ask at interview.
  • The place, filmed as it is, including the less glamorous corners.
  • Proof of progression, from someone who started where the candidate would start.
  • A bit of honesty about what's hard. It filters out the wrong people early and makes everything else more believable.

We've written about why real people on camera matter more now, and recruitment is where that bites hardest. Candidates are deciding whether to spend most of their waking week with these people. Show them the people.

How is video different for a recruitment agency?

An agency sells to two sides at once. Candidates need to trust the consultant enough to hand over their career. Hiring clients need to trust the agency enough to hand over a role. That splits the film work in two.

For candidates: consultant introductions, short sector updates and honest stories from people you've placed. For clients: a hiring manager explaining why they came back for a second hire, filmed with their permission and their sign-off on the edit. That second kind is the one most agencies never make, and it's the one that does the selling, for the same reason any customer story beats a company talking about itself.

If an agency offers to make employer brand films for its clients, remember you're filming somebody else's workplace and staff. Their HR team needs to agree what's filmed, who's in it and where it's used, in writing, before anyone turns up.

Which video types suit recruitment and HR?

  • An employer brand film. Two to four minutes on what the organisation is like to work for, for the careers page and LinkedIn.
  • Role videos. One short film per job family, so each advert has something specific attached.
  • Day-in-the-life pieces. Loose, observational, cut vertical for social.
  • Welcome and onboarding films. The people a new starter will meet, before they meet them.
  • Careers fair and graduate event coverage.

One honest note. For compliance training, policy walkthroughs and anything process-heavy in onboarding, an animated explainer or screen-based e-learning is usually the better tool. We don't make animation, and live action of someone reading a policy aloud helps nobody.

La Fromagerie was made as a brand documentary rather than for hiring, and it shows what staff voices can carry. It's told by the founder, the cheesemongers and the wholesale side, each describing the same business from where they stand, filmed in shops that were open and trading. Swap the cheese for your workplace and that's most of what a good employer brand film needs: several people who actually do the work, in the place they do it.

Six recruitment film ideas

  1. The person who got promoted from the role you're hiring for, explaining how.
  2. A manager's honest answers to the five questions every candidate asks.
  3. The first week, filmed with a real new starter who's happy to take part.
  4. A hiring manager's story for an agency, on why they came back.
  5. A consultant's monthly sector briefing, sixty seconds, straight to camera.
  6. The apprentice or graduate cohort, filmed at the start and again a year on.
Candidates are deciding whether to spend most of their week with these people. Show them the people.

What do HR teams need to be careful about?

General guidance, not legal advice, but these come up every time.

  • Staff consent. Footage of an identifiable person is personal data under UK GDPR. Between an employer and an employee, agreement isn't always freely given, because people may not feel able to say no to their boss. Make taking part genuinely optional, use a clear release and explain what happens to the footage if they leave.
  • Equality. Under the Equality Act 2010, adverts mustn't discriminate. Words like "young, energetic team" and who's shown on screen can imply a preference you didn't intend. Show your team honestly, and don't stage a workforce you don't have.
  • Confidential information. Candidate records, client names and salary bands on screens. Check every background.
  • Shelf life. People leave. Plan for refreshing the film, and agree with each person how long their footage stays up.

How to brief your team before a film shoot covers the release forms and the practical side in more detail.

Nobody has ever accepted a job because of a drone shot of the car park. Plenty have turned one down after meeting the manager.

How long should a recruitment video be, and what does it cost?

Sixty to ninety seconds for job adverts and social, two to four minutes for the careers page, and under a minute for each role video. Shorter is nearly always better for a role video, because it's competing with the advert text for the same thirty seconds of attention.

On cost, typical UK market ranges, not our quotes: under £2,000 for a freelancer filming a simple interview piece in a day, £2,000 to £8,000 for a small production company with one or two shoot days and a few cut-downs, and £8,000 to £30,000 for documentary-style employer brand work with research and several voices. The main drivers are the number of sites, the number of people and roles, how many versions you need for different platforms and subtitles. The efficient way to do it is to film several role videos and the main film on the same day, which is exactly what planning where a film will be used before the shoot makes possible.

If you're hiring this year and want the careers page to do more of the work, tell us what you're recruiting for.
items.author: Earl Duncan

faqs.q: Should we use actors in a recruitment video?
faqs.a: No. Candidates are trying to find out what your real workplace and real people are like, and actors answer that question with a fiction. Once a new starter realises the people in the film don't work there, the trust goes. Real staff who are a bit nervous on camera are far more persuasive than polished performers, and a decent interviewer can help them relax.

faqs.q: What if someone in the film leaves the company?
faqs.a: Agree this up front. A good release form says how long the footage can be used and what happens if the person leaves. Many organisations keep the film running for an agreed period, then refresh it. Building the film from several voices helps, because losing one person means recutting a section rather than reshooting the whole thing.

faqs.q: Can recruitment agencies film their clients' workplaces?
faqs.a: Yes, with the client's written agreement covering what's filmed, who appears, where it's used and who owns the footage. The client's staff need to give their own consent too, ideally through the client's HR team. Agree the sign-off process before the shoot, because a hiring client will want approval of anything showing their premises and people.

faqs.q: Do recruitment videos need subtitles?
faqs.a: Yes. Most social video is watched with the sound off, and subtitles also make the film accessible to deaf and hard of hearing candidates, which matters for an employer saying it welcomes everyone. Burned-in subtitles suit social feeds, while a separate caption file works well on YouTube and most careers pages. Always have a person check them for names and job titles.

items.title: Recruitment videos and employer brand films
items.excerpt: What a recruitment or employer brand video should show, which formats work, who should be in it, the equality and consent rules to respect, and what it costs.
items.coverAlt: An engineer at work, smiling at camera
items.body:
A recruitment video shows candidates what working somewhere is actually like, so the right people apply and the wrong ones don't. An employer brand film is the broader version: why people join, why they stay and what the place is like on an ordinary Tuesday. Both work best with real staff, in the real workplace, being honest about the job.

Honesty matters more here than almost anywhere. Oversell a job and you'll fill it, and then fill it again in six months.

What should a recruitment video show?

  • The actual work. What someone in the role does all day, including the dull parts.
  • The people. Colleagues and, ideally, the manager they'd report to.
  • Where it leads. Training, progression, people who started where the candidate would start.
  • The hard bits. Early starts, travel, weather, pressure. Said plainly.
  • The place. The site, the van, the office, the kitchen.
  • The practical stuff. Hours, shifts, location, and pay range if you can share it.

Why do so many recruitment videos look the same?

Because they're made to look like a good place to work rather than to show a particular one. A drone shot of the building, people laughing at laptops, someone saying "we're like a family", upbeat music. Candidates have seen it hundreds of times and discount all of it, the same way buyers discount a company praising itself.

What cuts through is specific and human. A named person explaining what they found hard in their first month. An apprentice showing the first thing they built. The manager admitting the job involves a lot of driving. I've written about why this matters more as AI-made content spreads in why real people on camera matter more now.

Which formats work?

  • An employer brand film, two to four minutes, for the careers page and the first conversation.
  • Role films, sixty to ninety seconds each, a day in the life of one specific job.
  • Vertical clips for social, especially for school leavers, apprentices and graduates.
  • Short staff answers to the questions candidates actually ask at interview.

The common thread is the work itself and the people doing it. Our Virtus Energy film was made for prospective partners rather than candidates, but it's built the way a good recruitment film should be: interviews with the installers doing the work, footage captured on live jobs, and an installer who thinks nothing of driving from Liverpool to Norfolk for a job.

If a new starter is surprised by their first week, the recruitment film didn't do its job.

Who should be in it?

Your own staff, chosen for being honest and comfortable rather than senior or photogenic. A short pre-interview helps find the people with real stories. Give them a sense of the questions without scripting answers, and send them how to give a good answer in a film interview. People who are a bit nervous at the start are usually the most convincing by the end.

Every recruitment film made in the last decade seems to contain a slow-motion high five. You're allowed to be the exception.

What rules and sensitivities should you respect?

General guidance, so run the final cut past HR or an employment adviser:

  • Don't imply who you want by age, sex or any other protected characteristic. The Equality Act 2010 applies to recruitment, and lines like "a young, energetic team" can suggest age discrimination, on screen as much as in a job ad.
  • Show your real team. Staging a diverse line-up you don't actually have is misleading, and candidates notice on their first day. If you're working on it, say so honestly.
  • Don't promise what you can't deliver. Pay, progression, flexible working. If it's in the film, it should be true for the role.
  • Consent and leavers. Staff should agree to public use, and you'll need a plan for when someone in the film moves on. Who owns the footage covers the licensing side.

Where do recruitment videos get used?

The careers page, job posts on LinkedIn and job boards, social channels, school and college careers events, open days, trade shows and the email inviting someone to interview. A film sent with an interview invite also means candidates turn up already knowing who they'll meet. Where to put your brand film covers recruitment as one of several places a film earns its keep.

Measure it like any other hiring channel. Track how many applications come through the careers page, ask candidates at interview whether they watched it, and notice whether the people who apply are a better fit. Fewer, better applications is a good result, even if it doesn't look like one on a dashboard.

How is it made, and what drives the cost?

Research comes first: short conversations with staff to find the people and stories worth filming. Then usually one or two shoot days around real work, scheduled so the business keeps running. From one shoot you can cut the main film, several role films and a batch of vertical clips. Cost depends on the number of roles, sites and people, and how many cuts you need. As general UK market ranges from our free playbook, most corporate video sits between £2,000 and £8,000, while documentary-style films with research, multi-day shoots and a full set of cuts run from around £8,000 to £30,000.

The same shoot can often feed your onboarding videos too, if everyone's agreed to both uses. Preparing the team properly helps on the day, and briefing your team before a shoot covers how. If you're hiring and want candidates to see the real job, talk to us.
items.author: Earl Duncan

faqs.q: Should we use actors or our own staff?
faqs.a: Your own staff, almost always. Candidates are trying to work out what the real team is like, and actors answer the wrong question. Staff can be nervous or less polished, but that reads as genuine. Actors only make sense for scripted scenarios, like showing a difficult customer situation, where nobody real should be identifiable.

faqs.q: What if staff don't want to be filmed?
faqs.a: Respect it and don't pressure anyone. Plenty of people are happy to be filmed working but not interviewed, so offer that option. Make it clear that saying no has no consequences. You only need a handful of willing, honest voices, and a film full of reluctant faces does more harm than good anyway.

faqs.q: Should a recruitment video mention salary?
faqs.a: If you can share a range in the job ad, mentioning it or showing it on screen helps, because pay is one of the first things candidates want to know. In a general employer brand film, specific figures date quickly, so it's often better to keep pay in the job ad and use the film for what text can't show.

faqs.q: Can a recruitment film be used for onboarding?
faqs.a: Yes, and it often should be, because new starters want to see the same things candidates do. Make sure everyone in it agreed to both public and internal use. You might add a short internal welcome from the founder for onboarding, but the core film can do both jobs from a single shoot.

stat.title: Trust in each source to give accurate information about a brand
stat.takeaway: People trust an employee more than the person at the top, so let your team describe the job rather than the boss.

source.name: Edelman, 2025 Edelman Trust Barometer Special Report: Brand Trust, From We to Me (15 markets)

items.title: Startup video: what founders should film first
items.excerpt: What video a startup or founder-led business needs first, what customers, hires and investors look for, six film ideas, the rules to watch and what it costs.
items.coverAlt: Two founders laughing on their stand
items.body:
The first video a startup or founder-led business should make is usually a short film of the founder explaining, in their own words, what problem they saw and why they're the one fixing it. Early on, nobody's buying a track record, because there isn't one. They're buying a person and a reason to believe them, and video shows both faster than anything else. Product demos, customer stories and hiring films come after, once there are customers and a team to film.

This is the startup and founder-led edition of our series on video by sector. If you want the bigger picture first, how video actually makes a business money covers the routes from a film to revenue.

Why does video matter more for a young business?

Because there's nothing else to lean on. An established firm has reviews, years of case studies and a name people half recognise. A startup has a website, a pitch and whoever's behind it. Everyone deciding whether to take a chance on you, a customer, a first hire, a supplier giving you terms, is really asking the same question: are these people serious, and will they still be here next year?

You can't answer that with copy. Every startup site says it's passionate and different. A founder on camera, talking plainly about the problem, answers it in about forty seconds, because people are very good at reading another person and very bad at reading a mission statement.

What do customers, hires and investors need to see?

Different things, from the same footage. Customers want to know you understand their problem better than they do, and that there's a real team behind the product. Hires are weighing up a job with no guarantees, so they want to see who they'd work with and why it's worth the risk. Investors and partners want clarity: can this founder explain the business simply, and do they sound like they'll keep going when it gets hard?

The useful part is that one well planned shoot can feed all three. A founder interview, some honest coverage of the team at work and a couple of early customers gives you a main film, a careers page piece and a stack of short cuts. Turning one film into a year of content goes through how that's planned.

Which video types suit a startup?

  • A founder story film. Why the business exists, told by the person who started it. Ages well, because it doesn't depend on this month's feature list.
  • Customer stories. Once you've got a few happy customers, their account beats yours every time. There's more in testimonial videos that don't sound like testimonials.
  • Product demos. Honestly, if you're a software company, a clean screen recording or an animated explainer will show the product better than live action ever will. We don't make animation, and I'd point you to a good motion designer for that part.
  • Hiring and team films. Short, real, filmed where the work happens.
  • Build-in-public clips. Rough, frequent, often on a phone, and that's fine for this job.

Carreducker is about as founder-led as a business gets. Deborah Carre and James Ducker met as apprentices under the same master shoemaker at John Lobb, finished their apprenticeships and eventually set up on their own. Every pair takes 210 steps and around six months. They finish each other's sentences, so we shot the interview as one conversation rather than two takes cut together, and the film carries both halves of the business, the making and the teaching. That's the founder film at its simplest: the people, the work and the reason, with nothing added.

Six film ideas for founder-led businesses

  1. Why I started this. The founder, filmed where the problem actually lives, not in a hired studio.
  2. The first customer. The person who took a chance on you, telling it their way.
  3. The bit nobody sees. The workshop, the warehouse, the code review, the tasting. Whatever happens behind the product.
  4. A week with the team. Cut for the careers page and for the next hire.
  5. The thing that nearly went wrong. Told honestly, it's often the most watched film a young company makes.
  6. The launch, filmed as it happens. Nothing staged, nothing repeated.
Early on, nobody's buying a track record. They're buying a person and a reason to believe them.

What should founders be careful about on camera?

A few things catch young businesses out. This is general guidance, not legal advice.

  • Claims. The UK advertising rules (the CAP Code) expect you to hold evidence for objective claims before you publish them. "The UK's first", "twice as fast" and "trusted by hundreds" all need backing up.
  • Anything that invites investment. A video asking people to invest can count as a financial promotion, which is regulated. Take proper advice before that goes anywhere public.
  • Consent. Anyone identifiable needs to agree to being filmed, and a signed release is the sensible way to record it. That includes early customers and friends helping out.
  • What's in the background. Whiteboards, screens, roadmaps and investor decks have a way of drifting into shot. Brief your team and tidy first.

A pitch deck has twenty slides. A founder film needs one sentence the founder actually believes.

How much does startup video cost?

It depends on what you're making, and typical UK market ranges are wide. As a rough guide, and these are market ranges rather than our quotes: under £2,000 usually buys a freelancer for a day or less, an interview, some B-roll and a short edit. £2,000 to £8,000 buys a small production company, one or two shoot days and a couple of cut-downs. £8,000 to £30,000 is where documentary brand films sit, with proper research, multi-day shoots, a specialist grade and mix and a full set of cuts.

The things that move the number are shoot days, the number of locations and people, the crew, how many versions you need and the licence. For most early-stage businesses my honest advice is to film the weekly stuff yourselves on a phone with a decent mic, and save the money for one properly made film when you've got something real to say: a launch, a raise, a first big customer. The film budget calculator will give you a rough figure in a couple of minutes.

When is it too early for a proper film?

When the product changes every month. A polished film about features you'll scrap by spring is money gone. A founder story, on the other hand, holds up, because why you started rarely changes even when what you sell does. If you're not sure, start with the story and leave the specs to screen recordings you can redo in an afternoon.

If you've got a founder with something to say and want to know whether there's a film in it, tell us about the business. We'll say so either way.
items.author: Earl Duncan

faqs.q: Should a founder film themselves or hire someone?
faqs.a: Both, for different jobs. Founders filming short, regular updates on a phone is cheap and builds familiarity. A considered film about why the business exists is worth commissioning, because the founder can't interview themselves, light themselves and judge their own answers at the same time. Most founders also say better things when someone else is asking the questions.

faqs.q: Can a startup video help with fundraising?
faqs.a: It can help investors get a sense of the founder before a meeting, and a short film is easy to forward inside a fund. It won't replace the deck, the numbers or the conversation. If a video invites the public to invest, for example on a crowdfunding page, it may be a regulated financial promotion, so get proper advice before publishing.

faqs.q: What if we don't have customers to film yet?
faqs.a: Film the founder and the team, and the work itself. The problem you're solving, the people building it and the process behind the product are all real and worth showing. Customer stories can come later, and they'll be stronger for waiting until the results are genuine rather than borrowed from a pilot that's barely started.

faqs.q: How long should a founder story film be?
faqs.a: Usually two to four minutes for the main version, with a sixty to ninety second cut for the top of the website and short verticals for social. The test is whether every section earns its place. A founder with a genuinely good story can hold attention longer, but most films get better when the weakest minute is cut.

stat.title: UK businesses born in 2019 still trading five years later
stat.takeaway: Customers and hires know most new businesses don't last, so anything that shows who's behind yours, and why it'll stick around, does real work.

source.name: Office for National Statistics, Business demography, UK: 2024 (released 20 November 2025)

items.title: Customer onboarding and customer service videos
items.excerpt: How customer onboarding and customer service videos cut support queries: which questions to film first, the right format, ideal length and where they belong.
items.coverAlt: A resident talking to camera outside his building
items.body:
Customer onboarding videos help new customers get set up and get value quickly after they buy. Customer service videos answer the questions people keep asking, so they can sort things out themselves. They're the same family: practical, made for people who've already paid you, and judged by fewer support tickets, fewer returns and fewer customers giving up in the first month.

They're also the least glamorous video a business makes, which is partly why they're so often missing.

What's the difference between onboarding and customer service videos?

Onboarding videos are proactive and come in a sequence. A short welcome, then setup, then the first useful thing the customer can do. They arrive by email, in the app or in the box, timed to when the customer needs them.

Customer service videos are reactive. A searchable library, one problem per video: how to reset it, why the light's flashing, how to read your bill. People find them when something's gone wrong, often while slightly annoyed.

Which questions should you turn into videos first?

Ask your support team for the ten questions they answer most. Then look for the ones that involve a physical step people get wrong, the ones that lead to returns or cancellations, and the ones that take longest to explain by email. Those are your first videos. You don't need a hundred. A dozen good ones covering the most common problems will take a lot of pressure off a support team.

Once they're live, check they're working. Watch whether tickets on those topics fall, ask the support team which links they send most, and look at where people stop watching. A video that loses everyone at the same moment usually has a confusing step right there, and that's a cheap fix.

What format works best?

Being honest about the tools:

  • Software and apps: screen recording with a clear voiceover. A crew rarely adds anything.
  • Physical products: live action, close up, from the customer's point of view, in a normal home or workplace rather than a studio.
  • Abstract things like how a tariff, a warranty or a billing cycle works: simple animation or graphics often explain them better than a person can.
  • The welcome: a real person from the business on camera. It's the start of a relationship, and a face helps.

As part of our content partnership with Plug In Stations we've made app tutorials as well as reviews and comparisons. A full walkthrough like the one below serves people who've just had a charger fitted as much as people still deciding.

What makes a good how-to video?

  • The title is the question. Use the exact words customers type, such as "why is my charger flashing blue", not your internal name for the issue.
  • The answer comes first. No intro, no logo sting.
  • One task per video, with chapters if it's longer.
  • Exact screens and buttons, matching the current version.
  • Captions and a transcript on the help page, which also helps people find it through search.
  • A calm, friendly tone. The viewer's probably frustrated. Don't be chirpy at them.
Title every help video with the exact words a frustrated customer would type into a search bar.

How long should they be?

Thirty seconds to three minutes per task covers most of them. A welcome video works at one to two minutes. A full product or app walkthrough can be longer, ten minutes or more, as long as it's chaptered so people can jump to the part they need. There's more on length in how long a brand film should be, and the principle holds: as long as it needs, not a second more.

Where should they live?

Everywhere the question comes up. The help centre, onboarding emails, inside the app, a QR code on the packaging or the installation manual, and on YouTube, where a lot of people go first when something isn't working. Support teams can send links in replies instead of writing out the same twelve steps again.

Two other things worth knowing, as general guidance rather than legal advice. If you're in financial services, the FCA's Consumer Duty expects firms to support customers' understanding, and clear video can help with that, though you should test that customers actually understand it. And make videos accessible: captions as standard, and an audio described version where important information is only shown visually. Our char.gy film was delivered with an audio described version for exactly that reason.

No one will ever make a documentary about resetting a password. Make that video anyway.

How are they made, and what drives the cost?

Treat it as a library rather than a one-off. Write a short script per video, batch record them in one session, edit with a consistent template, and give someone the job of checking them whenever the product changes. Cost depends on the number of videos, how often the product changes, the format and how many languages you need. Many screen-recorded help videos can be made in house at very little cost, and a phone handles a lot of the physical ones. AI subtitles and translation speed things up, but need checking, as covered in the unglamorous AI tools that save edit time.

Where outside help earns its keep is the welcome film and the physical product videos customers will watch most. As general UK market ranges from our free playbook, a short shoot with a freelancer is usually under £2,000, and most corporate video sits between £2,000 and £8,000. If a demo would do the job before the sale, see product and app demo videos, or tell us what your customers keep asking.
items.author: Earl Duncan

faqs.q: Should help videos go on YouTube or stay private?
faqs.a: Put general how-to videos on YouTube as well as your help centre, because many customers search there first and it helps new buyers see the product is well supported. Keep anything account specific, confidential or only for certain customers in your own help platform, unlisted or behind a login.

faqs.q: How do we keep help videos current when the product changes?
faqs.a: Give each video an owner and log which product version it shows. When an update changes a screen or a step, the owner flags the affected videos and they're re-recorded. Short, single-task videos make this manageable. A help library full of outdated screens generates the very support queries it was meant to prevent.

faqs.q: Should support staff appear on camera?
faqs.a: For the welcome and for physical product help, it's a good idea. Customers like seeing the people they might later speak to, and support staff know exactly where customers get stuck. Only film people who are happy to do it, explain where the videos will appear, and plan for replacing their section if they leave.

faqs.q: Do help videos need a voiceover?
faqs.a: Most benefit from one, because people often watch while doing the task and can't read text and act at the same time. Add captions too, for people watching on mute or with hearing loss. Very short clips showing a single physical step can work with on-screen text alone if the action is obvious.

stat.title: Video marketers who say video has helped them reduce support queries
stat.takeaway: More than half of businesses using video say it's cut their support load, so start with the questions your team answers every day.

source.name: Wyzowl, Video Marketing Statistics 2026 (266 respondents, late 2025)

items.title: Video for manufacturers: showing how things are made
items.excerpt: What video works for manufacturers: what buyers and recruits need to see, safety and confidentiality on the shop floor, six film ideas and typical UK costs.
items.coverAlt: Equipment mounted in a manufacturing facility
items.body:
Manufacturing video works when it takes a buyer inside the factory: the machines, the checks and the people who know the process well enough to explain it plainly. Procurement teams and engineers are judging capability and reliability, and a well made film of the shop floor shows both faster than a capability statement full of claims. It's also one of the best recruitment tools a manufacturer has.

This post covers what manufacturing buyers look for, which video types suit the sector, six film ideas, the safety and confidentiality issues to plan around, and what it costs.

What do manufacturing buyers want to see?

Proof that you can make what they need, to the standard they need, every time. That means the equipment you actually run, the inspection and quality steps, how much you can produce, and the experience of the people doing it. Certifications matter, but a logo strip at the end of a video says less than a quality inspector explaining what they check and why.

Buyers also want to know what happens when something goes wrong. A film where an engineer talks frankly about a difficult job and how it was solved is more convincing than one where everything is perfect, because nobody believes everything is perfect.

A logo strip says you're certified. An inspector explaining what they check says you mean it.

Which video types suit manufacturers?

  • Capability or factory film. What you make, how and with what, told by the people on the floor.
  • Process film. One product or part from raw material to dispatch.
  • Customer case study. A client explaining the problem you solved for them.
  • Recruitment and apprenticeship film. What the work and the people are really like.
  • Trade show content. A film for the stand screen, plus short pieces from the show itself.

Some things are better animated. If the selling point is what happens inside a sealed machine, at a microscopic scale or in a chemical process, a good 3D animator will explain it more clearly than any camera. We don't do animation. The two often work well together: live action for the people and the shop floor, animation for the part you can't see.

Six film ideas for manufacturers

  1. One part, start to finish. Sheet, bar or pellet to finished, inspected and boxed.
  2. The quality inspector. What they look for, what fails, and why it matters to the customer.
  3. The apprentice and the trainer. Two generations of the same skill.
  4. The awkward job. A customer problem nobody else would take on, and how it was solved.
  5. The night shift. For plants that run around the clock, the people who keep it going.
  6. The customer's side. Your product in use at their site, explained by them.

Why should recruitment be part of the plan?

Because skills shortages hit manufacturing harder than most sectors. In the government's Employer Skills Survey, about a third of manufacturing vacancies were hard to fill because applicants lacked the skills, against 27% across the economy as a whole. Young people rarely see inside a modern factory. A film that shows them the work, the kit and the people doing it is one of the few recruitment tools that changes that.

What does a shop-floor case study look like?

Our film at Alpha Manufacturing was made for Easee. Alpha work in sheet metal and had Easee chargers installed at their own site, which put them in a rare position for a case study: a manufacturer talking about a manufactured product, from the point of view of people who understand how things are actually made.

A factory is a hard place to film. It's loud, it's lit for work rather than for cameras, and production doesn't stop because a crew has turned up. The interviews were recorded on the shop floor around live production, and we covered the manufacturing process itself, not just the product on the wall, so the case study made sense next to the press brakes and welding bays. For smaller, hand-made production, our film with Carreducker, where every pair takes 210 steps and six months, shows the same idea at the other end of the scale. There's more on that in filming craft: making the invisible process visible.

What should manufacturers plan for before filming?

General guidance, not legal or safety advice. Your own safety and compliance people should sign off the plan.

  • Safety on camera and behind it. The crew need an induction, PPE and hearing protection. Nobody should be filmed with a guard removed or PPE missing, because the film becomes a record of it.
  • Confidentiality. Agree in advance what can't be shown: customer parts, drawings on screens, proprietary tooling or processes. Walk the route before filming and move anything sensitive.
  • Customer names and logos. A recognisable customer part or logo in shot needs that customer's agreement.
  • Environmental claims. Anything about recycled content, low emissions or sustainability needs evidence under the CMA's Green Claims Code.
  • Origin claims. If the film says made in Britain, make sure that's accurate for the product shown.

Every factory has a whiteboard with something on it that the legal team would rather nobody filmed. Find it before the camera does.

How long should a manufacturing video be?

Capability films usually work at two to four minutes for the website and sales team, with a one minute version for trade show screens and LinkedIn. Process films can be shorter or longer depending on the product, and engineers will happily watch detail that would bore a consumer. Recruitment films work best at two to three minutes with short verticals. Where to put your brand film once it's made covers how the cuts get used.

What does manufacturing video cost?

These are typical UK market ranges, taken from what production companies and freelancers generally charge, not our quotes:

  • Under £2,000. A freelancer, a day or less on site, an interview and some B-roll, a short edit and library music. Fine for social content and simple pieces.
  • £2,000 to £8,000. A small production company or experienced freelance team, one or two shoot days, a proper edit and often a couple of cut-downs. Most corporate video sits here.
  • £8,000 to £30,000. Documentary brand films and higher-end brand content. Real research, multi-day shoots, a crew, a specialist grade and mix, a full set of cuts.
  • £30,000 and up. Agency-led campaigns, scripted work with cast and art direction, built sets, broadcast advertising.

Manufacturing shoots cost more when production can't stop and filming has to work around shifts, when several sites are involved, when noise means every interview needs careful sound, and when trade show deadlines compress the edit. They cost less when the site is prepared, the route is agreed and the right people are free on the day, which our post on briefing your team before a shoot helps with. The film budget calculator gives a rough figure. If your shop floor has a story in it, get in touch.
items.author: Earl Duncan

faqs.q: Can you film in a factory without stopping production?
faqs.a: Usually, yes, and the footage is better for it. A small crew works around the line with a safety escort, filming the process as it happens. Interviews are often recorded in a quieter spot or during a break, with lav mics to cut through the noise. Agree with the production manager in advance which areas and times work best.

faqs.q: How do we stop competitors learning our process from the video?
faqs.a: Plan it before the shoot. Agree with the crew what can't be filmed, walk the route together, cover or move sensitive drawings and screens, and review the rough cut specifically for confidential detail. A good crew can make a process look impressive without showing exactly how it's done, using close-ups and framing rather than revealing settings or tooling.

faqs.q: Who should we put on camera in a manufacturing film?
faqs.a: The people who do the work and can explain it plainly. Engineers, inspectors, operators and apprentices are usually more convincing than a managing director reading key messages, because buyers trust the people closest to the product. The best contributors talk naturally about what they do, so short pre-interviews help choose who'll come across well.

faqs.q: Is a trade show video worth making on its own?
faqs.a: It's better as part of something bigger. A film made only for one stand screen gets watched for a few days. If the same shoot produces a capability film for your website, short pieces for LinkedIn and a loop for the stand, the cost is spread across a year of use instead of one event.

stat.title: Share of vacancies hard to fill because applicants lack the skills, by sector (UK, 2024)
stat.takeaway: A third of manufacturing vacancies are skills-shortage vacancies, so a film that shows people what the work really is helps you hire as well as sell.

source.name: Department for Education, Employer Skills Survey 2024: UK research report

items.title: Employee onboarding videos: what new starters need
items.excerpt: What employee onboarding videos should cover, how to make a welcome film feel real, how long each part should be, and the consent and data points to plan for.
items.coverAlt: Two people looking at a product on a show stand
items.body:
Employee onboarding videos help new starters understand the business, the people and the practicalities, ideally before their first day and during their first few weeks. The good ones do two separate jobs. One is the welcome: why the company exists, who's who and how things are done. The other is practical: systems, policies and where everything is. The first deserves a properly made film. The second suits short, cheap videos that are easy to update.

Mixing the two is the most common mistake. A heartfelt founder story doesn't belong in the same video as how to book annual leave.

What should an onboarding video cover?

  • A welcome from the person at the top, in their own words, not read from a script.
  • The story of the business. Where it came from and why it exists.
  • The people. Who they'll work with and who to ask about what.
  • How work is actually done. Values shown in practice rather than listed.
  • What customers say. New starters should hear who they're working for.
  • A tour, for sites where finding your way around matters.
  • The practical modules. Systems, safety, policies, the first week.

Why use video for onboarding at all?

Consistency, mainly. Every new starter gets the same welcome whether they join on a Monday at head office or on a night shift at another site. People can watch it before day one, when they're keen and nervous and have time. Founders who used to welcome everyone personally can't once a business grows, and a film keeps some of that. And managers stop repeating the same hour of introductions every few weeks.

It's also still fairly rare, which means a good one makes an impression on someone who's only just decided to trust you with their career.

How do you make a welcome film feel real?

Use real staff rather than actors. Let the founder tell the story unscripted. Show the actual work, including the unglamorous bits. And be honest about what's hard, because the new starter is about to find out anyway, and they'll trust everything else more if the film didn't pretend.

Our documentary for La Fromagerie is a founder story told alongside the cheesemongers and the wholesale side, who fill in what the business actually is now. It was made as a brand film, but a film built like that, with several real voices and the work going on around them, is exactly what a new starter needs to see.

I wrote about how that one was made in the story behind the La Fromagerie film. If you've already got a brand film, a cut of it can often become the heart of your onboarding without another shoot.

Show a value in action once and you'll never need the slide that lists it.

How long should onboarding videos be?

A welcome film works at three to six minutes. Practical modules are better at one to three minutes each, one topic per video, so people can find the one about expenses without sitting through the one about fire exits. A site tour can run two to four minutes. Resist the urge to make one long induction video. Nobody concentrates for forty minutes in their first week, and it'll be out of date in six months.

What about consent, data and people leaving?

Some general points worth checking with HR or a data protection adviser:

  • Footage of identifiable people is personal data under UK GDPR. Tell staff where the film will be shown, internally or publicly, and how long it'll be used.
  • Consent from employees is tricky, because of the power imbalance between employer and employee. The ICO's guidance says consent often isn't the most appropriate lawful basis at work, so many employers rely on another basis and give people a genuine way to opt out of appearing.
  • People leave. Agree up front what happens to footage of someone who leaves, and build the film so their section can be replaced.
  • Keep internal films internal. If an onboarding film might later be used publicly, for recruitment say, tell people that before filming.

Ownership and licences matter here too, and they're covered in who owns the footage when you commission a film.

Whoever stars in your welcome film will hand in their notice the week it's finished. Shoot it in sections.

How is it made, and what drives the cost?

The welcome film is usually one well planned shoot day: the founder interview, a few team conversations, the tour and coverage of the work. The practical modules can be screen recordings or phone videos made by the people who own each process. Preparing staff makes a big difference on the day, and how to brief your team before a film shoot covers it.

Cost depends on the number of people and locations, whether you need several sites, and how many modules there are. As general UK market ranges from our free playbook, a short shoot with a freelancer is usually under £2,000, and a small production company over one or two days typically sits between £2,000 and £8,000. Planning onboarding cuts into a brand film shoot is often the cheapest route, which is the idea behind turning one brand film into a year of content.

The practical side overlaps with training videos, and the welcome film has a lot in common with recruitment films, so it's worth planning them together. If you'd like to, get in touch.
items.author: Earl Duncan

faqs.q: Should onboarding videos be public or private?
faqs.a: Usually private, or at least unlisted. Practical modules about systems and policies belong in your intranet or learning platform. The welcome film is the exception that can work publicly, because it doubles as a recruitment tool, but only if everyone in it agreed to public use before filming. Decide that early, because it changes what people are comfortable saying.

faqs.q: Can our brand film double as an onboarding video?
faqs.a: Often, yes. A documentary-style brand film already tells the story of the business through real people, which is most of what a welcome film needs to do. You may want a slightly different cut with an extra internal message from the founder, but it can save a whole separate shoot if it's planned at the start.
