faqs.q: Who should present the onboarding film?
faqs.a: Ideally the founder or managing director for the welcome, and the people who actually own each process for the practical modules. New starters want to see the faces they'll meet. A professional presenter can make it smoother, but it puts a stranger between the new starter and the business they've just joined.

faqs.q: How often should onboarding videos be updated?
faqs.a: Review them at least once a year, and straight away after big changes like a move, a new system or a change of leadership. Modular videos make this much easier. A welcome film that's honest about the business's story tends to age well, while practical modules date quickly and need an owner who checks them.

stat.title: Video marketers who've made each type of video
stat.takeaway: Only about one in six video marketers has made an employee onboarding video, so a good one still stands out to a new starter.

source.name: Wyzowl, Video Marketing Statistics 2026 (266 respondents, late 2025)

items.title: Video for construction and architecture firms
items.excerpt: What video works for builders, contractors and architects: what clients need to see, safety and green claims on camera, six film ideas and typical UK costs.
items.coverAlt: An engineer working on a wall of cabling
items.body:
Construction and architecture video works when it shows finished work through the eyes of the client who paid for it, and the process through the people who actually built it. A prospective client is about to trust you with a large sum of money and a building they'll live or work in for decades. They need proof you deliver, and a sense of what you're like to deal with when something goes wrong, which it always does somewhere.

This post covers what construction and architecture clients look for on video, the formats that suit the sector, six film ideas, the safety and claims issues to respect, and what drives the cost.

What do construction clients need to see?

Every contractor says the same things about themselves. Quality, on time, on budget. None of it means much coming from the people being paid. What a prospective client believes is evidence: the finished work in detail, the scale of what changed, a site that was kept safe and tidy, and above all the client's own account of how it went.

For architects the question shifts a little. Clients want to understand how you think, how you listen and how a brief becomes a building. A practice film that shows a real conversation with a real client does that better than a slideshow of finished photography.

Quality, on time, on budget. Every contractor says it. Only the client saying it counts.

Which video types suit construction and architecture?

  • Client case studies. The homeowner or client tells the story of the project, start to finish.
  • Project films and time-lapse. A build condensed into a few minutes, with interviews from the people on site.
  • Recruitment and apprentice films. What the work is really like, for the people you want to hire.
  • Practice films. For architects and designers, how the studio works and what it cares about.
  • Tender and bid films. A short film of the team and a comparable project, sent with a submission.

For schemes that haven't been built, CGI fly-throughs and architectural visualisation are the right tool. Planning consultations and design competitions need people to see a building that doesn't exist yet, and live action can't do that. We don't make CGI. Where we come in is once there are real people and real places to film.

Why does recruitment belong in a construction video plan?

Because finding people is one of the biggest constraints in the industry. CITB's workforce outlook says construction needs tens of thousands of extra workers every year to the end of the decade, and a firm that shows young people what the work and the team are really like has an advantage over one with a job ad and a logo.

Six film ideas for builders, contractors and architects

  1. The client's account. Filmed once they've moved back in, in their own words.
  2. A build in four minutes. Time-lapse from a fixed camera, cut with short interviews at key stages.
  3. The apprentice. Their first year, and the person who trained them.
  4. The work nobody will see. Foundations, structure, waterproofing. Why it matters and how it's done properly.
  5. A year on. The architect and the client walk round the building after people have lived with it.
  6. The site manager's walkround. For tenders, showing how a live site is run.

What does a client-led construction film look like?

Our Barry Road film was made for a London builder who took on a full house renovation in East Dulwich. Rather than a walkthrough narrated by the builder, the film is the homeowner's account: what they wanted, what it was like to live through, and what they ended up with.

It was filmed once the work was finished and the family had moved back in, covering the whole property from the bathroom through to the kitchen extension and the garden. Before and after floorplans are cut in so the scale of the work reads on screen. The result is an edit the builder can send to someone who's deciding whether to trust them with a house. Our Nimrod Road film takes the same approach. If you want to try something similar, our post on testimonial videos covers how to ask the client and what to ask them.

What should construction firms watch out for on camera?

General guidance, not legal or safety advice. Your own health and safety lead has the final say on site.

  • Safety on screen. Anyone filmed must be working safely, with the right PPE. A missing harness or an unguarded edge in a promotional film is a public record of a breach.
  • Site rules for the crew. Film crews need inductions, PPE and supervision like any visitor. The principal contractor controls the site under CDM 2015, so agree access in advance.
  • Drones. Useful for scale and progress, but the operator must follow CAA rules, and cranes and neighbours complicate things.
  • Environmental claims. If the film calls a building sustainable, low carbon or net zero, the CMA's Green Claims Code expects you to back it up.
  • Client permission. A private home or a commercial client's building needs their agreement before it appears in your marketing, including security details and anything confidential.

Hi-vis is the most honest costume in film. Leave it off for one shot and someone in the comments will notice.

How long should construction videos be?

Client case studies usually work at three to five minutes, because the person watching is weighing a big decision and will give it the time. Time-lapse and progress films can be shorter, one to three minutes. Recruitment films work best at two to three minutes plus short verticals for the social platforms younger people actually use. Our post on how long a brand film should be explains how to judge it.

What does construction video cost?

These are typical UK market ranges, taken from what production companies and freelancers generally charge, not our quotes:

  • Under £2,000. A freelancer, a day or less on site, an interview and some B-roll, a short edit and library music. Fine for social content and simple pieces.
  • £2,000 to £8,000. A small production company or experienced freelance team, one or two shoot days, a proper edit and often a couple of cut-downs. Most corporate video sits here.
  • £8,000 to £30,000. Documentary brand films and higher-end brand content. Real research, multi-day shoots, a crew, a specialist grade and mix, a full set of cuts.
  • £30,000 and up. Agency-led campaigns, scripted work with cast and art direction, built sets, broadcast advertising.

Construction projects get more expensive when they run over months (repeat visits for progress or time-lapse), cover several sites, need drone work or have to fit around restricted site access. A single client case study, filmed in a day once the work is finished, is at the more manageable end. The film budget calculator will give you a rough number. If you've got a finished project and a client who'd talk about it, tell us about it.
items.author: Earl Duncan

faqs.q: When's the best time to film a construction case study?
faqs.a: Once the work is finished and the client has lived with it for a little while. By then they can talk about the result as well as the process, and the rooms look lived in rather than freshly handed over. If you want progress footage too, plan it from the start, because you can't go back and film the foundations later.

faqs.q: What if our client doesn't want to be on camera?
faqs.a: You can still make a strong film. The site manager or the architect can tell the story, with the finished work, plans and progress footage doing the rest. A written quote from the client on screen is weaker than them speaking but still useful. Some clients are happy to be heard and not seen, which works well too.

faqs.q: Can we film on a live construction site?
faqs.a: Yes, with the principal contractor's agreement, a site induction for the crew and the right PPE. Filming usually has to work around the programme rather than the other way round, so agree times in advance and plan for noise. Interviews are often better recorded in a quieter space like the site office, with the action filmed separately.

faqs.q: Is time-lapse worth it for a building project?
faqs.a: For projects that change dramatically, like a new build, an extension or a big fit-out, it's one of the most watchable things you can make. It needs a secure camera position, a power source and someone checking it regularly, so it's best set up at the start. On a small internal refurbishment there's often too little visible change to justify it.

stat.title: UK construction workforce, 2025 and the level CITB projects for 2030
stat.takeaway: CITB says that means around 41,200 extra workers needed every year to 2030, so showing people what working for you is like is part of winning work.

source.name: CITB, Construction Workforce Outlook 2026 to 2030

items.title: Training videos people actually finish
items.excerpt: What training videos suit, when to use screen recording, animation or live action, how long modules should be, the safety points to respect and what it costs.
items.coverAlt: A gloved hand working on an electrical unit
items.body:
A training video teaches people how to do something, and how to do it the same way every time. It suits tasks that are easier shown than described, that lots of people need to learn, and that need doing consistently across shifts or sites. It doesn't replace hands-on practice or proper assessment for anything risky, and the best training films are built to sit alongside both.

Most training video is made in house, quickly, and that's often fine. This post is about when it's worth doing properly, and what properly looks like.

Which kinds of training suit video?

  • Procedures. How to set up, install, clean, check or hand over something.
  • Safety and compliance. The parts people must understand, not just sign for.
  • Product training. For installers, resellers and partners who sell or fit what you make.
  • Situations. Difficult conversations, complaints, safeguarding scenarios, shown rather than described.
  • Knowledge capture. The person who's done the job for twenty years and carries half the business in their head.

That last one is underrated. When an experienced person retires or leaves, what they knew usually leaves with them. A few filmed conversations and demonstrations can keep a surprising amount of it.

Live action, screen recording or animation?

Pick by what's being taught. Being honest about it:

  • Software and systems: screen recording. Clean, cheap, easy to update.
  • Abstract rules and concepts: data protection principles, how a policy works, how a process flows between teams. Simple animation or clear graphics usually explain these better than people talking, and they're cheaper to update when the rules change.
  • Physical tasks, tools and sites: live action, filmed from where the learner will stand.
  • Experience and judgement: live action interviews with the people who have it.

We work in live action, so the last two are where we're useful. For the first two, an in-house screen recording or a specialist animator will serve you better.

What makes a training video work?

  • One task per video. Learners come back to find one thing. Make it easy to find.
  • The learner's angle. Over the shoulder or point of view, so left is left and the tool's held the way they'll hold it.
  • The real environment and real kit. A spotless demo bench looks nothing like a loft, a kitchen or a plant room.
  • The expert, not a presenter. The person who does the job knows what goes wrong. Coach them, don't replace them.
  • Show the mistake. What wrong looks like is often more useful than what right looks like.
  • Text where it matters. Torque settings, part numbers and checklist steps on screen, long enough to read.
  • Captions and chapters. For noisy sites, for accessibility, and for skipping to the bit you need.
Film the person who actually does the job, in the place they actually do it.

If the expert is nervous on camera, that's normal. A conversation with someone off camera usually gets a better result than asking them to present. How to speak on camera when you're not a presenter is a good thing to send them beforehand.

How long should training videos be?

Short. Two to six minutes per module is a good working range, with longer courses split into chapters rather than one long film. People watch training in the gaps of a working day, often on a phone, and they rewatch the bit they need when they're actually doing the task. A forty minute induction video gets played on a second monitor while everyone does their emails.

What about safety, accessibility and the rules?

Some general points, not legal advice:

  • Watching a video doesn't prove competence. Under the Health and Safety at Work etc. Act 1974, employers have to provide the information, instruction, training and supervision people need. For risky tasks, watching a film is the start, followed by supervised practice and a check. Your health and safety lead should decide where video fits.
  • Everything on screen teaches. If someone's working at height without the right equipment, or skips a step, that's what gets copied. Have a competent person watch the shoot and the rough cut.
  • Accessibility. Captions, transcripts and readable on-screen text help everyone and support the reasonable adjustments employers are expected to make under the Equality Act 2010.
  • Consent. Staff appearing in training films should know where the film will be used and agree to it.

If a training film shows someone up a ladder without the right kit, that's the only bit anyone will remember.

How is a training video made, and what drives the cost?

Start with the subject expert and a simple shot list per module: the steps, the angles, the mistakes to show. Shooting several modules in one day on one site is far more efficient than one at a time. Then the edit, on-screen text, captions and export in whatever format your learning system takes.

Cost is driven by the number of modules, locations, graphics, languages and review rounds, and compliance reviews can add more rounds than people expect. As general UK market ranges from our free playbook, a freelancer with a short shoot and a simple edit is usually under £2,000, and a small production company over one or two days typically sits between £2,000 and £8,000. For quick internal how-tos, a phone and a cheap microphone will do a lot. AI tools now make subtitles and first-draft translations quick, though they need a person checking them, as I cover in the unglamorous AI tools that save edit time.

Training often overlaps with induction, which has its own post on employee onboarding videos. If you've got expert knowledge you'd like captured on film before it walks out of the door, talk to us.
items.author: Earl Duncan

faqs.q: Can we film training videos on our own phones?
faqs.a: Yes, for plenty of internal how-tos a phone is enough. Use a tripod or clamp, film from the learner's angle, get close, and use a clip-on microphone because sound is where phone videos usually fall down. Bring in a crew when the training is customer facing, needs to last years, or covers something where clarity really matters.

faqs.q: How do we keep training videos up to date?
faqs.a: Keep them short and modular, one task per video, and record the date and the process version each one covers. When a step changes, you replace that module rather than the whole course. A simple spreadsheet listing every video, its owner and when it was last checked stops outdated training quietly staying in circulation.

faqs.q: Should training videos include quizzes?
faqs.a: For anything that matters, some kind of check is worth having, and most learning systems let you add questions after a video. A quiz confirms the key points landed, but it isn't the same as competence. For practical or risky tasks, a supervised check on the job is still the real test.

faqs.q: Can training videos be translated?
faqs.a: Yes. Translated subtitles are the simplest option and keep the original expert's voice. Dubbed voiceover suits graphics-led or screen-recorded videos better than talking heads. AI translation gives a quick first draft, but have a fluent speaker who knows the work check it, especially for safety instructions where a mistranslated word could matter.

stat.title: Video marketers who think 30 seconds to 2 minutes is the most effective video length

bars.label: Say 30 seconds to 2 minutes works best

stat.takeaway: That's a marketing view, but it's a useful nudge for training too: break long courses into short, single-task modules.

source.name: Wyzowl, Video Marketing Statistics 2026 (266 respondents, late 2025)

items.title: Video for property and estate agents: what works
items.excerpt: What video works for estate agents, developers and property managers: what buyers check, material information and privacy rules, six film ideas and costs.
items.coverAlt: A renovated kitchen opening onto the garden
items.body:
Property video works when it answers the questions photos can't: how the rooms connect, how much light there really is, what the street is like, and who you'll be dealing with. For estate and letting agents that means honest walkthroughs. For developers and property managers it means explaining a project to the people it affects. And for anyone selling renovation work, it means letting the homeowner tell the story.

This post covers what buyers, tenants and residents need to see, which video types suit the sector, six film ideas, the rules around listings and privacy, and what drives the cost.

What do buyers and tenants want to see on video?

The things that make them book a viewing or rule a place out. How you get from the front door to the kitchen. Whether the second bedroom fits a bed and a wardrobe. Where the light comes from at the time of day they'd be home. What's next door, and how loud the road is. Photos are chosen to flatter; a steady walkthrough at a normal pace shows how a home actually works.

They also want to know who they're dealing with. An agent, a developer or a managing agent is a stranger handling one of the biggest decisions of someone's life. Seeing the actual people, talking normally, does a lot of quiet work before the first phone call.

Photos are chosen to flatter. A steady walkthrough at a normal pace shows how a home actually works.

Which video types suit property businesses?

  • Listing walkthroughs. Agent-led or with no presenter, one continuous route through the property.
  • Neighbourhood guides. The high street, the station, the park, filmed honestly.
  • Agency and branch films. The team and how they work, for vendors choosing who to instruct.
  • Project and resident films. Explaining works, changes or a new service to people who didn't commission it.
  • Renovation case studies. The homeowner's account of a project, for builders and designers to send to the next client.

For homes that don't exist yet, CGI is the better tool. Off-plan buyers need to see finished interiors and the building in its setting, and architectural visualisation does that far better than filming a site in mud. We don't make CGI. A live-action film works alongside it once there are real people to film: the developer, the site team, the first residents.

Six film ideas for property businesses

  1. The friend's tour. Walk the house the way you'd show a friend round, in one take, at a normal pace.
  2. The street at both ends of the day. 8am and 6pm, so buyers see the school run and the commute.
  3. The owners' account. Why they bought, what they changed and what it's like to live there.
  4. Meet the branch. Who answers the phone and who does the viewings.
  5. Before the works start. A project explained to residents, with the people responsible on camera.
  6. A year of a development. Short updates from the site team, which turn into a story by completion.

What does a homeowner-led property film look like?

Our Nimrod Road film is about a Victorian house in Tooting that had sat empty after the previous owners died. The couple who bought it wanted the period features kept and the ground floor opened up, with a project starting in September and a baby due at the end of November. It was finished in eight weeks, two weeks inside the estimate.

It was filmed after the family had moved in, so the before only existed in the original listing photos, and those are cut in against the finished rooms. We filmed the street and the neighbourhood too, because part of their story is why they chose to buy there. Our Barry Road film in East Dulwich works the same way, with before and after floorplans cut in so the scale of the work reads on screen. For resident communication, our project overview for residents and freeholders shows the other side of property video: a captioned film that answers the questions residents ask before works start. Why the client's voice carries so much weight is covered in testimonial videos that don't sound like testimonials.

What rules apply to property video?

General guidance, not legal advice. Agents in particular should check their own professional body's guidance.

  • Material information. National Trading Standards has published material information guidance for property listings, and a listing video is part of the listing. It shouldn't leave out or disguise something a buyer needs to know.
  • Lenses and editing. A very wide lens can make a small room look huge. Some width helps people understand a space, too much misleads them, and so does cutting around the railway line at the bottom of the garden.
  • Drones. Aerial footage needs an operator following the CAA's drone rules, including registration and limits on flying near people and buildings.
  • Privacy in occupied homes. Tenants should agree before their home is filmed. Hide family photos, post with names on it, alarm panels and anything that tells a stranger when the house is empty.
  • Consent from people on camera. Homeowners, residents and staff who appear should agree in writing to how the film will be used.

There's a lens that can make a box room look like a ballroom. Buyers own tape measures.

How long should property videos be?

A listing walkthrough usually works at one to three minutes, depending on the size of the property. Neighbourhood guides can run longer on YouTube, where people searching for an area will happily watch five minutes. Renovation case studies and branch films sit around two to five minutes, with short cuts for social. Resident explainers should be as short as the information allows, captioned, and easy to send round before a meeting.

What does property video cost?

These are typical UK market ranges, taken from what production companies and freelancers generally charge, not our quotes:

  • Under £2,000. A freelancer, a day or less on site, an interview and some B-roll, a short edit and library music. Fine for social content and simple pieces.
  • £2,000 to £8,000. A small production company or experienced freelance team, one or two shoot days, a proper edit and often a couple of cut-downs. Most corporate video sits here.
  • £8,000 to £30,000. Documentary brand films and higher-end brand content. Real research, multi-day shoots, a crew, a specialist grade and mix, a full set of cuts.
  • £30,000 and up. Agency-led campaigns, scripted work with cast and art direction, built sets, broadcast advertising.

Listing videos usually sit at the bottom of those ranges and are often bundled per property, because they're repeatable and quick. Brand films for agencies, project films for developers and homeowner case studies cost more, because they involve interviews, more than one location and a proper edit. Drone work, twilight shoots and presenter-led pieces all add to the day. The film budget calculator will give you a starting figure, and where to use your brand film helps plan the cuts. If you've got a project worth telling properly, get in touch.
items.author: Earl Duncan

faqs.q: Should an estate agent present listing videos on camera?
faqs.a: It helps if they're comfortable doing it. A relaxed agent pointing out what they'd notice on a viewing builds trust in them as well as the property. A stiff, scripted presenter does the opposite. If nobody on the team enjoys being filmed, a steady walkthrough with on-screen captions for key details works perfectly well and is quicker to make.

faqs.q: Are video tours better than 360 virtual tours?
faqs.a: They do different jobs. A 360 tour lets someone explore at their own pace, which is great for checking layout. A video tour controls the route and the pace, and can include a person, the street and the light at different times of day. Many agents use a 360 tour for detail and a short video to make people want to book a viewing.

faqs.q: Can we film a tenanted property for a listing video?
faqs.a: Usually, but with the tenants' agreement and enough notice under their tenancy. Agree a time, ask them to clear personal items, and keep personal photos, post and security details out of shot. Tenants are far more cooperative when they're asked properly. This is general guidance rather than legal advice, so check your obligations.

faqs.q: What's the best time of day to film a property?
faqs.a: When the light is best in the rooms that matter most, which depends on which way the house faces. A south-facing garden or living room often looks best from late morning to mid-afternoon. Many agents also add a short twilight exterior with the lights on. Avoid filming in harsh midday sun if the main rooms face it directly.

items.title: Sales videos your sales team will actually use
items.excerpt: What sales videos are, which ones help close deals, how long they should be, how to put video into a proposal properly and what drives the cost of making them.
items.coverAlt: Two people in conversation on an exhibition stand
items.body:
A sales video is a film made to be sent by a person, during a sale. It goes in a follow-up email, inside a proposal, before a first call or after a pitch. Its audience is someone already talking to you, and its job is to answer the questions a buyer will ask their colleagues when your salesperson isn't in the room.

That makes it a very different brief from an advert, and it's why so many marketing videos never get used by sales teams. They were made for a stranger, and the salesperson needs something for a person who's halfway to yes.

What counts as a sales video?

  • A customer story. A client explaining what they bought, why, and how it went.
  • A process film. What actually happens after someone signs, step by step.
  • A team introduction. The people the buyer will deal with, so the first meeting isn't with strangers.
  • A personal video from the account lead. A short, phone-recorded message for one prospect. Cheap and surprisingly effective.
  • An objection answer. One short film for the question that stalls the most deals.
  • A project overview for stakeholders. For the people who have to approve the decision without being in the sales meetings.

That last one is easy to overlook. We made a project overview to explain a communal charging installation to residents, freeholders and managing agents. The audience wasn't the buyer, but the work couldn't go ahead without them, so the film had to be clear enough for residents and useful enough for the contractor to send ahead of a meeting.

Why do sales teams ignore most of the videos marketing makes?

Because they're too long, too general and made for the wrong stage. A two minute brand piece is brilliant on a homepage and awkward in a reply to a procurement manager who asked about installation timescales. Add videos nobody can find a link for and you get a sales team that sends PDFs instead.

The fix is to start with the sales team. Ask which questions come up on every call, which objections stall deals, and who else gets involved before a decision. Then make videos that answer those, and put the links somewhere every salesperson can grab them in ten seconds.

Which sales video does the most work?

In my view, the customer story. A buyer discounts most of what a seller says about themselves, because the seller is being paid. A customer who's already handed over the money has no reason to oversell, and the viewer knows it.

Our Barry Road renovation film was made exactly for this. It's the homeowner giving their own account of a full renovation, with before and after floorplans cut in, and it's an edit the builder can send to a prospective client who's deciding whether to trust them with a house.

The Car Planet film works the same way for a commercial buyer. The whole film is the customer talking, and the installer never makes the claim about themselves, which is what makes it usable in a sales conversation. I've written more on getting this right in testimonial videos that don't sound like testimonials.

The person who's already paid you is the one voice a buyer fully believes.

What goes into a good sales video?

  • A specific buyer. One type of customer per film. A homeowner and a facilities manager want different things.
  • The risk they're worried about. Disruption, cost overruns, being let down. Name it and answer it.
  • Proof. The work, the result, the customer, on screen.
  • The people. The faces they'll actually deal with.
  • One next step. Usually a call, a site visit or a quote.

Build it to be forwarded. The person you send it to will often pass it to someone who's never heard of you, so it has to make sense on its own, with a title and thumbnail that explain what it is.

How long should a sales video be?

A personal video: thirty to ninety seconds. A customer story: two to four minutes, plus a sixty second cut for the first email. A process film: three to five minutes is fine, because someone who's about to commit genuinely wants the detail. The rule is that length should match how far along the buyer is. Early on, keep it short. Close to a decision, people will watch every minute if it answers their questions.

How do you put video into a proposal?

With a link, not an attachment. A thumbnail image in the proposal PDF linked to a page where the video plays is the most reliable approach, because embedded video in PDFs is patchy across readers. A short landing page per proposal works well too, and a QR code does the job on anything printed. Host videos somewhere that shows you views, so the sales team can see when a prospect has actually watched. If you're assembling proposal PDFs, our free PDF tools can merge and compress them.

Attaching a 400MB video file to a proposal email is a reliable way to never hear back. Send a link.

How are sales videos made, and what do they cost?

Personal videos cost nothing but a phone and five minutes. Customer stories and process films usually come from one well planned shoot day with the customer, the team and the work, plus the edit. Filming customers needs their written consent, and they should approve anything said about results before it goes out. As general UK market ranges from our free playbook, most corporate video sits between £2,000 and £8,000, while documentary-style films with research, multi-day shoots and a full set of cuts run from around £8,000 to £30,000.

If you're working out whether it'll pay for itself, how video makes a business money covers the routes, and where to use your brand film covers the sales side in more detail. Or tell us which deals keep stalling, and we'll tell you whether a film would help.
items.author: Earl Duncan

faqs.q: Should salespeople record their own personalised videos?
faqs.a: Yes, for one-to-one messages it's one of the cheapest things a sales team can do. A short phone video naming the prospect, referencing their situation and suggesting a next step feels personal in a way an email doesn't. Keep it under a minute, record somewhere quiet with decent light, and don't script it word for word.

faqs.q: How do we get a customer to agree to be filmed?
faqs.a: Ask the customers who are already happy and already talk about you, and make it easy for them. Explain where the film will be used, how long the filming takes, and that they'll see it before it goes out. Many people say yes because it promotes their business too, so offer them the film for their own use.

faqs.q: Should a sales video mention prices?
faqs.a: Usually not specific prices, because they change and the video will outlive them. It's helpful to be honest about how pricing works, for example that quotes are fixed or that a survey comes first. That sets expectations without dating the film, and keeps the actual number for the conversation where it can be explained.

faqs.q: How can we tell if a prospect watched the video?
faqs.a: Host it on a platform that reports views per link or per page, or use a sales tool that tracks when a link is opened. Most video hosting services and many email tools will show plays and how much was watched. Treat it as a signal to follow up, not as proof of interest on its own.

stat.title: How people say they'd most like to learn about a product or service
stat.takeaway: Very few people want a sales call to be how they learn, so send the video first and use the call for the questions it raises.

source.name: Wyzowl, Video Marketing Statistics 2026 (266 respondents, late 2025)

items.title: Video for ecommerce brands: what actually sells
items.excerpt: What video an online shop needs: product page clips, how-tos and brand films, what shoppers check before buying, the ad rules to know and typical UK costs.
items.coverAlt: A boxer hitting pads in a dark gym, filmed for a sports brand
items.body:
Ecommerce video has one main job: to stand in for the shop floor. It shows the product at its real size, in use, from every angle, so someone can feel confident buying something they can't pick up. That's product video, and it does most of the selling. A brand film sits above it and gives people a reason to buy from you rather than from a cheaper lookalike on a marketplace.

Most online shops need both, in very different quantities. This post covers what online shoppers need to see, which video types an ecommerce brand needs, six film ideas, the advertising rules that catch people out and what it costs.

What do online shoppers need to see before they buy?

Everything they'd check in a shop. How big it is next to a hand or a body. What the material looks like up close and in daylight. How it opens, folds, fits, pours or plugs in. What arrives in the box. And, more and more, who's behind it, because a small brand competing on a marketplace page is otherwise just another listing with a lower review count.

Honest product video also helps after the sale. When people can see exactly what they're getting, there are fewer surprises when the parcel arrives. Show it the way it is and let that be enough.

Which videos does an online shop actually need?

  • Product page videos. Short, often fifteen to forty five seconds, silent-friendly, one per product or range.
  • How-to and setup videos. For anything that needs assembling, fitting or using properly.
  • A brand film. The founder, the reason the business exists, how the product is made or chosen.
  • A making-of or process film. Especially for handmade or small-batch goods. Our post on filming craft businesses explains why showing the process justifies the price.
  • Customer and creator content. Real customers using the product. There's a full guide in UGC for businesses.
  • Ad creative. Many short variations for paid social, so you can test which opening works.

Two honest caveats. For a big catalogue, product video is a volume job best done in a product studio with a turntable and consistent lighting, not by a documentary crew. And for anything where the selling point is inside the product, the layers of a mattress or the workings of a gadget, 3D animation will usually explain it better than any camera. We don't do animation. Where we fit is the brand film and the human side: the founder, the workshop, the customer.

Six film ideas for ecommerce brands

  1. Why this exists. The founder on the problem they couldn't find a product for.
  2. Where it's made. The workshop, the factory or the supplier, filmed as it is.
  3. The honest test. The product put through real use, with the results shown straight.
  4. Packing day. The people who pick, wrap and post the orders. Small brands win on care, and this shows it.
  5. The hardest user. The customer who uses it more than anyone, in their own words.
  6. The material. Where the leather, the coffee, the wool or the clay comes from, and why it costs what it does.

What does a good ecommerce brand video look like?

The Dollar Shave Club launch video from 2012 is the one everyone in ecommerce gets shown, usually for the jokes. Watch it again for what's actually in it. The founder on camera in his own warehouse, explaining exactly what you get and how it works, in under two minutes. It's a founder film with a sense of humour.

The comedy suited that brand and that moment, and I wouldn't copy it. What travels is the structure: a real person, a real place and a plain offer. That works just as well delivered quietly by a maker at a bench. It's also a reminder that people trust a face over a logo, which we've written about in why real people on camera matter more now.

Which advertising rules apply to ecommerce video?

General guidance only. The ASA and CMA publish detailed guidance, and anything borderline is worth checking.

  • Demonstrations must be fair. If the video shows what a product does, it has to do that for the customer. Speeding up, filtering or editing a result to make it look better than it is can be misleading.
  • Ads must be obviously ads. Paid creator content needs labelling. The ASA's guidance on recognising ads on social media is the place to start.
  • Reviews must be real. Fake or undisclosed incentivised reviews are banned under the CMA's unfair commercial practices rules, and that includes video testimonials.
  • You need rights to everything in it. Customer clips, music and footage all need permission for the way you're using them, and paid ads usually need broader licences. See music licensing for brand videos.

If the mug in the video looks bigger than the mug in the box, your returns team will tell you before your analytics do.

How long should ecommerce videos be?

Product page clips should be as short as they can be while still answering the question, often well under a minute, and they should make sense on mute because most people scroll with the sound off. How-to videos run as long as the task takes. A brand film for an online shop usually works at two to four minutes on the about page and YouTube, cut down to thirty to ninety seconds for ads. Every platform wants a different shape, and our free video resizer handles the reformatting for small jobs.

What does ecommerce video cost?

These are typical UK market ranges, taken from what production companies and freelancers generally charge, not our quotes:

  • Under £2,000. A freelancer, a day or less on site, an interview and some B-roll, a short edit and library music. Fine for social content and simple pieces.
  • £2,000 to £8,000. A small production company or experienced freelance team, one or two shoot days, a proper edit and often a couple of cut-downs. Most corporate video sits here.
  • £8,000 to £30,000. Documentary brand films and higher-end brand content. Real research, multi-day shoots, a crew, a specialist grade and mix, a full set of cuts.
  • £30,000 and up. Agency-led campaigns, scripted work with cast and art direction, built sets, broadcast advertising.

Product video is often priced per product or per studio day rather than per film, so the number of products drives it more than anything else. Brand films cost more when they involve several locations, models, a supplier visit abroad or a large set of ad variations. Our film budget calculator gives a rough figure, and how video actually makes a business money helps when you're deciding what it's worth. If you've got a founder story or a workshop worth seeing, tell us about it.
items.author: Earl Duncan

faqs.q: Do product videos really need sound?
faqs.a: They need to work without it. Most people browse with the sound off, so a product page video should make sense from the pictures and any on-screen text alone. Sound is a bonus for those who turn it on. A brand film is different, because it's usually carried by people talking, so it needs proper sound and subtitles.

faqs.q: Should we use AI-generated video for our product pages?
faqs.a: Be careful. A generated video that shows the product looking or behaving differently from the real thing risks misleading customers and causing returns. AI tools can help with backgrounds, edits and resizing, but the product itself should be filmed for real. For anything showing what a product does, real footage is the safer and more honest choice.

faqs.q: How many product videos does a small online shop need?
faqs.a: Start with your bestsellers and the products that get the most questions or returns. A short video on those pages usually does more than a thin clip on every listing. Add a single brand film for the about page and social, then build out product videos range by range as budget allows, ideally shooting several at a time.

faqs.q: Can we use customers' unboxing videos in our ads?
faqs.a: Only with the creator's permission, and for ads you want that agreement in writing, covering paid use, platforms and how long you can run it. A tag or a mention isn't permission. If the customer was given the product free or paid, that also needs to be clear to viewers. This is general guidance rather than legal advice.

stat.title: Share of Great Britain's retail sales made online, August 2026
stat.takeaway: Nearly three in every ten pounds spent in retail now goes through a screen, so the video on your product page is doing the job a shop assistant used to.

source.name: Office for National Statistics, Retail sales, Great Britain: August 2026

items.title: Product demo and app demo videos that people trust
items.excerpt: What product and app demo videos are for, how to film them so buyers believe them, how long they should be, where to use them and what drives the cost.
items.coverAlt: An engineer in hi-vis on site, filmed for a product demo
items.body:
A product demo video shows a product working, and an app demo shows the screens and what you do on them. Both answer the same two questions a buyer has: will it do what I need, and is it easy? The best demos show rather than claim, in conditions the viewer recognises, and they're honest about what was edited.

I've put them in one post because the thinking is the same. The filming is what changes.

What's the difference between a product demo and an app demo?

A product demo is about something physical: hands, a real environment, the thing doing its job and the result you can see. An app demo is mostly screen recording: real screens, realistic data, a cursor or a finger moving at a human speed, and zooms that guide the eye.

Within both there are a few distinct jobs:

  • The short marketing demo. The one or two moments that make someone want it.
  • The full walkthrough. For people who are seriously evaluating, often sent by sales.
  • Feature videos. One feature each, useful on product pages and in release notes.
  • Comparisons. This model against that one, or this plan against the other.

Mix those jobs up and you get a ten minute video on a homepage, or a thirty second clip sent to a procurement team who wanted detail.

What makes a demo believable?

Showing the product doing the hard thing, in real conditions, without a cut at the crucial moment. Buyers have seen enough polished demos to assume the polish is hiding something. A slightly rough, unbroken take of the key moment is worth more than a glossy montage.

The clearest example from our own work is an installation at a car showroom in Poole. The installer explains why he works with Easee, then runs a live RCD test on the unit to demonstrate one of its safety features rather than just claiming it. Electricians and specifiers don't take a product claim on trust, so the proof had to happen on camera, on a real site.

The strongest demo shows the product doing the hard thing, on camera, in one take.

Other things that help: a real user rather than a model, the product in the place it'll actually be used, and the result shown long enough to register. If a step is slow in real life, say so and speed it up visibly. People forgive a slow step. They don't forgive feeling tricked.

How do you film an app demo well?

Most of the work happens before you press record:

  • A clean demo account with realistic data. Empty dashboards look broken, and "Test User 1" looks unfinished.
  • Notifications off, battery and clock tidy, nothing personal on screen.
  • Record at high resolution so you can zoom in the edit without the text going soft.
  • Slow, deliberate movement. Real users are quick because they know the app. Viewers don't.
  • A script, scene by scene, written to match exactly what's on screen.

Be honest about the format here too. For most app demos, a clean screen recording with a voiceover and a few graphics is the right tool, and a live action crew isn't needed. Real people come in for context: someone holding the phone on a job, in a shop, on the sofa. That's what shows where the app fits into a life. If the app isn't finished, animated mock-ups of the interface are usually better than filming a half-working build.

Plan for change as well. Interfaces update constantly, so keep demos modular, one feature per clip, so a redesign means replacing one video rather than all of them.

How long should a demo video be?

A marketing demo works at thirty to ninety seconds. Feature videos sit around one to two minutes each. A full walkthrough for someone evaluating can happily run five to fifteen minutes, because that viewer wants detail and has chosen to watch. As part of our content partnership with Plug In Stations we've made app tutorials and comparison pieces, and those longer formats exist because buyers go looking for them on YouTube while they're making up their minds.

Where do demo videos get used?

Product pages, app store listings, sales follow-ups, trade stand screens (on mute, so the visuals must carry it), onboarding emails and help centres. App stores have their own rules for preview videos, and Apple, for one, expects previews to use footage captured from the app itself, so check the current spec before you cut. A demo also makes a good partner to a customer testimonial: the demo shows it works, the customer says it worked for them.

What can go wrong, and what are the rules?

The big risk is a demo that misleads. Speeding things up without saying so, showing a result the product can't reliably produce, cherry picking one perfect run out of fifty. If the demo runs as an advert, the UK advertising codes apply, and the Advertising Standards Authority has ruled against ads that used filters to exaggerate what a beauty product does. The general principle is simple: what's shown should be what a customer will get. This is general guidance, so check anything borderline with whoever signs off your marketing claims.

Every app demo has one moment where the loading spinner takes four seconds longer than it ever has before. Record it twice.

How is a demo made, and what drives the cost?

A physical product demo is usually one shoot day, in a studio or on location, with close-up lenses and a plan for exactly what the product will do and when. An app demo is a script, a screen capture session, voiceover and an edit with graphics. Costs move with the number of features, locations, graphics, versions and languages. As general UK market ranges, simple motion graphics add roughly £200 to £1,500 or more, cut-downs £150 to £600 each, and most straightforward corporate video sits between £2,000 and £8,000, all from our free playbook. For quick internal feature clips, a phone is often enough.

If what you really need is a clear overview of what the product is, that's an explainer, covered in when animation beats live action. And if you'd like a demo filmed on a real site with real users, tell us about the product.
items.author: Earl Duncan

faqs.q: Should a real customer appear in a product demo?
faqs.a: It helps a lot if you can arrange it. A real customer using the product in their own setting answers questions a staff member can't, like how it fits into an ordinary day. Get their written consent, agree where the video will be used, and let them use the product the way they normally would rather than scripting every move.

faqs.q: Can we film an app demo ourselves?
faqs.a: Yes, and for many feature clips you should. Built-in screen recording on a computer or phone, a quiet room and a decent microphone will get you a usable result. Where it's worth bringing in help is the flagship demo on your homepage, where pacing, graphics and sound make a visible difference.

faqs.q: How often should demo videos be updated?
faqs.a: Whenever the product looks or works noticeably differently from what's on screen. An outdated demo creates support questions and makes the product look neglected. Keeping demos short and modular, one feature per video, means you only replace the clips affected by a change rather than reshooting everything.

faqs.q: Should a demo video have music?
faqs.a: Usually a little, kept low under the voice. Music helps pacing in a short marketing demo, but it gets in the way in a detailed walkthrough where people are concentrating. Whatever you use, make sure it's properly licensed for every platform the video will appear on, including paid ads if it'll run as one.

stat.title: People who've bought or downloaded an app after watching an app demo video

bars.label: Bought or downloaded after an app demo

stat.takeaway: An app demo is often the last thing someone watches before they download, so make it show the app doing what they need.

source.name: Wyzowl, Video Marketing Statistics 2026 (266 respondents, late 2025)

items.title: Video for hotels and hospitality: what guests trust
items.excerpt: What video works for hotels, venues and travel businesses: what guests check before booking, privacy and pricing rules, six film ideas and typical UK costs.
items.coverAlt: Guests laughing at a summer party
items.body:
Hospitality video works when it shows a guest what staying, eating or drinking somewhere will actually feel like, and who'll be looking after them. Hotels, pubs with rooms, venues and travel businesses all sell an experience that only exists once someone turns up, so the film's job is to make that experience believable before they book. That means real rooms, real light, real staff and an honest sense of the place around it.

Most hotel video is a drone shot, a made bed, a pool and a slow pan across an empty bar. It's pleasant. It's also interchangeable with the place down the road. This post covers what guests and bookers look for, the video types that fit, six film ideas, the sensitivities to respect and what it costs.

What do guests want to see before they book?

Mostly reassurance. Is the room the size it looks. What does the view really look out on. Is the street noisy. Will the staff be pleasant or just polite. Is it the kind of place where I'll fit in. For an event planner or a corporate booker the questions get more practical: how many people fit, where does the coffee go, how does a day actually run.

Guests also check your video against everything else they can find, especially reviews and guest photos. If the film oversells, the reviews correct it, and the gap between the two does more damage than a plain video would have. Honest footage of a good place is enough.

Every hotel video gets checked against the guest photos in the reviews. Film it so it passes.

Which video types work for hotels, venues and travel?

  • Brand documentary. The owners, the building, the reason the place exists. Strongest for independents, family-run hotels and restored buildings.
  • Room and space tours. Plain, steady and useful. These belong on the booking page next to the price.
  • Event and wedding venue films. Walked through by the events team, for planners and couples comparing venues.
  • Staff and recruitment films. Hospitality is people-heavy, and a film showing what working there is like helps hiring.
  • Local guides. What's nearby, filmed honestly, which also gives you content that people search for.

For showing a conference layout or every room in a large property, a 360 virtual tour or a simple animated floor plan often does the job better than a film. They let people explore at their own pace. We don't make those, and I'd still recommend them where that's the question being asked. A documentary film answers a different one: would I like it here?

Six film ideas for hospitality businesses

  1. Before the guests wake up. Housekeeping, the breakfast setup, the deliveries. The work that makes a stay feel easy.
  2. The longest-serving member of staff. What's changed, what hasn't, and the guests they remember.
  3. The owner's walk. Round the neighbourhood, to the places they'd send a friend.
  4. The building's story. For anywhere old, restored or converted. What it was, and what it took.
  5. The events walkthrough. The events manager showing a planner how a real day runs, room by room.
  6. Returning guests. In their own words, with their consent. Our post on customer testimonial videos covers how to make that feel genuine.

Is there a good example of hospitality on film?

The BBC series Amazing Hotels: Life Beyond the Lobby is a useful one to study. Its presenters work alongside the staff at each hotel, and what holds the attention is the people and the machinery behind the stay, far more than the suites. That's the same instinct a good hotel brand film works on.

You don't need a TV budget to borrow the approach. One chef, one housekeeper and one owner talking honestly about the place will tell a guest more than a montage of amenities. There's more on why that kind of film lands in brand documentary vs corporate video.

What should hotels and venues be careful about on camera?

General guidance only, so check the specifics with a professional where it matters.

  • Guests' privacy. Guests are there to relax, not to be filmed. Shoot public areas at quiet times, get clear consent from anyone featured, and never show room numbers with people going in or out of them.
  • Accessibility claims. If the film shows or mentions step-free access or accessible rooms, make sure it shows them accurately. People plan around that information.
  • Prices and fees. If a video ad mentions a price, the CMA's guidance on unfair commercial practices is worth reading. Hiding mandatory fees behind a headline price, known as drip pricing, is banned.
  • Reviews and testimonials. Fake reviews are also banned under the same rules. Staff playing guests, or guests paid to gush without saying so, is a risk as well as a bad look.
  • Music. The licence that lets you play music in the bar doesn't cover putting it in a video. More in music licensing for brand videos.

A made bed has been filmed roughly a million times. The person who made it, almost never.

How long should a hospitality video be?

Room tours and booking page clips work best short, often under a minute each. A brand documentary for an independent hotel or venue usually sits between two and five minutes for the website and YouTube, with a sixty to ninety second cut and vertical pieces for social. Event venue films can run a little longer, because a planner comparing venues will genuinely watch the detail. Shoot in the season you sell. A garden filmed in February is a hard sell for a summer wedding.

What does hotel and hospitality video cost?

These are typical UK market ranges, taken from what production companies and freelancers generally charge, not our quotes:

  • Under £2,000. A freelancer, a day or less on site, an interview and some B-roll, a short edit and library music. Fine for social content and simple pieces.
  • £2,000 to £8,000. A small production company or experienced freelance team, one or two shoot days, a proper edit and often a couple of cut-downs. Most corporate video sits here.
  • £8,000 to £30,000. Documentary brand films and higher-end brand content. Real research, multi-day shoots, a crew, a specialist grade and mix, a full set of cuts.
  • £30,000 and up. Agency-led campaigns, scripted work with cast and art direction, built sets, broadcast advertising.

Hospitality projects get more expensive when they cover several outlets (rooms, restaurant, spa, events), need early mornings and late nights to work around guests, involve drone permissions, or need to be shot across two seasons. They get cheaper when the property can close a space for a few hours and the staff are briefed properly beforehand. Our guide to briefing your team before a shoot helps with that, and the film budget calculator gives a rough number. If you want to talk it through, get in touch.
items.author: Earl Duncan

faqs.q: Should a hotel film its rooms empty or with people in them?
faqs.a: Both, for different jobs. Empty, steady room tours are best on booking pages, where guests want to see the space clearly. Films with people in them, staff or consenting guests, do the emotional work of showing what a stay feels like. Using models who look like guests can work, but it starts to feel like an advert quickly.

faqs.q: Is drone footage worth it for a hotel?
faqs.a: Sometimes. It's good for showing a rural setting, a coastline or how a large property sits in its grounds. In a city it often shows rooftops and car parks. Drone flights also need a properly registered operator following CAA rules, and restrictions near airports and crowds can rule it out. Treat it as a few seconds of context, never the whole film.

faqs.q: When is the best time of year to film a hotel?
faqs.a: The season you most want to sell. A summer wedding venue should be filmed when the garden looks like it will on the day, and a cosy winter retreat in winter. Many hotels shoot twice a year, or film the core interviews once and add seasonal footage later. Quieter weeks are easier for access, as long as the place still looks alive.

faqs.q: Can we use guest footage from social media in our video?
faqs.a: Only with permission from the person who posted it, and ideally in writing that covers where you'll use it. A guest tagging you doesn't give you the right to reuse their video in your marketing. It's often the most believable footage you'll get, so it's worth asking properly. This is general guidance rather than legal advice.

items.title: Explainer videos: when animation beats live action
items.excerpt: What an explainer video is for, what goes in a good one, how long it should run, and an honest guide to when animation does the job better than live action.
items.coverAlt: A presenter explaining grants to camera with graphics beside her
items.body:
An explainer video is a short film, usually a minute or two, that tells someone what a product, service or idea is and why it matters to them. It's built for the moment when someone's interested but still confused. Done well, it saves a sales call. Done badly, it's ninety seconds of ukulele music and a cartoon mascot pointing at a laptop.

We make documentary-style films with real people in them, so you might expect me to say live action every time. I won't. There are jobs where animation is plainly the better tool, and I'll be straight about which ones.

What is an explainer video actually for?

Getting someone from "I don't get it" to "I get it, and I can see why I'd want it". That's a narrower job than a brand film has. A brand film is mostly about trust and feeling. An explainer should be judged on one thing, which is whether people understood it.

They tend to live where the confusion happens: near the top of a homepage, on a product or service page, in the first email after an enquiry, on a loop at a trade stand, and in the welcome sequence once someone's signed up. If you sell something new, technical or regulated, it's often the most useful two minutes of video you'll own.

When does animation beat live action?

More often than a live action studio would like to admit. These are the cases where I'd point you towards an animation studio without a second thought:

  • When the thing is invisible. Software back ends, data, insurance, pensions, how a drug works in the body, electricity moving around a house. There's nothing to point a camera at.
  • When it doesn't exist yet. A product that hasn't been manufactured, a building that's still a planning application, an app that's half built.
  • When the subject can't be filmed. Patients, children in care, people at risk, confidential sites. Animation lets you tell the story without anyone being identifiable.
  • When it'll change often, or needs many languages. Re-voicing an animation is simple. Re-shooting people, or dubbing them, is neither cheap nor convincing.
  • When the idea is a system. Ten things happening at once, in an order, with arrows. Diagrams were invented for this.

Our own launch film for a load balancer is a good example of the first point. You can't film electricity being balanced inside a consumer unit, so that film was built around motion graphics rather than beauty shots of the product. Graphics were the only honest way to show the thing working.

For a full animated explainer, hire a specialist animation studio. That's a different craft from ours, and a good one will beat a live action crew at it every time.

When is live action the better choice?

When trust is part of what's being bought. Services, people, places, physical products and anything where the buyer is really choosing who they'll be dealing with. A cartoon can explain a process clearly, but it can't show the person who'll turn up, the workshop, or the customer who's already happy. Faces do a lot of work that graphics can't.

Live action also suits explainers about something people already half understand but need to act on. The landlord explainer we made for Easee covers the chargepoint grants available to landlords. It had to be clear enough to act on without becoming a lecture, and it went out subtitled.

There's also a middle route that gets overlooked: a live action interview with simple graphics laid over the part you can't film. A real person explains, a diagram shows the bit nobody can see. I've written more about where effects earn their place in VFX for brand video.

What goes into a good explainer video?

  • The problem first, in the viewer's words. Not your company history, not your product name.
  • One idea. If you've got three products, that's three explainers.
  • Show, then tell. Every claim should have something on screen that proves or illustrates it.
  • A script written to be heard. Read it out loud. Somewhere around 130 to 160 words a minute is a comfortable speaking pace, so a ninety second script is a lot shorter than people expect.
  • One next step. Book a call, start a trial, read the guide. Pick one.
  • Captions. A lot of video is watched on mute, and captions matter for accessibility anyway.
If your script needs a second idea to make sense, you need a second video.

How long should an explainer video be?

For the version on your homepage or in an ad, sixty to ninety seconds is a sensible target, and two minutes is about the ceiling. Wyzowl's 2026 survey found 71% of video marketers think thirty seconds to two minutes is the most effective length. A longer walkthrough has its place further down the line, for people who are already evaluating you. There's more on judging length in how long a brand film should be, and the same test applies: cut until it hurts, then check nobody's confused.

What are the common mistakes?

Starting with who you are instead of what the viewer's struggling with. Jargon the team uses every day that no customer has ever said. Listing every feature. Stock footage of people shaking hands. A voiceover that sounds like it's reading a terms and conditions page. And a mascot, drafted in because nobody could agree on what the actual idea was.

If the first line of your script is the year you were founded, I can tell you roughly where people stop watching.

The other big one is making an explainer when you need something else. If people already understand what you do and simply don't trust you yet, a clearer explanation won't help. That's a job for a customer story or a brand film, which is the difference I go into in brand documentary vs corporate video.

How is an explainer made, and what drives the cost?

The steps are similar either way: a brief, a script, approval, then production. For animation that means style frames, a storyboard, voiceover, animation and sound. For live action it means a recce, a shoot day, the edit, graphics, grade and mix. The script is where most of the quality is decided, so it's worth getting signed off properly before anyone films or animates a frame. Writing a decent brief makes that stage much faster.

Cost is driven by length, the number of locations or scenes, the complexity of the visual style, voiceover, languages and how many cut-downs you need. As general UK market ranges from our free playbook: under £2,000 usually buys a freelancer, a short shoot and a simple edit; £2,000 to £8,000 is where most corporate video sits, with a proper edit and a couple of cut-downs. Simple motion graphics on a live action piece typically add £200 to £1,500 or more. Animation is usually priced by the second and by style, so get quotes against the same script. The film budget calculator helps you sanity check a number.

If you're not sure whether your explainer wants real people or animation, tell us what it needs to explain. If the answer is animation, I'll say so.
items.author: Earl Duncan

faqs.q: Should an explainer video have a presenter?
faqs.a: Only if the presenter is someone the viewer should trust, like the founder or the person who'll do the work. A hired presenter adds polish but rarely adds belief. For live action explainers, a real person from the business talking plainly usually beats a professional reading a script, and it gives you a face customers will recognise when they meet you.

faqs.q: Can we use an AI voiceover for an explainer video?
faqs.a: You can, and for internal or quickly updated videos it's often fine. For anything customer facing, listen carefully, because synthetic voices still flatten emphasis and mispronounce names and technical words. If you use one, don't clone a real person's voice without their agreement. A real voice artist remains the safer choice for a flagship explainer.

faqs.q: Do we need a different explainer for social media?
faqs.a: Usually a different cut rather than a different film. Social versions need the point in the first couple of seconds, captions burned in, and a vertical or square frame. Plan those cuts at the script stage so the key lines can stand on their own, rather than trying to squeeze a widescreen ninety second film into a phone afterwards.

faqs.q: Who should write the explainer script?
faqs.a: Whoever writes it, the person who answers customer questions every day should review it. Production companies and animation studios will often draft the script from your brief, which is sensible because writing for the ear is a skill. Your job is to check it's accurate, uses your customers' language and makes one clear point.

stat.title: What video marketers have mostly created
stat.takeaway: Live action is the default, so choose your format on purpose: animation stands out when the subject can't be filmed.
