items.title: Video for food and drink brands: what to film
items.excerpt: What video works for restaurants, food producers and drink makers: what customers want to see, rules on claims and alcohol, six film ideas and what it costs.
items.coverAlt: People at an outdoor food and drink event
items.body:
Food and drink video works when it shows the people, the place and the process behind what's on the plate or in the glass. A restaurant, a cheesemaker, a bakery or a small brewery is selling something nobody can taste through a screen, so the film has to give them a reason to trust it instead: who makes it, how it's made, and why it's worth the price. Glossy product shots help on a menu page. On their own they rarely make anyone care.

This post covers what food and drink customers actually look for, the video types that suit the sector, six film ideas, the rules worth knowing and what drives the cost.

What do food and drink customers want to see on video?

The same things they'd ask if they were stood at the counter. Where does this come from. Who made it. Is it actually any good, and why does it cost more than the supermarket version. Someone choosing a restaurant wants to see the room, the food and a sense of the people running it. A deli buyer or a restaurant ordering wholesale wants to know the supply is reliable and that the person behind it knows their stuff.

Most food video online answers none of that. Shallow depth of field, slow-motion pours, hands, a bit of music and nobody in it. It looks lovely and it could belong to anyone. I'd argue the people matter more in food than almost anywhere else, because taste is personal and trust is what you're really buying when you can't try before you buy.

Nobody can taste through a screen. So the film has to give them someone to trust instead.

Which types of video suit a food or drink business?

  • Brand documentary. The story of the business told by the people in it. Best for founders with history, producers and specialist shops.
  • Process film. How the thing is made, at its real pace. Bread, cheese, coffee roasting, brewing, butchery.
  • Menu and product content. Short clips of dishes and products for the website, delivery apps and social, usually shot on the same day as everything else.
  • Supplier stories. The farm, the dairy, the grower. A restaurant that buys well should show it.
  • Recruitment film. Kitchens are hard to staff, and a film showing what working there is really like does a job a job ad can't.
  • Opening and event coverage. Launches, tastings, a new site.

Animation has a place too, mostly for explaining something you can't point a camera at, like a fermentation process or a supply chain map. If that's the job, a good motion designer is the better hire. We film real people, and for most food businesses that's where the trust is.

Six film ideas for restaurants, producers and makers

  1. The origin. Where it started, and what nearly stopped it. Told by the founder, not a voiceover.
  2. One service. Prep to the last cover, cut to five minutes. The pass is where the character of a kitchen shows.
  3. The producer visit. The chef or buyer goes to the farm and talks to the person who grows it.
  4. The bit nobody sees. The early bake, the cheese being turned, the market run before anyone's awake.
  5. The regulars. Customers who've been coming for years, in their own words. There's more on getting that right in testimonial videos that don't sound like testimonials.
  6. The trade film. For wholesale buyers. Range, consistency, delivery and the people they'll actually deal with.

What did filming La Fromagerie show us?

La Fromagerie began with a wheel of Beaufort in a garden shed, then a market stall at Camden Lock and a shop in Highbury at eighty pounds a week. Thirty three years on it's three shops with walk-in cheese rooms and a wholesale business supplying restaurants across London. The film tells that story through four voices: the founder, the cheesemongers and the wholesale side.

Two decisions shaped it. We filmed while the shops were open and trading, around customers rather than after hours, in cheese rooms that are cold, dark and busy. And we kept several voices instead of one, so the film shows what the business actually is now rather than just where it came from. I'd recommend both to any food business. An empty shop at 7pm looks like a set. A busy one looks like a place people choose. The full story of how it was made is in La Fromagerie: the story behind a documentary brand film.

What rules apply to food and drink video?

This is general guidance, not legal advice, and it's worth checking anything specific with the relevant body or a solicitor.

  • Health and nutrition claims. In Great Britain, only claims on the GB nutrition and health claims register can be made, and that applies to what someone says in a video as much as what's on the pack. A founder saying a product "boosts your immune system" on camera is making a claim.
  • Alcohol. The CAP Code's alcohol section covers marketing, including your own website and social channels. Among other things, nobody who is or looks under 25 should play a significant role, and drinking can't be linked to social or sexual success.
  • The food should look like the food. Advertising rules expect what's shown to represent what customers actually get. Styling is fine. Swapping in a better-looking dish isn't.
  • Hygiene on set. The crew follow the kitchen's rules. Hair tied back, no kit on prep surfaces, hands washed, and nobody wanders behind the pass without being asked.
  • Customers in shot. Anyone identifiable and featured should agree to it, and notices for general filming are good practice. Someone halfway through a first date didn't sign up to be in your advert.

Food stylists famously used mashed potato for ice cream because the real thing melts under the lights. Cheese, mercifully, holds its nerve.

How long should it be, and where does it go?

A brand documentary for a food business usually lands between two and six minutes, for the website, YouTube and anyone deciding whether to stock you or book you. Then a sixty to ninety second cut for the top of the homepage, and a set of short verticals for Instagram and TikTok, which is where most people already watch food. Our post on how long a brand film should be goes into the reasoning, and how to turn one film into a year of content covers getting the short pieces out of the same shoot.

What does food and drink video cost?

These are typical UK market ranges, taken from what production companies and freelancers generally charge, not our quotes:

  • Under £2,000. A freelancer, a day or less on site, an interview and some B-roll, a short edit and library music. Fine for social content and simple pieces.
  • £2,000 to £8,000. A small production company or experienced freelance team, one or two shoot days, a proper edit and often a couple of cut-downs. Most corporate video sits here.
  • £8,000 to £30,000. Documentary brand films and higher-end brand content. Real research, multi-day shoots, a crew, a specialist grade and mix, a full set of cuts.
  • £30,000 and up. Agency-led campaigns, scripted work with cast and art direction, built sets, broadcast advertising.

What moves a food project around those ranges: whether you film during service or close for it, how many sites are involved (a farm visit adds a day of travel), whether you need a food stylist, how many people are interviewed and how many cuts come out the other end. Our film budget calculator will give you a rough figure in a couple of minutes. And if there's a story behind what you make, tell us about it.
items.author: Earl Duncan

faqs.q: Can you film in a restaurant during service without getting in the way?
faqs.a: Yes, with a small crew and a plan agreed with the head chef. Service footage is usually the best footage, because it's real. The usual approach is one camera, no big lights in the dining room, interviews done before or after service, and clear agreement about where the crew can and can't stand at the pass.

faqs.q: Do we need a food stylist for a brand film?
faqs.a: Usually not for a documentary-style film. The chef's own plating, filmed well, is more believable and costs nothing extra. A stylist earns their fee on product photography, packaging shots and ads where one dish has to look perfect for a long close-up. If a stylist is used, the food should still be what customers actually get.

faqs.q: Is phone video good enough for a restaurant's social media?
faqs.a: For day-to-day posts, often yes. A modern phone handles a dish on the pass or a quick clip of the room perfectly well, especially in good light. Where phone video struggles is sound and low light, which is why interviews and anything going on your homepage are usually worth filming properly. Many restaurants do both.

faqs.q: Do customers need to sign a release to appear in our video?
faqs.a: Anyone who's clearly identifiable and featured should give their consent, ideally in writing. People passing in the background of a busy room are usually handled with visible filming notices and by keeping them out of focus. This is general guidance rather than legal advice, so check anything unusual, such as filming children, with a professional.

items.title: Live action vs animated video: when each one wins
items.excerpt: Live action or animation? When each one wins, when to mix them, how cost and shelf life compare, and why we make live action and say so when animation's better.
items.coverAlt: A black and white frame of a fighter training on the bag
items.body:
Live action wins when the thing you're selling is people, places, craft or trust, and the viewer needs to see that it's real. Animation wins when the subject is invisible, abstract, sensitive, not built yet or changes often, or when you simply can't film it. Plenty of good films mix the two. We make live action, documentary-style, with real people. We don't make animation, and when animation is the better tool I'll say so and point you elsewhere.

What's the difference between live action and animation?

Live action is filmed with a camera: real people, real places, real things. Animation is made rather than filmed, and the main kinds you'll come across are:

  • Motion graphics. Designed shapes, text, icons and diagrams that move. The most common kind in business video.
  • 2D animation. Drawn characters and scenes, from simple explainer styles to hand-drawn work.
  • 3D animation. Modelled objects and environments, common for products and engineering.
  • Screen recording. Software captured as it's used, often with graphics added.

Then there's the mixed version: live action with graphics on top, like name captions, maps and diagrams. Most of our films include a little of that, and I've written about where it helps and where it hurts in VFX and motion graphics for brand video.

When does live action win?

When trust is the thing being bought. A viewer deciding whether to hire a builder, pay for a bespoke pair of shoes or support a charity wants to see the actual people and the actual work. Animation can explain a service, but it can't show you that the person who'll turn up is decent, skilled and real.

It also wins for craft, because the value is in watching a hand do something difficult at its real speed. On our signwriting film the whole point is a single unbroken brush line that either works or doesn't. An animation of that would miss the reason anyone cares.

And it wins on emotion carried by a face. Customer stories, founder stories, recruitment. As AI-made imagery spreads, real footage of real people counts for more, which I've gone into in why real people on camera matter more now.

When does animation win?

There are some clear cases, and I'd rather be honest about them.

  • The subject is invisible. Data moving, electricity, chemistry, software logic, something happening inside a pipe or a body.
  • The idea is abstract. A financial product, a process with lots of steps, a concept with no physical form.
  • The subject is sensitive. Abuse, illness, debt, anything where filming real people could harm them or put them off.
  • It doesn't exist yet. A product in development, a building not yet built.
  • It changes often. Software screens that'll look different in six months are cheaper to update in animation than to reshoot.
  • You can't film it. No access, no permission, or a location that's unsafe.

Tea and Consent, the animated short Thames Valley Police used in a consent campaign, is the best example I know of animation doing something live action couldn't. Stick figures and a cup of tea explain sexual consent clearly, with a bit of humour, and without putting a real person in an uncomfortable scene. Filmed with actors, it would have been heavier and much easier to argue with.

Can you mix live action and animation?

Yes, and it's often the best answer. Real people for the trust, graphics for the bit the camera can't see.

The UK launch film for the Easee Equalizer is a case where graphics had to lead. The Equalizer is a load balancer, and you can't film electricity being balanced inside a consumer unit. So the film was built around motion graphics rather than product beauty shots, visualising the whole home energy picture from solar through to the car on the drive, and written so it worked for installers and homeowners at once.

Going the other way, documentary films regularly use simple graphics to explain one thing: a map of where a business operates, a before and after floorplan, a number on screen. On the Barry Road renovation film, before and after floorplans were cut in so the scale of the work reads on screen.

Which is cheaper, live action or animation?

It depends far more on ambition than on format. A simple motion graphics explainer can cost less than a multi-day shoot, and detailed character animation or photoreal 3D can cost much more than a documentary.

Live action costs are driven by shoot days, crew, locations and edit time. Our free playbook Before the camera comes out sets out typical UK market ranges, not quotes: under £2,000 for a simple single-day piece, £2,000 to £8,000 for most corporate video, £8,000 to £30,000 for documentary brand films and higher-end brand content, and £30,000 and up for scripted work with cast and built sets. Simple animated elements inside a live action film, like titles and lower thirds, typically run £200 to £1,500 or more.

Full animation is priced by length, style, complexity and rounds of changes. We don't make it, so I won't put numbers on it here. Get two or three quotes from animation studios against the same brief and compare what's included, especially the number of revisions.

Animation can explain what you do. It can't show that the person who'll turn up is decent, skilled and real.

Which one ages better?

Both date, in different ways. Live action dates through clothes, hairstyles, people who've left the business and kit that's been replaced. Animation dates through style, because illustration trends move quickly, and through any interface it shows. A live action film built around a customer story or a craft tends to last well. An animation built around a product screen may need updating within the year.

How do you decide?

A few questions usually settle it:

  • Is the viewer deciding whether to trust people? Live action.
  • Is the main thing invisible or abstract? Animation, or graphics within live action.
  • Would filming real people put anyone at risk? Animation.
  • Does it exist and can you get access to film it? If not, animation.
  • Will the subject change in the next year? Lean towards animation, or keep the changeable bits in graphics.

I've been asked if we can animate a client's founder to save them being filmed. We can't, and honestly, they'd be the best bit.

If live action is the answer, here's how our films work. If it's animation, I'd still happily tell you what to look for in a studio. Get in touch either way.
items.author: Earl Duncan

faqs.q: Is animation better for explainer videos?
faqs.a: Often, when the thing being explained is invisible or abstract, like software, finance or a technical process. If the explainer is really about a service delivered by people, live action with a few simple graphics is usually more convincing. Many of the best explainers mix the two: a real person introducing the problem, and animation showing how the solution works.

faqs.q: Can AI generate animation for a business video now?
faqs.a: AI tools can produce animated clips and images quickly, and they're useful for rough ideas and storyboards. For a finished business film they still struggle with consistency, exact branding and accurate detail, and audiences increasingly notice. If you use them, have a person direct and check every frame, and be open about it where people would expect to know.

faqs.q: Does s4digital make animated videos?
faqs.a: No. We make documentary-style live action films, with real people in real places, plus the photography and short-form content around them. Our films include simple graphics such as titles, captions and maps where they help. If your project genuinely needs full animation, we'll say so and suggest what to look for in an animation studio.

faqs.q: Which gets more engagement, live action or animation?
faqs.a: There's no reliable rule, because engagement depends on the subject, the audience and how good the video is. Live action with real people tends to do well where trust and emotion matter. Animation can stand out in sectors where everyone else films the same talking heads. Test both if you can, and judge them on the result you actually wanted.

stat.title: The kind of video marketers mostly make
stat.takeaway: Live action is the default for most businesses, so choose animation on purpose when your subject can't be filmed, not just to look different.

items.title: Cyber security and SaaS video: making the work human
items.excerpt: How cyber security and SaaS companies can film invisible technical work: what buyers need to see, six film ideas, what to keep out of shot and when to animate.
items.coverAlt: A rendered product scene used in a launch film
items.body:
Cyber security and SaaS companies sell work nobody can see. The best videos for them put the people doing that work on camera, let a customer explain the problem that went away, and use screen recordings or animation only where they genuinely explain something better. Buyers choose software and security partners they trust, and trust comes from seeing who's behind the product.

Below is why technical work is hard to film, what buyers need to see, film ideas, what a security company must keep out of shot, and when live action isn't the right tool.

Why is invisible technical work so hard to film?

Because there's nothing to point the camera at. Code doesn't look like anything. A blocked attack looks exactly like a normal Tuesday. So the sector falls back on the same visual shorthand: a figure in a hoodie, green characters raining down a screen, a glowing padlock, a globe with lines across it. Everyone's seen it so often that it's become invisible too.

The way out is to film the people. The analyst on a night shift, the engineer who built the integration, the IT manager who used to dread Monday mornings. Your buyer is a person, often one who's been through a bad day already. The UK government's latest breaches survey found that 43% of businesses had experienced a cyber security breach or attack in the previous twelve months.

We faced a version of the same problem making the UK launch film for the Easee Equalizer, a load balancer whose entire value is invisible. You can't film electricity being balanced. That film was built around motion graphics rather than product shots, because graphics were the clearest way to show it.

What do software and security buyers need to see?

  • Who's on the other end. Especially for managed services and support, buyers want to know there are capable people awake when it matters.
  • Plain English. The person signing the contract is often a finance director or a founder, not an engineer.
  • Proof from customers. Someone like them saying what changed.
  • The product, honestly. What it actually looks like to use, not a mock-up.
  • Calm competence. Security buyers are nervous. A film that's frantic or scary doesn't help them choose you.
A blocked attack looks exactly like a normal Tuesday. So film the people who made it normal.

What films work for cyber security and SaaS companies?

  1. The people on watch. Analysts and support engineers talking about what a normal shift involves. It answers the question most buyers never ask out loud.
  2. A customer's own account. The problem before, the decision, what's different now. Where a client can't be named, it can still be done with voice, hands and an unbranded room.
  3. The founder film. Why the company exists, told by the person who started it, unscripted.
  4. Engineers explaining one thing. A short clip of your own expert explaining a concept at a whiteboard is more believable than a voiceover and more useful than a feature list.
  5. Product walkthroughs. A clean screen recording with a real person explaining it, kept short so it's easy to update.
  6. Recruitment. Engineering talent is hard to hire, and good people want to see who they'd work with.

Plain language and accessibility matter here as much as anywhere. Our film for char.gy explained a B Corp certification, a genuinely hard thing to earn and a genuinely boring thing to explain, by letting the people who did the work talk about it, and it was delivered with an audio described version.

What should a security company keep out of shot?

More than you'd think. Offices of security and software companies are full of things that shouldn't be on YouTube. Before and during the shoot, check for:

  • Screens showing live dashboards, client names, alerts, IP addresses or code
  • Whiteboards with architecture diagrams or project names
  • Badges, door codes, visitor books and Wi-Fi details on the wall
  • Staff who, for their own safety or their clients', shouldn't be identifiable

Have your own security lead review the final cut frame by frame. Claims need the same care. The advertising code requires documentary evidence for objective claims, which makes words like "unhackable" or "100% secure" a bad idea on top of being tempting fate. And many contracts stop you naming clients at all, so check before you film anyone. This is general guidance, not legal advice.

If your film has someone in a hoodie typing green code in a dark room, I'm afraid the stock library has already won.

Live action, screen recording or animation?

Each does a different job, and the honest answer is usually a mix. Live action for people, culture and customer stories, which is where we work. Screen recordings for the product itself, because nothing shows software better than the software. Animation and motion graphics for architecture, data flows and how an attack is stopped, because those are diagrams at heart. We don't make animation, but we're happy to say when it's the better tool. I'd avoid AI avatars as presenters. In a sector built on trust, a synthetic face sends the wrong message, as I've written in what AI can and can't do for brand video.

What does it cost, and what goes wrong?

As UK market ranges, not quotes from us: under £2,000 for a freelancer's day of interviews, £2,000 to £8,000 for a small production company's interview-led film with cut-downs, and £8,000 to £30,000 for documentary films with research and several shoot days. Software teams also need to budget for keeping demos current, since a walkthrough can date with the next release.

The common mistakes: stock hacker imagery, jargon nobody outside the team understands, demos that are out of date within months, and sensitive screens caught in the background. If you'd like to plan a film properly, get in touch, or read our free guide Before the camera comes out.
items.author: Earl Duncan

faqs.q: How do we make a customer story if the client won't be named?
faqs.a: Focus on the person and the problem rather than the logo. You can film someone's voice over shots of their hands, their desk or an unbranded room, describe them by role and sector, and leave out anything identifying. It's still more convincing than a written case study. Agree what can and can't be shown with the client in writing before the shoot.

faqs.q: Should a SaaS company use an AI avatar instead of filming staff?
faqs.a: For anything about trust, I wouldn't. Avatars are quick for internal training or frequently updated help content, but buyers judging a software or security partner want to see real people. A synthetic presenter can suggest there's nobody there, which is the exact worry you're trying to answer. Film your team for the important pieces and keep avatars, if at all, for routine updates.

faqs.q: How often should product demo videos be updated?
faqs.a: Whenever the interface changes enough that a viewer would be confused, which for many SaaS products is every few months. Keep walkthroughs short and focused on one task each, so you can replace one clip without remaking a whole series. Keep the human, evergreen films separate from the product demos, because those can last for years.

faqs.q: Can engineers who hate being on camera still be in the film?
faqs.a: Yes, and they're often better than they expect. A relaxed conversation about something they know well usually brings out good answers, especially with no script. Filming them working, or at a whiteboard, takes the pressure off. Our posts on preparing for being filmed and speaking on camera have practical tips worth sharing with them beforehand.

stat.title: UK organisations that had a cyber security breach or attack in the last 12 months
stat.takeaway: Your buyer has quite possibly been through an attack already, so a film that shows calm, capable people will land harder than any padlock graphic.

source.name: Department for Science, Innovation and Technology, Cyber Security Breaches Survey 2025

items.title: Teaser videos: what they're for and how to cut one
items.excerpt: What a teaser video is, when one makes sense, how it differs from a trailer, what goes in a good one, how long it should be and how to cut one from your film.
items.coverAlt: Car headlights in a dark car park, a moody cinematic frame
items.body:
A teaser video is a short clip released before something launches, a product, a film, an event, a new site, to make people want to see the real thing. It shows a little, holds most of it back, and points to a date or a place to go. Most run six to thirty seconds. A teaser only works if there's something worth waiting for, and an audience that's already at least slightly interested. Tease to nobody and nothing happens.

When does a teaser actually make sense?

When there's a moment coming and you've got enough time before it to build some anticipation. Product launches. The release of a brand film or a documentary. An event with tickets on sale. A rebrand or a new website. A big announcement.

A teaser is really a specialised kind of promotional video: same audience, same eventual ask, just released earlier and holding more back.

It makes less sense when the thing being teased is small, or when your audience is so small that nobody's waiting for anything. A teaser borrows attention against a future payoff. If the payoff's modest, a straightforward announcement is more honest and usually works better.

What's the difference between a teaser and a trailer?

A teaser comes earlier and gives away less. It's about mood and a question. A trailer comes closer to release and tells more of the story, who's in it, what happens, why you should care. Films often release both: a teaser months out and a trailer in the final weeks. Businesses can borrow the same pattern for a big launch, though for most a single teaser followed by the real thing is plenty.

The first teaser for Star Wars: The Force Awakens, released about a year before the film came out, is a near-perfect example of the form. No plot. A handful of striking images, a voice asking a question, and the Millennium Falcon at the very end with the music swelling. It tells you almost nothing and makes you want everything. Few businesses have nearly forty years of fans waiting, but the structure scales down: a few images, one question, one reveal.

What goes into a good teaser?

  • One strong image or moment that sticks. Better one great shot than ten good ones.
  • A question the viewer wants answered. What is it, who's that, what happens next.
  • Sound that does work. In a short piece, sound design and a single line of dialogue carry a lot.
  • Enough to know what it is. Mystery is good. Confusion isn't.
  • A date or a destination. When it lands, or where to sign up to be told.
  • Consistency with the final thing, so the payoff feels like the promise was kept.

How long should a teaser video be?

For social, six to thirty seconds, and the shorter end is often stronger. For a film or documentary release, up to a minute is fine. Past that it's becoming a trailer, which is a different job. If you're running a sequence, two or three short teasers spaced over a couple of weeks tends to beat one longer one.

Can you cut a teaser from the main film?

Yes, and for most businesses it's the cheapest and most consistent route. With a documentary-style brand film, a teaser can be as simple as one line from an interview laid over one strong shot, ending before the line resolves. The viewer gets the voice, the place and a reason to come back.

It works best when it's planned at the shoot. A few shots framed with the teaser in mind, a moment of quiet before someone speaks, a reveal that can be held back. I've written more on that in turning one brand film into a year of content. Events work the same way: content from one show can tease the next one, which is what happened with the Fully Charged South and North shows, where the first produced the material that promoted the second.

What are the common mistakes?

  • Too vague. Nobody can tell what's being teased, or who from.
  • Giving it all away. If the teaser contains the best moment, the launch has nothing left.
  • Too long a gap. Months between a small brand's teaser and the release, and people forget.
  • No date and no next step. Interest with nowhere to go evaporates.
  • Teasing something that slips. Announce the date only once you're sure of it.
  • A teaser for a teaser. If you need three rounds of build-up, the thing itself may not be strong enough yet.
Mystery is good. Confusion isn't. The viewer should know exactly what they're waiting for.

A teaser is the only piece of marketing where saying less is the brief. Enjoy it while it lasts.

How is a teaser made, and what does it cost?

If it's cut from footage you already have, it's an edit job, and in our free playbook Before the camera comes out cut-downs sit at a typical UK market range of £150 to £600 per cut, depending on whether it's a simple reframe or a new structure with captions. That's a market range, not a quote. Add music if the main film's licence doesn't cover the new use, and check that the licence covers paid placement if you plan to promote it. There's more on that in music licensing for brand videos.

A standalone teaser with its own shoot follows the usual budget bands. A simple one-day piece often sits under £2,000, and anything with cast, art direction or a built set moves quickly into the higher bands.

For our films, a teaser is one of the short pieces we'd plan from the same shoot as the main film. If you've got a launch coming up and want the build-up planned properly, tell us about it.
items.author: Earl Duncan

faqs.q: How far ahead of a launch should a teaser go out?
faqs.a: For most businesses, one to three weeks before is about right. That's long enough to build interest and short enough that people still remember when the real thing arrives. Big launches with established audiences can tease further out. If you're releasing more than one teaser, space them a few days apart and make each one reveal a little more than the last.

faqs.q: Should a teaser include our logo?
faqs.a: Usually yes, somewhere, so people know who it's from. It doesn't need to open on the logo. A brand mark at the end, a product people recognise, or a familiar face is often enough. The only exception is a deliberate mystery campaign, and those only work if the reveal is strong enough to be worth the wait.

faqs.q: Can a teaser be a still image instead of a video?
faqs.a: It can, and a striking still with a date works well on some platforms. Video tends to perform better in feeds because movement catches the eye and sound adds a lot of mood. A good compromise is a very short clip, five or six seconds, that's almost a still image with one small movement and a line of sound.

faqs.q: Do teasers work for B2B companies?
faqs.a: They can, for genuine moments like a product launch, a major report, an event or a new service line. Keep them clear about what's coming and who it's for, because B2B audiences are less patient with pure mystery. A short clip from the interview that sits at the heart of the launch, with a date, usually works better than abstract imagery.

stat.title: Video marketers who've made a teaser video

bars.label: of video marketers say they've created teaser videos

stat.takeaway: Teasers are a common tool, so yours needs a genuinely strong image and a clear date to stand out from everyone else building up to something.

source.name: Wyzowl, Video Marketing Statistics 2026 (survey of 266 respondents, late 2025)

items.title: Health and safety videos and site inductions that stick
items.excerpt: How to make health and safety films and site induction videos people watch, what the law asks for in general terms, six film ideas and filming safely on site.
items.coverAlt: An engineer in hi-vis talking to camera on site
items.body:
A good health and safety video shows real workers on your real site talking about the hazards they actually face, short enough to hold attention, and followed by a conversation that checks people understood. Safety films and site induction videos stop supervisors repeating the same briefing forty times and make sure everyone hears the same thing. But under the construction regulations a film can only ever be one part of an induction.

Below is what makes a safety film work, what the law asks for in general terms, film ideas, how to film safely on a live site, and when animation is the better choice. The legal section is general guidance, not health and safety advice. Your competent person and your own risk assessments come first.

What makes a safety film people actually watch?

Recognition. People switch off when the film's clearly from somewhere else, voiced by an actor and full of hazards that don't apply to them. They pay attention when they see their own site, their own equipment and someone they know saying "this is the bit that'll catch you out".

  • Your own site. The actual gate, the actual muster point, the actual forklift route.
  • Experienced workers talking. A supervisor with twenty years on the job carries more weight than any presenter.
  • Stakes. Why the rule exists, said plainly.
  • Short sections. A few minutes each, not one long sit-through.

It's also worth remembering what the harm actually looks like. Most of it isn't the dramatic accident. HSE's figures show far more people made ill by work, through stress, strain and repetitive damage, than injured in a single event. A good programme of films covers the slow stuff as well.

What does the law say about inductions and safety information?

General guidance only, for Great Britain. Employers must give employees comprehensible and relevant information on the risks identified by their risk assessment and the measures in place, along with adequate training. On construction projects, the Construction (Design and Management) Regulations 2015 say the principal contractor must ensure a suitable site induction is provided, and HSE's guidance for principal contractors describes that as site-specific.

What that means for video:

  • A film can carry the standard part of an induction consistently, every time.
  • A person still needs to cover what's changed today, answer questions and check understanding.
  • "Comprehensible" covers language. If your workforce includes people whose first language isn't English, subtitled or translated versions help, and translations should be checked by a fluent speaker.
  • It has to stay current. A film showing last year's layout is worse than no film.

Safety films have a reputation as the twenty minutes before the biscuits come out. It's a reputation the genre has worked hard for.

What safety films work best?

  1. A modular site induction. Welcome, layout, rules, emergency routes and welfare, filmed as separate sections so one can be reshot when the site changes without redoing everything.
  2. Toolbox talk shorts. Two or three minutes on one topic, led by the people who do the work, ready to play on a phone at the start of a shift.
  3. The day it went wrong. Someone who had an incident or near miss explaining it in their own words. Nothing lands harder. It needs their full consent, real care, and usually waiting until any investigation is closed.
  4. Visitor and contractor inductions. For factories, warehouses and depots, a short film people watch before they arrive saves time at the gate.
  5. Task-specific how-tos. Isolation, manual handling, a particular machine, shown by your most experienced operator at the real pace of the job.
  6. A safety culture film. Leaders and workers talking about why it matters here. Useful for recruitment as well.

How do you film safely on a live site?

The crew is a hazard too. They need their own induction, the right PPE, a briefing on where they can and can't stand, and someone from site with them. Production rarely stops for a camera, and it shouldn't have to. When we filmed on a working shop floor for Alpha Manufacturing, the interviews had to happen around live production, in a place that's loud and lit for work rather than cameras.

The other thing is what ends up in frame. A safety film with someone in the background missing their eye protection becomes training material for exactly the wrong thing, and it's the detail everyone remembers. Check every shot for PPE, guarding, housekeeping and correct technique, and have a competent person review the cut before it's used. We did something similar on a live installation at a car supermarket, filming tight on engineers working around moving vehicles with nothing stopped for us.

A safety film with someone in the background missing their eye protection becomes training material for exactly the wrong thing.

Live action or animation for safety training?

Live action for your site, your people and your procedures, because recognition is the whole point. Animation for what you can't or shouldn't film: a fall from height, a gas leak, an explosion, the inside of a machine, or a reconstruction of a serious incident. Showing those with real people ranges from impractical to tasteless, and a clear animated sequence does the job better. That's specialist work we don't make, but the two combine well. Our post on graphics and effects covers when they're worth paying for.

How much does a safety or induction film cost?

As UK market ranges, not quotes from us: under £2,000 for a freelancer's day of simple coverage, £2,000 to £8,000 for a small production company making a proper interview-led film with several sections, and £8,000 to £30,000 for larger documentary-style projects with research and several shoot days. For inductions, think about the update cost as well as the first build. A modular film that's cheap to refresh is better value than a polished one that's out of date by spring.

The usual mistakes: too long, filmed somewhere else, wrong PPE in shot, no check of understanding afterwards, and no plan to update. If you'd like to plan one, get in touch, or start with our free guide Before the camera comes out.
items.author: Earl Duncan

faqs.q: Can a video replace a face-to-face site induction?
faqs.a: Not completely. A film can deliver the standard information the same way every time, which is valuable. But on construction projects the induction needs to be suitable and site-specific, and someone should cover what's changed that day, answer questions and check people have understood. Treat the video as the consistent core and the conversation as the part that makes it work. General guidance only.

faqs.q: How long should a site induction video be?
faqs.a: As short as it can be while covering what people need. Break it into sections of a few minutes each, such as welcome, rules, emergency procedures and welfare, so attention doesn't drift and sections can be updated on their own. If the full set runs long, consider which parts everyone needs and which only apply to certain roles or areas of the site.

faqs.q: Should we film real incidents or reconstructions?
faqs.a: A real person telling the story of their own incident is usually the most powerful option, with their full consent and once any investigation is closed. Reconstructing a serious incident with actors can feel uncomfortable, and showing it graphically rarely helps. For the moment of the incident itself, simple animation or a clear diagram often explains what happened better and more respectfully.

faqs.q: Do we need translated versions of safety videos?
faqs.a: If people on your site don't all read or speak English well, yes, it's worth it. The duty is to give information people can understand, and subtitles or translated versions are a practical way to do that. Have translations checked by a fluent speaker who understands the work, because machine translation can get technical safety terms badly wrong.

stat.title: Working people in Great Britain affected by work, 2024/25 (thousands)
stat.takeaway: More people are made ill by work than injured by it, so a safety film programme should cover strain and stress as well as accidents.

source.name: HSE, Health and safety at work: key figures for Great Britain 2024/25

items.title: Event videos: conferences, launches and live events
items.excerpt: What event videos are, the kinds you can get from one day, what to plan before the doors open, lengths, common mistakes and what drives the cost of coverage.
items.coverAlt: A crowd gathered for the opening ceremony at Southwick D-Day 80
items.body:
An event video is any film made from a conference, launch, exhibition, competition, seminar or other live event. That covers a short highlight film, full recordings of talks, interviews with speakers or guests, social clips and photography, and an event can produce all of them at once. The single most useful thing to do is decide before the day which of those you need, because each one needs different coverage, and you can't go back for it afterwards.

What kinds of event video are there?

  • Highlight film. The story of the day in one to two minutes, for selling the next one and showing sponsors what they bought into.
  • Full session recordings. Talks and panels recorded end to end, for people who couldn't attend and for your own archive.
  • Interviews. Speakers, exhibitors, partners or attendees on camera, usually in a quieter corner.
  • Social clips. Short vertical moments, ideally posted while the event is still happening or the day after.
  • Photography. Usually wanted, and easiest when it's planned alongside the video.

What is an event video for?

Usually one of four things, and it helps to know which.

Selling the next one. The seminar with Rafael Lovato Jr and Demian Maia at London Fight Factory was cut into a highlight edit the gym can use to sell the next seminar. The reactions in the room are what make that kind of film worth watching.

Keeping the value going. Exhibiting costs a lot and the value drains away the moment the doors close. For Road at the Installer Show, we filmed across three days at the NEC, with interviews with three brands on the stand and a bank of b-roll so Road could keep posting long after everyone went home.

Recording something that matters. Some events need a proper record more than a sales tool.

Content for everyone involved. Sponsors, speakers and exhibitors all want something to share, which spreads the event further than your own channels can. Short vertical clips do most of that work, and the rules in social media videos for business apply to them too.

For the eightieth anniversary of D-Day in Southwick, where the landings were planned, the coverage included the arrivals, the procession, the opening ceremony and the full panel talk recorded end to end. A commemoration is a single-take event with no rehearsal, and a camera has to stay out of the way of the thing it's there to record.

What should you plan before the day?

  • The running order, with the moments that can't be missed marked clearly.
  • Sound for talks. A feed from the venue's sound desk is usually far better than a mic at the back of the room. Ask the venue or AV team well before the day.
  • Who matters. A list, with photos if possible, of the speakers, guests and sponsors who must be filmed.
  • Consent. Tell attendees they may be filmed when they register and with signs at the door, get speakers to agree to recording and publication, and offer a simple way to opt out. Take extra care with children. This is general guidance, so check your own data protection position.
  • A quiet spot for interviews, away from the noise of the main room.
  • Turnaround. When you need each piece by, because a highlight film a month later has missed its moment.

How long should an event video be?

Highlight films: sixty seconds to two minutes. Social clips: fifteen to forty five seconds. Interviews: one to three minutes each. Session recordings: as long as the session, with the dead time trimmed. If you only get one piece, make it the highlight film, then cut the social clips from it.

What are the common mistakes?

  • Only wide shots of the room. The good moments are small: a face, a handshake, a reaction. That needs close coverage.
  • No sound plan. Talks recorded on a camera mic from thirty metres away are hard to listen to.
  • Slow turnaround. Social clips are worth most within a day or two. For Fully Charged, assets had to be turned around fast enough to sell tickets for the next show while they still mattered.
  • No one on the ground who knows who's who. The camera person can't spot your biggest sponsor in a crowd.
  • Stopping the event for the camera. It breaks the thing you're filming.
At a live event nothing can be asked for twice, so the planning is the coverage.

The best moment at any event happens about four seconds after you've lowered the camera to change a battery. Plan for two cameras.

How is event video made, and what does it cost?

The cost is mostly people and time on the day, then turnaround. More rooms and more simultaneous sessions mean more operators. Full talk recordings need a locked-off camera and good sound for each room. Fast turnaround means an editor working during or straight after the event.

Our free playbook Before the camera comes out gives typical UK market ranges, not quotes. A camera operator usually runs £400 to £1,200 a day including basic kit, a second camera £350 to £800, a sound recordist £350 to £650, a stills photographer £400 to £1,200, and an editor £300 to £600 a day. Each extra cut-down typically adds £150 to £600. Simple single-day event recaps often fall under £2,000, while multi-day coverage with several outputs usually sits in the £2,000 to £8,000 band or above. You can add up your own version with the film budget calculator.

Event coverage is one of the things we do alongside our films. If you've got something coming up, tell us the date and what you need from it. And if the event footage is going to feed your content for months, this post on getting a year out of one shoot applies just as well.
items.author: Earl Duncan

faqs.q: Can event footage be live streamed as well as recorded?
faqs.a: Yes, but it's a different job with different kit. Live streaming needs a stable internet connection, a vision mixer or streaming setup and someone dedicated to running it, alongside the cameras. If you want both, plan it as a streaming job with recording built in, and expect the cost to rise. For many events, fast edited clips are more useful than a live stream.

faqs.q: How quickly can we get event videos back?
faqs.a: Social clips can often be turned around the same day or the next if an editor is planned in. A highlight film usually takes a few days to two weeks depending on the edit and changes. Full session recordings take longer if they need tidying, captions and graphics. Agree the deadlines for each piece before the event, not after.

faqs.q: Do we need permission to film attendees at a UK event?
faqs.a: Generally you should tell attendees in advance that filming will take place, explain how the footage will be used, and give them an easy way to avoid being filmed. Speakers should agree to being recorded and published. Extra care applies to children and to sensitive events. This is general guidance, so check your own data protection obligations for anything unusual.

faqs.q: Is it worth filming a small event?
faqs.a: Often, yes, if you plan to run it again or the people there are your best customers. A small event filmed well can look busy and warm, which helps sell the next one. Keep the coverage proportionate: one experienced shooter, a short highlight film and a few social clips is usually enough for a small gathering.

items.title: Healthcare video: real clinicians, real consent
items.excerpt: What patients need to see in a healthcare video, how consent and medical claims work in general terms, six film ideas and when animation is the better tool.
items.coverAlt: An empty consultation room at golden hour with a camera set up for an interview
items.body:
Patients want to see who'll be treating them, what will actually happen, and that they'll be treated with dignity. A good healthcare video shows real clinicians explaining things plainly in the place patients will visit, includes patients only with proper written consent, and makes no claim you can't back up with evidence. That applies whether you're a private clinic, a dental practice, a physio, a care provider or a healthtech company.

Below is what patients look for, how consent and claims work in general terms, film ideas, and where animation is the better tool. The consent and advertising sections are general guidance, not legal or regulatory advice. Your professional regulator's standards, your data protection lead and your own policies come first.

What do patients need to see before choosing a clinic?

The clinician, more than anything. Nurses and doctors are among the most trusted people in Britain. In the Ipsos Veracity Index, nine in ten people said they trust nurses to tell the truth, and around eight and a half in ten said the same of doctors. That's a huge asset most healthcare marketing wastes by putting a voiceover and stock footage where the clinician should be.

  • The person treating them. Their manner, how they explain things, whether they seem to listen.
  • The place. The entrance, the waiting room, the treatment room. Anxious patients find it calming to have seen it first.
  • What happens, step by step. From arrival to aftercare, without euphemism.
  • Realistic expectations. What a treatment can do, and what it can't.
  • Accessibility. Subtitles as standard, and clear speech. Health audiences include people with hearing and sight loss.

How does patient consent work when filming?

General guidance only. For doctors, the GMC's guidance on making and using visual and audio recordings of patients says consent, usually in writing, is needed for recordings used in widely accessible public media, whether or not the patient will be identifiable. It also says patients should be under no pressure to agree. Other professions have their own regulators and standards, so check yours.

Data protection matters too. The ICO treats health data as special category data needing extra protection, and a patient filmed in a clinic is revealing something about their health just by being there. In practice:

  • Ask away from treatment. Never in the chair or on the couch, and never in a way that could feel linked to their care.
  • Explain exactly where it'll be used and for how long, and how they can change their mind.
  • Check the background. Screens, appointment lists, whiteboards, other patients in the waiting room. Film in closed hours where you can.
  • Use staff for demonstrations where a patient isn't needed, and don't present them as patients.
  • Take extra care with capacity. In care settings, some residents can't give consent themselves, and that needs proper handling under your policies.

Every clinic film seems to need a slow-motion shot of someone in a white coat walking down a corridor. I've never heard of anyone choosing a clinic because of it.

What claims can a healthcare video make?

Only ones you can prove. The advertising code says marketers must hold documentary evidence for objective claims, and its section on medicines and health products goes further, requiring evidence for health claims and barring the advertising of prescription-only medicines to the public. That last one catches out aesthetics clinics more than anyone. A patient saying "it cured my back pain" in your film counts as your claim. Before-and-after footage needs to be real, unaltered and representative. If in doubt, ask the ASA's advice service before you publish.

A patient saying "it cured my back pain" in your film counts as your claim.

What films work for healthcare providers?

  1. Meet the clinician. Short, unscripted profiles of the people who treat patients, talking about their work and how they approach it.
  2. Your first appointment. The route from the front door to the treatment room, and what happens there. Hugely reassuring for nervous patients.
  3. A patient's own account. With written consent, after treatment, focused on the experience rather than the medical result.
  4. Clinicians answering common questions. One question per clip, general information, clearly labelled.
  5. Recruitment. Healthcare is short of people. Staff talking honestly about the place they work is a strong pull.
  6. A day in a care home. For care providers, families want to see daily life and how staff treat residents. It needs the most careful consent of all, and it's often the film that matters most.

Cleveland Clinic's Empathy film is a good example of the human side done well. It follows people through a hospital with short captions about what each one's carrying. No product, no claim, nobody selling, and it says more about the place than any brochure could.

Live action or animation for medical video?

Live action for people, places and reassurance. Animation for what happens inside the body. If you need to show how a joint replacement sits, how a drug acts or what a scan is looking for, medical animation is clearer and more accurate than anything a camera can do, and that's specialist work we don't make. Healthtech products are usually best shown with screen recordings, with your clinicians and team on camera for the why. I've written about when graphics earn their place.

What does it cost, and what goes wrong?

As UK market ranges, not quotes from us: under £2,000 for a freelancer's day of interviews, £2,000 to £8,000 for a small production company's interview-led film with cut-downs, £8,000 to £30,000 for documentary films with research and several shoot days. Healthcare shoots often run around clinic hours and infection control, so allow for an early start or a closed day. Briefing your team before the shoot saves a lot of trouble.

The common mistakes: stock doctors with stethoscopes, claims that outrun the evidence, patient details visible in the background, and filming patients who felt they couldn't say no. If you'd like to plan a film properly, get in touch.
items.author: Earl Duncan

faqs.q: Can we film patients in the background of a clinic film?
faqs.a: It's best to avoid it. Someone visible in a clinic waiting room is revealing something about their health just by being there, and they haven't agreed to appear. Film in closed hours, use staff, or frame shots so nobody else is identifiable. If anyone recognisable does appear, you'd need their consent. This is general guidance, so check with your data protection lead.

faqs.q: Do staff need to sign a release to appear in a healthcare video?
faqs.a: It's good practice, yes. Staff are people with their own data rights, and appearing in marketing isn't automatically part of their job. Explain how the film will be used, get written agreement, and let anyone who'd rather not appear stay out of shot without it being held against them. Agree what happens to the film if they leave.

faqs.q: Can a private clinic use before-and-after footage?
faqs.a: Often, but carefully. Before-and-after images and video must be genuine, not altered to exaggerate the result, and representative of what patients can expect. You'll need the patient's written consent, and the claims involved need evidence like any other. Check the advertising code's rules on health claims and, for aesthetics, the rules on prescription-only medicines before you publish.

faqs.q: Should a care home film its residents?
faqs.a: It can, and families often value it most, but it needs real care. Some residents can't give consent themselves, so follow your policies on capacity and involve families where appropriate. Film ordinary daily life with dignity, avoid anything a resident might find embarrassing, and make it easy for anyone to stay out of the film. General guidance only.

stat.title: Who people in Britain trust to tell the truth
stat.takeaway: Your clinicians are some of the most trusted people in the country, so let them speak on camera rather than a voiceover.

source.name: Ipsos, Veracity Index 2025 (1,022 British adults, 5 to 11 November 2025)

items.title: Social media videos for business: what works
items.excerpt: What social media videos are for a business, which types work, how long they should be, how to keep them going every week, and the mistakes that waste a shoot.
items.coverAlt: Coaches and teammates shouting from the corner at a jiu-jitsu event
items.body:
Social media videos are short videos made to be watched in a feed: Instagram Reels, TikTok, YouTube Shorts, LinkedIn and Facebook. For a business they're mostly vertical, mostly under a minute, made to make sense with the sound off, and posted regularly rather than once. Nobody's paying to put them in front of people, so each one has to stop a scroll on its own merits. The businesses that do well with them usually show the real work, often, and don't overthink each post.

What kinds of social video work for a business?

Most of what works falls into a handful of types:

  • The work happening. A job from start to finish, a process, the satisfying bit.
  • One thing explained. A question customers ask all the time, answered in under a minute.
  • The people. Who does the work, in their own words.
  • A customer story, cut down from a longer film.
  • Behind the scenes. The bits a customer never normally sees.
  • A reveal. Before and after, what we found, how it turned out.

Which ones suit you depends on the business. A trade with a satisfying visual process has it easy. A consultancy has to lean on people and explanation. Either can work.

Why does vertical matter so much?

Because that's how people are holding the screen. Most time online now happens on a phone, and the feed formats on the big platforms are built around the vertical frame. A horizontal film dropped into a vertical feed sits as a small letterbox with empty space around it, and it looks like what it is: something made for somewhere else.

That doesn't mean everything has to be shot vertical. It means the vertical versions need planning at the shoot, with framing that leaves room to crop, or separate vertical setups for the shots that matter.

How long should social media videos be?

Most land between fifteen and sixty seconds. Quick hooks and reveals sit at the short end. Explanations and stories need more. The honest rule is that a video can be as long as it stays interesting, and most business videos stop being interesting sooner than their makers think. The platforms do allow longer videos, and some topics earn it, but the first three seconds decide whether anyone gets to the rest.

How do you keep it going every week?

By batching. The businesses that post consistently aren't filming every day. They capture a lot in one go and cut it into many pieces.

For Super Efficient, one day on a drainage job in Enfield fed an eight minute YouTube film, a run of vertical shorts and two carousels. Each short was given a different job: the satisfying clear, the reveal, natural sound with no music, the education piece and the commercial one. The captions were written separately for homeowners and for commercial property, because they're not the same buyer even when the footage is.

For two grappling competitions, the vertical reels were built per fight and per fighter, hooked in the first three seconds and finished on the hero moment, so competitors would share them themselves.

The training content we shot with Isaac Chamberlain for Boxraw is a good example of the work itself being the content. It was filmed around a real session rather than staged, because a boxer mid-session isn't a model, and interrupting to reset a shot breaks the thing you came to film. Then it was cut for the brand's social channels.

What are the common mistakes?

  • Posting the whole brand film. Cut it down. Nobody watches five minutes in a feed they're scrolling past.
  • Music on everything. Sometimes the real sound is the hook. The jetter and the water on the Super Efficient shorts were left alone for that reason.
  • No captions. Plenty of people watch with the sound off.
  • Chasing trends that don't fit. A dance trend from a drainage firm is a brave choice.
  • A burst then silence. Ten posts in a week and nothing for two months does more harm than a steady one a week.
  • Judging it on one post. Social builds over months. One video rarely tells you much.

If a post does well on its own, it's often the best candidate for paid promotion, which works differently and is covered in brand video ads for social and online.

The businesses that post consistently aren't filming every day. They capture a lot in one go and cut it into many pieces.

Every content day, someone asks if we can do a trend. I always ask which one, and the answer's always the one that finished last week.

Do you need a production company, or is a phone enough?

For a lot of everyday social content, a phone is genuinely enough if the sound and light are sorted. I've written a full post on when phone video is enough. Where professional help earns its money is in planning a content day so it feeds weeks of posts, in sound that holds up, in the editing, and in the time it frees up for you to run the business.

What does social media video cost?

Our free playbook, Before the camera comes out, puts the under £2,000 band, a freelancer, a day or less on site and a short edit, as fine for social content. That's a typical UK market range, not a quote. Vertical cut-downs from existing footage typically run £150 to £600 each, depending on whether they're just reframed or rebuilt with a new structure and captions.

Ours are content days and monthly partnerships, priced on the same one-shoot, many-outputs idea. If you want help keeping a feed going without losing days to it, get in touch.
items.author: Earl Duncan

faqs.q: How often should a business post video on social media?
faqs.a: As often as you can keep up for months, not weeks. For most small businesses that's one to three videos a week. Consistency matters more than volume, because a steady rhythm builds an audience that expects you, while bursts followed by silence tend to reset everything. Batching your filming makes a regular schedule far easier to hold.

faqs.q: Should the business owner be on camera?
faqs.a: It usually helps, because people buy from people, and an owner who's comfortable talking about the work is hard to beat. It doesn't have to be every video. Staff, customers and the work itself can carry plenty of posts. If the owner is nervous, start with them talking while working rather than straight to camera.

faqs.q: Do we need different videos for each platform?
faqs.a: Not entirely different, but adjusted. The same vertical edit can often run on Reels, TikTok and Shorts, with captions and text placed to avoid each app's buttons. LinkedIn audiences tend to accept slightly longer, more explanatory videos, and YouTube rewards longer horizontal videos alongside Shorts. Write the caption separately for each.

faqs.q: What should we do if a social video gets no views?
faqs.a: Look at the first three seconds before anything else, because that's where most videos lose people. Then check the length, captions and whether the topic is something your audience actually cares about. One quiet video tells you very little. Look for patterns across ten or twenty posts and do more of what keeps people watching.

items.title: Video for insurers: show the people behind the policy
items.excerpt: What insurance customers need to see in a video, FCA and consent points in general terms, six film ideas for insurers and brokers, and when animation is better.
items.coverAlt: A couple at home after moving house, filmed for a brand
items.body:
Insurance buyers want proof that someone will be there when they claim. A good insurance video shows the people who actually handle claims, customers who've been through one, and plain explanations of what's covered, all within FCA rules that say communications must be fair, clear and not misleading. Insurers, brokers and MGAs all sell a promise that only gets tested later, and film is one of the few ways to show it before then.

Below: what customers need to see, the rules and sensitivities in general terms, film ideas, which formats suit insurance, and what it costs. The regulatory section is general guidance, not compliance advice.

What do insurance customers need to see?

People, mostly. Insurance is a product nobody wants to use, bought from companies people tend not to trust. The FCA's Financial Lives survey found insurance companies were the least trusted kind of financial institution. But people trusted their own insurer far more than insurers in general, which tells you something useful. Trust grows from contact with a real organisation and real people, and video is a way of giving people that contact before they need it.

What that means in a film:

  • The claims people. Who answers the phone when a pipe bursts at midnight, and how they talk.
  • What happens when you claim. The steps, roughly what's needed, what people can expect.
  • Honesty about cover. What a policy is for, and where it stops.
  • Expertise, for brokers. A commercial broker sells knowledge of a client's sector. Showing them on a client's site, understanding the business, says more than a list of specialisms.

What rules and sensitivities apply to insurance video?

General guidance based on UK rules. Insurance distribution is regulated by the FCA, and the core standard for communications and financial promotions is that they must be fair, clear and not misleading. The Consumer Duty also expects firms to communicate in a way customers can understand. On camera, that tends to mean:

  • No implied guarantees. One happy claim story can suggest every claim gets paid, quickly. Keep the edit honest about what was true for that customer.
  • Speed claims need evidence. If someone says "paid in a week", it has to be true and not presented as typical unless it is.
  • Cover described accurately. A film that makes a policy sound broader than its wording is a complaint waiting to happen.
  • Care with claimants. People who've claimed have often been through a fire, a flood, a crash, an illness or a death. Consent needs to be informed and unhurried, and anyone who might be vulnerable needs extra care.
  • Personal data. Claim details are personal data, and for life, health and protection products they may include health information, which gets extra protection under UK GDPR. Agree what can be said before the camera rolls.

A sensible rule of thumb is to film claim stories only once the claim's settled, with the customer's written agreement and compliance involved from the questions stage.

Nobody has ever finished an insurance advert and thought, now I'd love to read the policy wording. Make the film do the explaining.

What films work for insurers and brokers?

  1. A claim story, told by the customer. What happened, who helped, what it felt like. With consent and after settlement, this is the most persuasive film an insurer can make.
  2. Meet the claims team. Handlers and loss adjusters talking about the job. Most customers have never pictured the person on the other end.
  3. What happens when you claim. A calm, practical process film that sits on the claims page and gets sent to people at the worst moment of their year.
  4. The broker who knows your trade. A commercial broker filmed with a client in their workplace, a kitchen, a workshop, a site, talking through risks in that client's language.
  5. Risk advice for commercial clients. Short films from your risk specialists on preventing the common losses in a sector. Useful enough that clients share them.
  6. Recruitment. Claims and underwriting roles are hard to picture from outside. Let people who do them explain.

Which video types suit insurance?

Documentary-style live action for claims stories and people, because it's believable. Our post on testimonial videos that don't sound like testimonials goes into how to film customers so they sound like themselves.

Emotional, scripted advertising has a place too. Thai Life Insurance's Unsung Hero is a well known example: a three minute story about a young man doing small kindnesses every day, with the insurer only appearing at the very end. It's scripted with actors, which is a different job to what we do, but it shows that insurance films work best when they're about life rather than the policy.

And be honest about animation. Explaining an excess, how no claims discount works or the difference between buildings and contents cover is often clearer with simple motion graphics than with anyone talking. We don't make animation, but we'd happily tell you when it's the right tool.

Insurance sells a promise that only gets tested later. Film is one of the few ways to show it before then.

How much does an insurance video cost, and how is it made?

As UK market ranges, not quotes from us: under £2,000 for a freelancer's day of simple interviews, £2,000 to £8,000 for a small production company's interview-led film with cut-downs, and £8,000 to £30,000 for documentary films with research, several shoot days and a full set of cuts.

The hidden cost in insurance is time rather than money. Finding customers who'll talk about a claim takes weeks, consent and compliance add steps, and a claims story often means filming in someone's home. Start the search for willing customers early, ideally through your claims team, who know who had a good experience. Setting a budget first makes the rest easier.

What mistakes do insurers make with video?

  • Stock happy families on sofas. Every insurer has them, so they say nothing.
  • Actors playing claimants without saying so. It feels hollow, and it can mislead.
  • Filming before a claim is settled. Things can change, and so can the customer's feelings.
  • Overselling speed or cover. It'll come back as a complaint.
  • Making one film and stopping. A claims story can feed social, email and the claims page for a year. Here's how one film becomes a year of content.

If you'd like to talk through a film, get in touch, or read our free guide Before the camera comes out first.
items.author: Earl Duncan

faqs.q: Can we film a customer while their claim is still open?
faqs.a: It's usually better to wait until the claim's settled. An open claim can change, and filming during it can feel like pressure on someone who's already stressed. Once it's settled, the customer can decide freely and speak with hindsight, which makes for a better film anyway. Get written consent and involve compliance before filming. This is general guidance, not compliance advice.

faqs.q: Should insurance brokers make their own videos?
faqs.a: Yes, especially commercial brokers. What a broker sells is judgement and knowledge of a client's sector, and that's hard to show in text and easy to show on film. A broker walking a client's site and talking through risks in plain language does more than any list of specialisms. Short risk-advice clips also give clients something genuinely useful to share.

faqs.q: Do we need to show the small print in a video?
faqs.a: A film doesn't need to recite the policy wording, but it mustn't give a misleading impression of the cover. If a film describes what a policy does, it should be accurate, and where significant limits apply, viewers shouldn't come away thinking they don't. Point people to the policy documents for detail. Your compliance team should review any film that describes cover.

faqs.q: How do we find customers willing to be filmed?
faqs.a: Ask your claims team. They know who had a good experience and who might be glad to talk about it. Approach people gently, explain exactly where the film will be used, and make it easy to say no. Give them time to decide. A small thank you is fine, but be careful that payment doesn't shape what they say, and be open about it where required.

Low trust in insurance companies in general
High trust in their own contents insurance provider

stat.takeaway: People trust the insurer they know far more than insurers in general, so letting customers meet your actual people on film is worth the effort.
