items.title: Brand video ads for social and online, explained
items.excerpt: What brand video ads are, when paid video is worth it, what goes in an ad that stops a scroll, lengths and formats, UK ad rules, and what drives the cost.
items.coverAlt: A woman talking to camera outdoors in a brand film
items.body:
A brand video ad is a short video you pay to put in front of people, on YouTube, Meta's apps, TikTok, LinkedIn or across websites and streaming services. Unlike a film on your own website, it turns up uninvited, so it has to earn attention in the first second or two, make sense with the sound off, and give the viewer one clear thing to do. Get those three right and a modest budget can work hard. Get them wrong and you're paying to be scrolled past.

How is a video ad different from organic social video?

Organic video reaches the people who already follow you, plus whoever the platform decides to show it to. An ad reaches exactly who you pay to reach: by location, age, interests, job title or people who've visited your website. That targeting is the whole point, and it changes how you make the video. An ad can be aimed at a cold audience who's never heard of you, or at warm people who've already watched something and need a nudge. Those are two different videos.

The creative rules overlap with social media video, but an ad has to work harder, because nobody chose to watch it.

When is paid video worth it?

When three things are in place. There's something specific to sell or sign up for. There's a landing page that does its job once someone clicks. And you've got creative good enough that people would watch it even if it weren't paid. Paying to push a weak video just shows a weak video to more people.

The Christmas raffle we made with Plug In Stations and Ohme is a good example of an ad with a clear job. It was built as a Facebook ad rather than an organic post, with a golden ticket download as the reason to complete the form, because a giveaway that collects likes from people who only want the free thing is money wasted. It brought in a thousand entries and two paid installs on top of the two winners.

What goes into a video ad that works?

  • A first second worth stopping for. Movement, a face, a question on screen, something happening. Not a logo.
  • Captions burned in. Assume the sound's off until proven otherwise.
  • One message. The single thing you want remembered.
  • The brand visible early, in the product, on a van, on a uniform, so people know who it's from even if they leave at five seconds.
  • One call to action, matched to what happens after the click.
  • Several versions. Different hooks and lengths, so the numbers can tell you which works.

Real people help here as well. Ads that look like real footage of real customers or real work tend to sit more naturally in a feed than polished studio work. That's the thinking behind UGC, and behind most of what we make.

How long should a video ad be, and in what shape?

Short, and in more than one shape. As a rough guide:

  • Six seconds for YouTube bumper ads and quick reminders. One image, one line.
  • Fifteen seconds for most feed and story placements.
  • Thirty to sixty seconds for warmer audiences who already know you.
  • Longer only for in-stream placements where the viewer can skip, and you've earned it.

For shapes, vertical 9:16 for stories, Reels, Shorts and TikTok, 4:5 or 1:1 for feeds, and 16:9 for YouTube and websites. The Fifth Gear sponsorship for Easee needed idents at five, ten and fifteen seconds that could land the brand before anyone decided whether to look up, and survive being seen dozens of times without becoming irritating. That second problem is real for any ad that runs for weeks.

What rules apply to video ads in the UK?

Online ads in the UK fall under the CAP Code, which the Advertising Standards Authority enforces. In plain terms, ads mustn't mislead, claims need evidence you can produce if challenged, and there are extra rules for things like health, finance, children and comparisons with competitors. If an influencer or creator is paid to post, it has to be clear that it's an ad. This is general guidance rather than legal advice, so check the ASA's own resources or a specialist for anything borderline.

The other rule worth knowing is music. Library tracks often have separate licences for paid advertising, and a track that's fine on your website may not be cleared for a paid campaign.

What are the common mistakes?

  • A TV-style ad shrunk onto a phone, with the important bit in the middle of a horizontal frame
  • Five seconds of logo before anything happens
  • No captions
  • One version, run until it stops working, with nothing to replace it
  • Sending clicks to the home page instead of a page about the offer
  • Judging it on views when the goal was enquiries
Paying to push a weak video just shows a weak video to more people.

The algorithm doesn't care how much the shoot cost. It cares whether somebody stopped scrolling.

How are video ads made, and what do they cost?

There are two separate costs: making the ads, and the media spend to show them. Keep them apart in your head and in the budget.

Making them follows the usual market ranges, which we list in our free playbook Before the camera comes out. They're typical UK market ranges, not quotes. A simple ad from a freelancer can sit under £2,000. A small production company with one or two shoot days and a handful of versions usually lands between £2,000 and £8,000. Agency-led campaigns with cast, art direction and broadcast advertising start at around £30,000. The cheapest route to lots of versions is shooting once and cutting many times, at roughly £150 to £600 per extra cut. Our guide to turning one film into a year of content covers how to plan for that at the shoot.

Media spend is entirely separate and set by you. Even a small test budget across a few versions tells you more than any amount of guessing.

We make the footage. Where a client wants ads run, that's managed by a specialist, and the spend is always paid separately. If you've got something worth putting money behind, tell us what it is.
items.author: Earl Duncan

faqs.q: How much should we spend on video ads?
faqs.a: Start with a test budget you're comfortable losing while you learn, spread across two to four versions of the ad, and run it long enough to get a meaningful number of clicks or leads. Once one version clearly outperforms the others, put more behind it. There's no universal figure, because costs vary a lot by platform, audience and how competitive your sector is.

faqs.q: Can we turn our brand film into ads?
faqs.a: Yes, and it's one of the most efficient routes. The strongest moments from the interview and the most visual shots can be recut into short vertical and square versions with a new hook at the start and captions throughout. It works best when the cut-downs were planned at the shoot, so there's enough footage framed for vertical and enough short, self-contained lines.

faqs.q: Which platform is best for B2B video ads?
faqs.a: LinkedIn is the obvious one, because you can target by job title, industry and company size, though it's usually more expensive per click. YouTube can work well for search-led audiences, and Meta can be surprisingly effective for business owners of smaller firms. Test a small budget on two platforms and let the cost per lead decide.

faqs.q: How often should we refresh video ads?
faqs.a: When performance drops, which happens as the same audience sees the same ad repeatedly. For a small audience that can be a few weeks. For a broad one it can be months. Having several versions ready from the start makes this easy, because you can rotate a new hook in rather than commissioning a whole new ad every time.

Share of all UK digital ad spend that went on video

stat.takeaway: Video is where a growing share of UK ad money goes, so the feed your ad lands in is more crowded every year and the first second matters more.

items.title: Financial services video: earning trust on camera
items.excerpt: What financial services and fintech video needs to show, FCA financial promotion rules in general terms, six film ideas and why every cut-down needs sign-off.
items.coverAlt: An engineer in hi-vis working on street equipment
items.body:
Financial services and fintech video has one main job: helping people trust you with their money. That means showing the real people behind the firm or the app, explaining things in plain English, and staying inside the FCA's rules on financial promotions, which apply to a video in the same way they apply to a print advert. Get those three right and a film does a lot of the slow trust-building work that adverts can't.

Below is what buyers need to see, the regulatory points in general terms, film ideas for advisers, wealth firms and fintechs, and what drives the cost. The regulation section is general guidance, not compliance advice. Your compliance team, or whoever approves your promotions, decides.

What do people need to see before trusting a financial firm?

Proof that there are capable, decent people behind the numbers. The FCA's own research shows how low the starting point is. In its Financial Lives survey, fewer than four in ten UK adults said they had confidence in the financial services industry.

That shapes what a film needs to show. For an adviser or wealth manager, the product is the relationship, so the client wants to meet the person and hear how they think. For a fintech, the product's an app, and the worry is the opposite: is there anyone there at all? For a B2B fintech selling to finance teams, buyers want to see the people running operations and the care they take.

  • Faces and names. Who founded it, who runs it, who picks up when something goes wrong.
  • Plain explanations. What the product does, in words a non-specialist can follow.
  • Customers like them. Real people describing the experience, handled carefully (more on that below).
  • A sense of steadiness. Nobody wants their pension handled by a firm that seems excitable.

What rules apply to financial promotion videos?

General guidance only, based on the FCA's published rules for the UK. If you're regulated, the core standard is in COBS 4.2.1R: a communication or financial promotion must be fair, clear and not misleading. The FCA is media neutral, so a ninety second film and a fifteen second vertical clip count just as much as a brochure.

  • Who can communicate it. Under the financial promotion restriction, an unauthorised business generally needs its promotions approved by an authorised firm with the right permission. The FCA's financial promotions pages set out the gateway for approvers.
  • Balance. Benefits and risks need to be presented fairly, and any required risk warning has to be prominent. On screen that means readable, and on long enough to read.
  • Social media. The FCA's guidance on financial promotions on social media applies the same standards to posts and clips, and warns that influencers promoting regulated products without approval may be committing a criminal offence.
  • Consumer understanding. The Consumer Duty expects firms to communicate in a way customers can actually understand, which is a decent brief for any film anyway.
  • Testimonials and past performance. A happy client talking about returns is a claim. Treat it like one.

The practical point people miss is the cut-downs. Every vertical edit and every fifteen second clip is a promotion in its own right. If the risk warning lives at the end of the main film and the short version stops before it, you've made a non-compliant ad from a compliant one. Plan sign-off for every cut, not just the hero film.

Every financial film reaches the moment where compliance asks for the risk warning to be bigger. They're usually right, annoyingly.

What films work for financial services and fintech?

  1. The founder or adviser film. Why the firm exists and how it thinks, told by the person who started it. Interview-led, unscripted, filmed where they actually work.
  2. The people behind the app. For fintechs, the support team, the engineers and the person checking for fraud. It answers the "is anyone there?" question without a word of marketing copy.
  3. Customer stories. Real customers on what changed for them, with consent, compliance review and no promise that results will repeat. Our post on testimonials people believe covers the approach.
  4. Plain-English explainers. Your own experts explaining one topic at a time: what a pension transfer involves, how a business loan is assessed. General information, clearly labelled.
  5. B2B case studies. A client's finance lead explaining why they chose you and how the switch went, which is what other finance leads want to hear.
  6. Recruitment films. Financial firms compete for the same people. Honest staff voices help.

Which video types suit financial services?

Live action interviews for anything about trust and people. That's where we work, and it's where the sector's usually weakest, because so much financial marketing hides behind skylines and handshakes.

For how a product works, be honest about the tool. How interest compounds, how a payment moves between banks, how a fund is structured: animation and motion graphics usually explain these more clearly than a person talking, and that's not something we make. For app walkthroughs, a clean screen recording beats filming a phone in someone's hand. The strongest results usually mix them, with a real person for the reasons and graphics for the mechanics. I'd steer clear of AI avatars presenting anything to do with money. Real people on camera matter most where trust is thin.

Every vertical edit and every fifteen second clip is a promotion in its own right.

How much does a financial services video cost?

As UK market ranges, not quotes from us: under £2,000 for a freelancer's day of talking heads, £2,000 to £8,000 for a small production company's interview-led film with cut-downs, and £8,000 to £30,000 for documentary-style brand films with research, several shoot days and a full set of cuts.

Financial work tends to cost a bit more time than money. Compliance review adds rounds, and every cut needs checking. Build that into the schedule from the start, and agree who signs off what before anything's filmed. The questions in how to write a video brief help here.

What mistakes do financial firms make with video?

  • Stock footage of city skylines. It tells people nothing about you, and they've seen it a thousand times.
  • Actors posing as customers without saying so. Beyond feeling hollow, it can mislead, which is the one thing the rules ask you not to do.
  • Risk warnings lost in the edit. Especially in vertical cut-downs.
  • Jargon. If your own experts can't explain it simply on camera, the edit can't fix it.
  • Forced fun. A light tone works for some fintechs. A light tone about risk doesn't.

If you're weighing up a film, our free guide Before the camera comes out covers planning, or get in touch.
items.author: Earl Duncan

faqs.q: Do fintech videos on social media count as financial promotions?
faqs.a: Often, yes. If a clip invites or encourages someone to engage in a regulated financial activity, it's likely to be a financial promotion, whatever the format or platform. The FCA's social media guidance applies the same fair, clear and not misleading standard to posts and short videos. This is general guidance only, so check each piece with your compliance team or approver.

faqs.q: Can we use real customers in a financial services video?
faqs.a: Yes, and they're usually the most convincing people you can put on camera. Get their written consent, be clear where the film will be used, and have compliance review what they say. Watch for anything that sounds like a promise of returns or suggests their result is typical. Customers talking about service, clarity and how they were treated are usually safer ground than performance.

faqs.q: Who signs off a financial promotion video?
faqs.a: For an authorised firm, usually its own compliance function, under its approval process for financial promotions. An unauthorised business generally needs an authorised firm with the right permission to approve it. Agree who signs off before the shoot, share the interview questions in advance, and plan review time for every cut, including vertical and short versions. This is general guidance, not regulatory advice.

faqs.q: Can we use actors instead of real customers?
faqs.a: You can use actors, but be careful how they're presented. If a viewer would reasonably think they're watching a genuine customer, that's likely to mislead. Many firms use actors for scenarios and label them clearly, and save testimony for real customers. Real staff and real customers tend to be more persuasive anyway, because viewers can usually tell when someone's performing.

items.title: Promotional videos: what makes one actually work
items.excerpt: What a promotional video is, how it differs from an advert, when it works, what goes in a good one, how long to make it, and what drives the cost in the UK.
items.coverAlt: Visitors at a brand stand at a trade show
items.body:
A promotional video is a short film made to get a particular person to do a particular thing: buy, book, sign up, enquire or turn up. It promotes something specific, a product, a service, a launch, an offer or an event, rather than the business in general. It works when it's about one thing, for one kind of viewer, and when it shows enough proof that the ask at the end feels reasonable.

It's a slightly baggy term, and people use it to mean anything from a launch film to a sales page video. That's fine. What they have in common is that they all end with a request.

What's the difference between a promotional video and an advert?

An advert is defined by where it runs: paid placement on TV, YouTube, Meta, TikTok or LinkedIn. A promotional video is defined by its job, and it can live in lots of places you don't pay for. A product page, a launch email, a screen on a trade stand, a link a salesperson sends after a call. The same film can do both, and often does, but a promotional video doesn't have to fight a thumb in a feed the way an ad does. I've covered paid placements in brand video ads for social and online.

When does a promotional video work?

When there's something real to promote and a clear moment to promote it. Product launches. A new service. An event with tickets to sell. A seasonal offer. A milestone the business can genuinely be proud of.

Timing matters as much as the film. When we covered two Fully Charged shows in the same year, the content from the South show was used to promote the North one, which meant the real deadline wasn't the end of the edit. It was the start of ticket sales for the next show.

It works less well when the business is trying to promote everything at once, or when nobody's yet sure what the offer is. A film can't fix a muddled offer. It just makes the muddle more expensive.

What goes into a good promotional video?

Most good ones follow roughly the same shape, even when they look nothing alike:

  1. A hook in the first few seconds. A moment, a problem or a person the viewer recognises.
  2. The thing itself, shown working, in use, or in the hands of someone who uses it.
  3. Proof. A customer, a demonstration, a number you can stand behind.
  4. The offer, said plainly.
  5. The ask. One action, with the place to do it.

Starting with the person rather than the product is often what makes the difference. The three films we made for Easee were each built around a moment that actually triggers a charger purchase: moving house, passing your test, being a landlord with a grant to claim. The charger follows the life event, because nobody wakes up wanting a charge point.

The video Dollar Shave Club launched with in 2012 is still the example people point to, and for good reason. One product, one founder walking through his own warehouse talking straight to camera, every claim landed with a joke, and an offer at the end that's impossible to misunderstand. It's a scripted comedy piece, which isn't how we work, but the structure underneath it is exactly the five steps above.

How long should a promotional video be?

  • Paid social and feeds: fifteen to thirty seconds, with the point made in the first three.
  • Launch films and web headers: sixty to ninety seconds.
  • Product or sales pages: up to two or three minutes, because someone who's on that page is already interested.

Make the longest version first and cut down from it. Building a long film out of a thirty second ad rarely works.

Where do promotional videos get used?

The landing page for the offer, the launch email, social posts and stories, paid ads if there's budget, sales follow-ups, event screens and partner channels. If a distributor or partner is going to share it, give them a version without your own call to action in it, or with theirs. There's a fuller list in where to put your film once it's made.

What are the common mistakes?

  • Listing features. Ten features in sixty seconds and the viewer remembers none of them.
  • A long logo sting up front. The first three seconds are the most valuable in the film. Don't spend them on an animation of your logo.
  • No ask, or three asks. Pick one.
  • Baking in a date or price. Make a version without the date so the film keeps working after the offer ends.
  • One cut for every platform. A horizontal film squashed into a vertical feed looks like an afterthought.
  • Music that drowns the voice. If someone's speaking, they win.

Every promotional video brief I've seen wants it to go viral. I'd settle for the right two hundred people watching it to the end.

A film can't fix a muddled offer. It just makes the muddle more expensive.

How is a promotional video made, and what does it cost?

Brief, script or interview plan, a shoot, an edit, then the versions. Promotional films are more often scripted than our documentary work, though the most convincing ones I see still lean on real customers and real use rather than actors.

On cost, the typical UK market ranges in our free playbook, Before the camera comes out, are a useful starting point. They're market ranges, not quotes. A simple promotional piece from a freelancer in a day can come in under £2,000. One or two shoot days with a small production company and a few cut-downs usually lands between £2,000 and £8,000. Scripted work with cast, art direction or built sets runs from £30,000 up.

The lines that move it most are shoot days, crew, locations (studios typically £400 to £2,000 or more a day), motion graphics (£200 to £1,500 or more), music, and the number of cut-downs at £150 to £600 each. A commercial music track runs into thousands, and library licences don't always cover paid ads, which I've explained in music licensing for brand videos. To rough out your own numbers, try the film budget calculator.

If the thing you're promoting has a real story behind it, a founder, a craft, a customer whose life changed, that's where we come in. Tell us about it.
items.author: Earl Duncan

faqs.q: Should a promotional video be scripted?
faqs.a: It can be, and short promotional pieces often are. Scripts work best when the people delivering them are actors or comfortable presenters. If your own team or customers are on camera, an interview with good questions usually sounds more natural, and you can still plan the structure and the key lines you need to get from them before the shoot.

faqs.q: Can we reuse footage from an older film in a promotional video?
faqs.a: Usually, yes, as long as you own or have a licence for that footage, the music is cleared for the new use, and anyone on camera agreed to appear in marketing. Check whether your original contract gave you the right to re-edit the footage. Mixing old and new material works best when the colour and framing are matched in the edit.

faqs.q: Do promotional videos need subtitles?
faqs.a: Yes, in almost every case. A lot of video is watched with the sound off, especially in feeds and offices, and subtitles help people who are deaf or hard of hearing. Burned-in captions suit social platforms, while a separate caption file suits YouTube and your website. Proofread them, because automatic captions often get names and technical words wrong.

faqs.q: How do we know if a promotional video worked?
faqs.a: Decide what it was meant to do before it goes out, then measure that. If it was meant to sell tickets, track tickets sold from the page it sits on. If it was meant to drive enquiries, count enquiries and ask new leads where they heard about you. Views are a useful signal, but they aren't the result you paid for.

items.title: Video for law firms: what clients need to see
items.excerpt: What clients want to see in a law firm video before they call, the SRA publicity rules in general terms, six film ideas for legal practices and what they cost.
items.coverAlt: Two people shaking hands at a front door
items.body:
Clients choosing a law firm want to see who'll actually handle their matter, how that person talks, and what happens after they pick up the phone. A good law firm video shows real solicitors explaining things plainly, in their own offices, without a script. It also has to be accurate about fees and outcomes, because the SRA expects your publicity to be accurate and not misleading, and a film is publicity.

The regulatory part below is general guidance, not legal advice, which I realise is an odd thing to tell a law firm. Your compliance officer has the final word.

What do clients need to see before they choose a law firm?

Most people come to a solicitor at a bad moment. A divorce, a death in the family, a dismissal, a house purchase that's wobbling. They're anxious, often out of their depth, and they're trying to work out one thing above everything else: will this person look after me?

A website full of practice areas and a stock photo of a gavel can't answer that. Video can, because it shows the things people judge without realising they're judging them. Tone of voice. Whether the solicitor explains a term or assumes you know it. Whether they look at you or at their notes. In practice, clients want to see:

  • The actual people. The solicitor they'd be dealing with, not only the senior partner who'll never see their file.
  • Plain English. Someone who can explain a process without hiding behind it.
  • What happens next. The first meeting, roughly how long things take, how they'll be kept updated.
  • Some sense of how you charge. Not a quote, but enough that the cost doesn't feel like a trap.
  • Calm. A grieving family or a frightened employee wants to feel the temperature drop a little while they watch.

The best legal films feel like a first meeting that went well.

The best legal films feel like a first meeting that went well.

What rules apply to law firm marketing videos?

This is general guidance based on the SRA's published rules for firms in England and Wales. It isn't legal advice, and if you're regulated by someone else, the Law Society of Scotland or the Bar Standards Board for example, check your own regulator's rules.

The SRA Code of Conduct for Solicitors says any publicity about your practice must be accurate and not misleading, including anything about your charges. The usual traps all apply on camera:

  • Results. A client story can imply every case ends that way without anyone saying it. Past outcomes don't predict the next one, so the edit shouldn't suggest they do.
  • Fees. If a film mentions price, it has to match what you actually charge. The SRA's Transparency Rules already require price and service information on your website for certain services, such as residential conveyancing, probate and some employment matters, so keep the film consistent with that page.
  • Information that sounds like advice. A short "your rights at work" explainer is useful marketing. Make it clear it's general information and that everyone's situation is different.
  • Confidentiality. A client's affairs stay confidential unless they agree otherwise. A client story needs their informed, written agreement, and even then you'd keep out anything that identifies the other side or details they haven't cleared.
  • Unsolicited approaches. The Code bars unsolicited approaches to members of the public to advertise your services, current and former clients aside. A film on your website or on a channel people choose to follow is a different thing, but how you push it out is worth a quick check with compliance.

None of this is hard. It just means compliance sees the interview questions before the shoot and the cut before it goes live, rather than afterwards.

Lawyers make good interviewees. They're used to being asked questions. They're less used to being asked how something felt.

What films work well for law firms?

  1. Meet the solicitors clients actually deal with. Short profiles of the solicitors clients actually deal with, filmed in their own office, talking about why they do this kind of work and what they wish clients knew at the start. They work quietly on the team page and in follow-up emails.
  2. What happens at your first meeting. What to bring, what you'll be asked, how the fee conversation works. It answers the questions people are too embarrassed to ring up and ask.
  3. Short answers to common questions. A run of one-minute clips, each answering one thing people genuinely search for: how long probate takes, what happens if there's no will, whether you need a solicitor for a settlement agreement. General, clearly labelled, and useful for months.
  4. A client's own account. Where a client's willing and the matter allows it, someone explaining in their own words what it was like. It's the most persuasive film a firm can make, and needs the most care. More on that in testimonial videos that don't sound like testimonials.
  5. Trainee and recruitment films. Firms compete hard for good people. Current trainees and associates talking honestly about the work will beat a careers brochure.
  6. Community and pro bono work. If the firm runs free advice clinics or does long-standing local work, filming it shows character without anyone having to claim it.

Which video types suit a legal practice?

Interview-led live action does most of the heavy lifting, because what you're selling is people and judgement. The documentary approach suits it: real solicitors, no autocue, questions they answer in their own words. I've written about how that differs from a standard corporate video, and why viewers believe it more.

There's an honest exception. Some legal processes are easier to follow as a diagram: the stages of a conveyancing transaction, the order things happen in probate, how a claim moves through a tribunal. Simple animation or motion graphics will explain a sequence more clearly than a person describing it, and that's not something we make. A good combination is a solicitor on camera for the reassurance, with a few clean graphics for the steps.

A partner answering a topical question on LinkedIn doesn't need a crew. Sometimes a phone is enough.

How much does a law firm video cost?

It depends what you're making, and the UK market is wide. As rough market ranges, not quotes from us: a simple talking-head set filmed by a freelancer in a day can come in under £2,000. A small production company making a proper interview-led film with a couple of cut-downs typically sits between £2,000 and £8,000, which is where most corporate video lands. Documentary-style brand films with research, several shoot days and a full set of cuts generally run from £8,000 to £30,000.

The cheapest way to get a lot is to film several things at once. One well planned day can give you several profiles, a first-meeting film and some short answers. Our film budget calculator shows where the money goes.

What mistakes do law firms make with video?

  • Filming only the senior partner. They may be the face of the firm, but they're rarely who the client deals with day to day.
  • Scripts and autocue. Solicitors reading prepared words sound like they're reading a disclaimer. Let them talk, then edit.
  • Leaving compliance until the end. A late note can mean a reshoot. Bring them in at the questions stage.
  • No plan for where it goes. A film that lives only on the About page barely gets watched. Where to put it once it's made covers the options.

If you'd like to plan one properly, our free guide Before the camera comes out walks through the whole process, or get in touch and tell us what you're working on.
items.author: Earl Duncan

faqs.q: Can a solicitor give legal advice in a marketing video?
faqs.a: It's safer to give general information than advice. A short film explaining how probate usually works is helpful and good marketing. Advice depends on someone's facts, which a video can't know. Say on screen or in the caption that it's general information and that people should speak to a solicitor about their own situation. As always, this is general guidance and your compliance officer should check it.

faqs.q: Do we need a client's permission to mention their case on camera?
faqs.a: Yes. A client's affairs are confidential, so you'd need their clear, informed agreement, ideally in writing, before their matter appears in any film. Even with that agreement, keep out details that could identify other parties or that the client hasn't specifically cleared. Many firms find it easier to film clients talking about the experience of working with them rather than the legal detail.

faqs.q: How long should a law firm video be?
faqs.a: Shorter than most firms expect. A solicitor profile works at around sixty to ninety seconds, a process film at two to three minutes, and a short answer clip at a minute or less. A longer firm film can work on your website if it holds attention. Our post on how long a brand film should be goes into the detail of picking a length for each place it'll be seen.

faqs.q: Should we put our fees in a video?
faqs.a: Only if the figures will stay accurate, because a film sticks around longer than a price list. If you do mention fees, they need to match what you actually charge and what your website says under the SRA Transparency Rules. Often it's better for the film to explain how you charge and point people to the price page, which you can update without reshooting anything.

items.title: Corporate videos: what they are and when they work
items.excerpt: What a corporate video is, the main kinds, what goes in a good one, how long it should be, the usual mistakes, and the UK market ranges that drive the cost.
items.coverAlt: A team lined up on their exhibition stand
items.body:
A corporate video is any film a business makes about itself for a business audience: who the company is, what it does, how it works, or something it needs staff, customers, partners or investors to understand. Company introductions, case studies, recruitment films, internal updates and project overviews all count. They work when they answer one question that one kind of viewer is already asking, and they fail when they try to answer everything for everyone.

The phrase has a bad reputation, and some of it's earned. Most people picture a managing director reading lines in front of a logo wall. That's a style, though, and you don't have to make that one. I've written separately about how a brand documentary differs from a corporate video. This post is the plain guide to the format itself.

What counts as a corporate video?

It's a broad label. The common kinds are:

  • Company introduction. Who you are, what you do, where you are. Usually for the website and sales material.
  • Case study. One project or one customer, told properly. Often the hardest working film a business owns.
  • Recruitment film. What it's actually like to work there, for people deciding whether to apply.
  • Internal and training films. Onboarding, safety, a new process, a message from leadership.
  • Project or milestone film. A big job finished, an anniversary, a number reached.
  • Investor or stakeholder film. Results, plans or a funding story for a small, specific audience.

What is a corporate video actually for?

One job per film. A company introduction exists so a stranger can work out in a minute or two whether you're the right kind of business for them. A case study exists so someone weighing up the same decision can see how it went for someone else. A recruitment film exists so the right people apply and the wrong ones don't.

The useful question before anything else is who's watching and what they're trying to decide. Sometimes the answer is surprising. On a communal charging project we filmed, the audience wasn't the buyer at all. It was residents, a freeholder and a managing agent who hadn't commissioned the work, so the video had to answer the questions residents ask before the works start, and be useful enough for the contractor to send ahead of a meeting.

What goes into a good corporate video?

The good ones share a few things, whatever the budget.

  • The right person speaking. Someone the viewer would actually deal with, or a customer who's already been through it. People believe a customer far more than a company talking about itself.
  • Proof shown, not claimed. If you say it's safe, show the test. If you say you're tidy, show the site.
  • The real place. Your workshop, your office, your site, running as normal.
  • Something specific. A number, a date, a problem that got solved. "Quality and service" is said by every company in every sector.
  • A clear next step. What the viewer should do once it's finished.

The proof point matters more than most people expect. For an installation case study at a car showroom in Poole, the installer ran a live RCD test on camera to demonstrate a safety feature rather than just describing it, because installers and specifiers don't take a product claim on trust.

This case study at Alpha Manufacturing is a corporate video in the plainest sense, made for Easee to use with commercial buyers. It was filmed on a working shop floor, with interviews recorded around live production and the people who make the parts talking about running the product themselves. Loud, lit for work rather than cameras, and far more convincing for it.

How long should a corporate video be?

As short as the job allows. Rough guides that hold up in practice:

  • Company introduction: sixty seconds to two minutes
  • Case study: two to four minutes, with a short cut for social
  • Recruitment: one to three minutes
  • Training: as long as the task needs, split into chapters if it runs long

There's more on judging length in how long a brand film should be. The short version is that a film is too long the moment the viewer has what they came for and it keeps going.

Where do corporate videos get used?

The website first, usually on the home page, the about page or the service page the film relates to. Then sales emails and proposals, LinkedIn, recruitment ads, screens at events and onboarding packs. The B Corp film we made for char.gy runs as the principal video on their About and Local Government pages, and it was cut eleven ways from one shoot so it works wherever they post. Planning those versions before the shoot is cheaper than inventing them afterwards.

What are the most common mistakes?

  • Making it for the board. Everyone internal signs it off, and nobody outside cares.
  • A script read by someone who isn't an actor. Even a good script sounds stiff when a non-actor reads it.
  • Trying to include everyone. Every department gets ten seconds and the film has no spine.
  • Claims with nothing behind them. Passionate, innovative, customer-focused. The viewer skips past the lot.
  • One version only. A four minute horizontal film doesn't work on a phone in a feed.
  • No subtitles. A lot of business video gets watched with the sound off.
A corporate video earns its keep when it answers one question a real viewer is already asking.

If your company film opens on a drone shot of the car park, I promise nobody chose you because of the car park.

How is a corporate video made, and what does it cost?

The process is the same shape for most of them: a brief, some planning, a shoot of usually one or two days, an edit, a round or two of changes, then the cut-downs. A clear brief saves more money than anything else on the list.

On cost, our free playbook Before the camera comes out lays out typical UK market ranges. They're market ranges, not quotes from us. Under £2,000 usually buys a freelancer, a day or less on site, an interview, some B-roll and a short edit, which is fine for simple talking heads. Between £2,000 and £8,000 you're typically looking at a small production company or experienced freelance team, one or two shoot days, a proper edit and a couple of cut-downs. Most corporate video sits in that band.

What moves the number within a band is mostly days and people. A camera operator typically runs £400 to £1,200 a day including basic kit, a sound recordist £350 to £650, an editor £300 to £600 a day, motion graphics such as titles and lower thirds £200 to £1,500 or more, and each extra cut-down £150 to £600. The film budget calculator adds those up for you.

We make the documentary end of this, built from real people and real places, which takes longer and does a different job. If you're not sure which you need, here's how our films work, or tell us what the video has to do and we'll say honestly whether it's us.
items.author: Earl Duncan

faqs.q: Is a corporate video the same as a brand film?
faqs.a: Not quite. A corporate video explains the company, usually in the company's own words, and is often scripted. A brand film, especially a documentary-style one, is built from real people telling their own story and is cut to make the viewer feel something as well as understand it. Plenty of films sit somewhere in between, and the right choice depends on what the viewer needs.

faqs.q: Should our managing director present the corporate video?
faqs.a: Only if they're comfortable on camera and the viewer would genuinely deal with them. A relaxed interview usually works far better than presenting to camera, because people speak naturally when they're answering questions. Customers and front-line staff are often more convincing than the person at the top, since viewers expect leaders to say good things about their own business.

faqs.q: How long does a corporate video take to make?
faqs.a: A simple corporate video usually takes three to six weeks from brief to finished film. That covers planning, booking a shoot date that suits everyone on camera, the edit and a round or two of changes. Approvals are often the slowest part, so agree up front who signs it off and how many rounds of feedback there'll be.

faqs.q: Can we use one corporate video for years?
faqs.a: Yes, if you keep it free of things that date quickly. Avoid naming prices, staff numbers, specific offers or people who might leave, and keep the music and graphics fairly plain. A film built around a customer story or the work itself usually lasts longer than one built around a product line or a team photo.

stat.title: Types of video marketers say they've made
stat.takeaway: Most businesses make several kinds of video, so give each one a single job instead of asking one film to do all of them.

items.title: What's in a documentary shooter's kit bag
items.excerpt: The kit categories for a one-person or small-crew brand film day: camera, lenses, audio, lights, support, power, media and the small bits that save shoots.
items.coverAlt: Earl in headphones filming an interview outside, camera on a tripod
items.body:
A documentary shooter's kit bag for a brand film day covers seven jobs: making the picture, recording the sound, lighting, holding things steady, powering everything, storing the footage safely, and a pile of small bits that save the day more often than anything expensive. Everything in it has to earn its place, because you carry it all, often up stairs, often on your own.

I'm not going to list models. They change every year, and the categories and the thinking behind them matter far more. This is what goes in, and why.

What camera kit do you need for a documentary shoot?

A camera body that records a high quality, flexible file. For brand films that usually means a cinema camera or a high-end hybrid that records in log, a flat profile that keeps detail in bright skies and dark corners for the grade. Good low light performance matters too, because documentary means filming in the light a place has, not the light you'd choose.

Alongside the body, most shooters carry:

  • ND filters. Sunglasses for the lens, so you can keep a wide aperture and a natural shutter speed in bright light. Some cameras have them built in.
  • A monitor. A bigger, brighter screen than the camera's own, useful for judging focus and exposure properly.
  • A cage or rig. A frame around the camera with mounting points for the monitor, the mic receiver and a handle.

A backup plan matters as much as the camera. That might be a second body, or simply knowing exactly what you'd do if the main one failed on the day.

Zooms or primes?

Both have a case. Zooms cover several focal lengths in one lens, so you can go from wide to close without changing anything. In documentary, where moments happen once and don't wait, that speed counts for a lot. Primes, fixed focal length lenses, tend to be smaller, sharper and better in low light, and they make you move your feet, which often gives better framing.

A common pattern is a versatile zoom that lives on the camera for most of the day, plus one or two fast primes for interviews, low light and close detail. Mixing focal lengths in the edit, wide for the place, mid for the conversation and close for the hands and the detail, is a big part of what makes a film feel considered. I've written more about that in what cinematography means.

What audio kit goes in the bag?

More than most people expect, because sound is the part a viewer won't forgive. A typical small-crew audio kit includes:

  • Lav mics, usually on a wireless system, for interviews and people moving around
  • A shotgun or hypercardioid on a boom pole, with proper wind protection
  • A separate recorder, or a camera with good inputs and a backup record option
  • Closed-back headphones, worn the whole time
  • Spare cables, toupee tape for hiding lavs, and wind covers for every mic

For lavs outdoors I use URSA Fur Circles, small furry discs that sit over the capsule and take the edge off wind. They're tiny, cheap and live permanently in the bag. If you want the detail on each mic type, see lav mics explained, shotgun mics explained and how wireless audio works.

Which lights does a small crew bring?

Usually fewer than people expect. Many great interviews are lit with one big, soft key light, a bit of fill or negative fill, and a practical lamp in the background. So a small kit tends to be:

  • One strong LED light with a large softbox or diffusion for the key
  • One or two smaller lights for a back light, background or a bit of shape
  • A collapsible reflector that can bounce or block
  • A couple of dimmable household bulbs to swap into practicals

LEDs have made this much easier. They run cool, many can change colour temperature to match a window or a lamp, and some run on batteries, which helps when there's no socket where you need one. The principles are in interview lighting explained simply.

What support and grip do you need?

A proper video tripod with a fluid head is the foundation, for interviews and anything that needs to sit still and watch. I've written about why good tripods cost so much, and the short version is that it's one place not to economise. Beyond that, a gimbal or shoulder rig for movement, and grip to hold up the lights: stands, a C-stand or two, sandbags, clamps. That side of the bag has its own post, light stands, C-stands and grip explained.

Every shoot, without fail, something needs to be held exactly here. And without fail, the clamp that would hold it is in the car.

How do you power a full day of filming?

With far more batteries than seems sensible. A long documentary day can run ten hours or more, and you often can't plug in where you're filming. Camera batteries, larger batteries for lights and monitors, AA or rechargeable cells for wireless packs and recorders, and the chargers for all of them.

A few habits help. Charge everything the night before and label what's flat. Swap batteries at natural breaks, not when they die, because a battery never goes during the boring bit. Carry an extension lead and a multi-socket, so the moment you find a plug you can charge several things at once.

How should footage be stored and backed up?

As if losing it would end the job, because it would. A shoot day can't be bought back. The habits that matter:

  • Enough cards. More than you think you need, from reputable makers. Cheap cards fail at the worst time.
  • Record to two cards at once where the camera allows it.
  • Offload during the day to at least two separate drives, and check the copies before any card gets wiped.
  • A clear system. Labelled cards, a note of what's been backed up, and a rule that a card isn't reused until its footage exists in two other places.
A shoot day can't be bought back. Treat the cards accordingly.

What small bits earn their place?

The unglamorous stuff saves more shoots than the expensive kit. Most bags carry some version of:

  • Gaffer tape. Tapes down cables, fixes things, labels things and peels off without wrecking surfaces. Not the same as duct tape.
  • Spare batteries for everything, including the small ones nobody thinks about.
  • Clamps and cable ties. For mounting, tidying and improvising.
  • Lens cloths and a blower. Dust and fingerprints show up badly on a close-up.
  • A small torch, a multi-tool and marker pens.
  • A rain cover for the camera, even when the forecast is fine.
  • Spare cables and adapters. One broken lead can stop a whole interview.

What bags and cases work best?

It depends how you're travelling. Hard cases, the waterproof kind with foam inside, protect the most and stack well in a car, but they're heavy. Rolling cases save your back on long walks between a car park and a location. A camera backpack works when you need hands free or you're on public transport. Soft bags take stands and grip.

In London, where parking near a location can be impossible, the whole kit has to be movable by hand in as few trips as possible. That shapes everything above. The kit gets lighter, the choices get sharper, and every item has to justify the weight.

Our day on a drainage job in Enfield shows why a self-contained kit matters. One live job, filmed start to finish with no reshoots and no waiting for the camera, and it had to feed a long YouTube film, vertical shorts and carousels. When the work won't stop for you, everything you might need has to already be in the bag.

If you're commissioning a film, all of this is part of what a day rate covers, and it's why quotes vary as much as they do. There's more on that in how much a brand film costs in the UK, or tell us about the film you've got in mind.
items.author: Earl Duncan

faqs.q: Can one person film a brand documentary on their own?
faqs.a: Yes, and plenty of documentary work is shot by one person who directs, operates the camera and handles the sound. It works well for small spaces and sensitive subjects, where a big crew would change how people behave. The trade-off is time and attention. Sound in particular benefits from a second person, especially with more than one speaker or a noisy location.

faqs.q: Should you rent or buy filming kit?
faqs.a: Buy what you use every week and rent what you use occasionally. Core kit like a camera, a lens or two, a tripod and audio usually pays for itself quickly if you're filming regularly. Specialist lenses, big lights and extra cameras are often better hired for the day, which also lets you try them before committing. Rental houses usually include insurance options, which is worth checking.

faqs.q: How much does a documentary kit weigh?
faqs.a: A full small-crew kit for an interview and coverage can easily run to several cases and bags, often well over thirty kilograms once stands, sandbags and batteries are included. A stripped-down one-person kit can be carried in a backpack and one roller. The weight is usually set by the grip and lighting more than by the camera itself.

faqs.q: Do you need insurance for filming equipment?
faqs.a: Anyone filming professionally should have equipment insurance and public liability insurance. Equipment cover protects against theft, loss and damage, including on location and in transit. Public liability covers injury or damage caused to other people or their property, like a light stand falling over in a client's shop. Many locations and clients ask to see proof of public liability before a shoot.

items.title: The unglamorous AI tools that save edit time
items.excerpt: The everyday AI tools that save time in a real video edit, from transcripts to subtitles and noise reduction, what still needs a person, and when to disclose.
items.coverAlt: Earl in headphones monitoring sound during an interview
items.body:
The AI that actually earns its place in a video workflow today is the unglamorous kind. Transcribing interviews, searching hours of footage by what people said, cleaning up noisy audio, helping cut a person out from a background, drafting subtitles and translations, and getting shots from different cameras to roughly match. Each one turns hours of repetitive work into minutes. Each one still needs a person checking the result, and none of them decide what the film is about.

We've written separately about what AI can and can't do for brand video, which covers generated footage, and about why real people matter more as AI spreads. This one's about the edit suite. Less exciting. More useful.

Which AI tools genuinely save time in an edit?

I'll describe these by what they do rather than by product, because the names change every few months and most of the big editing apps now have some version of each built in.

Transcription

An interview-led film starts with hours of conversation. Automatic transcription turns all of it into text in the time it takes to make a coffee. That alone changes how an edit runs, because you can read an interview end to end before you've watched a frame.

Searching footage by what was said

Once there's a transcript, you can search it. Every time someone mentions a particular customer, the word "apprentice" or a specific year. Some editing software lets you build a rough cut by selecting lines of text, and the matching clips line up on the timeline. For documentary work, where the story is found in the footage rather than written beforehand, this is the biggest time saver of the lot.

Noise reduction and dialogue clean-up

Real places are noisy. Fridges, air conditioning, traffic, a busy shop floor. Dialogue tools can pull the voice forward and push the room back far better than the old filters did. They don't replace recording good sound on the day, but they rescue a lot.

Masking and rotoscoping help

Separating a person from the background used to mean drawing round them frame by frame. AI masking now does a decent first pass on its own, which makes jobs like brightening a face, blurring a background or tidying a distraction much quicker.

Subtitles and translation

A first draft of subtitles in minutes, and a first draft in another language not long after. Since so much video is watched on mute, and subtitles matter for accessibility as well, this one pays for itself.

The landlord explainer we made for Easee had to explain a government grant scheme clearly enough to act on, and it was delivered subtitled. That's the kind of film where every word on screen has to be right, because someone might make a decision on it.

Colour matching

When two cameras film the same interview, their pictures never quite match. Matching tools get them close automatically, so the colourist starts from a sensible base instead of from scratch.

What does a person still have to do?

All the judgement, and a lot of checking. The tools are quick and confident, and they're confidently wrong often enough that nothing goes out unchecked.

  • Transcripts mangle names, places and technical words. Fine for searching, not fine for subtitles.
  • Cleaned audio can go watery or robotic if it's pushed too hard. Someone has to listen on proper headphones and back it off.
  • Masks struggle with hair, fast movement and anything see-through, and the errors show up as a shimmer round the edges.
  • Translations for anything public should be checked by a fluent speaker, ideally one who knows your industry.
  • Colour matching gets shots consistent. The grade, the actual look of the film, is still taste.

Transcription software has a real gift for turning a client's surname into a breakfast cereal. Check every name.

And the big one. A transcript tells you what was said. It doesn't tell you how. The pause before an answer, the look away, the line that reads flat on the page and lands beautifully on screen. Picking those moments is the job, and I don't see software doing it for a film meant to make someone feel something.

A transcript tells you what was said. It can't tell you which moment will make someone feel something.

Does AI make editing cheaper?

It makes some of it faster. Logging, syncing, transcribing and versioning take a fraction of the time they used to. On a well run production, most of that saved time goes back into the story edit rather than off the invoice, because the story edit is where the quality lives.

The biggest single cost in a film is still the shoot, which no edit tool changes. We break down where the money goes in how much a brand film costs. Where AI helps your budget most is in the extras: more cut-downs, more subtitled versions, quicker turnaround on small changes.

Do you have to tell people AI was used in the edit?

For the jobs above, generally no. YouTube's altered or synthetic content rules are about realistic content that makes a real person appear to say or do something they didn't, alters footage of real events or places, or shows a realistic scene that never happened. Transcribing, captioning, cleaning audio and adjusting colour don't change what happened, so they're not what the label is for.

My own line is simple. If a tool tidies what happened, fine. If it changes what happened, say so, or better still don't do it. The grey area is voice. Some tools can patch a fluffed word in an interview using a clone of the speaker's voice. Technically impressive. But it's putting words in someone's mouth, and I'd only ever do it with that person's clear agreement, and I'd rather just ask them to say it again.

There's a second honesty question people forget, which is where your footage goes. Many of these tools process files in the cloud. If the interview covers anything confidential, unreleased products or people who haven't agreed to their words being stored by a third party, it's worth knowing which tools are used and where the data ends up.

What should you ask a production company about their AI use?

  • Which parts of the edit use AI tools, and who checks the output?
  • Will anything in the film be generated, or altered beyond tidying?
  • Will anyone's voice or face be synthesised, and with whose consent?
  • Where is our footage uploaded and processed?
  • Are subtitles and translations checked by a person before delivery?

A decent production company will answer all of those without fuss. If you'd like to ask us, get in touch, or see how our films are made from research to the final mix.
items.author: Earl Duncan

faqs.q: Can AI edit a whole brand film on its own?
faqs.a: Not one worth watching, in my view. Tools can assemble clips, suggest cuts and trim pauses, and that's handy for simple talking-head social posts. A brand film depends on choosing which moments carry the story and in what order, and on judging how a line lands rather than what it says. That's still a person's job, and it's most of what you're paying an editor for.

faqs.q: Is AI noise reduction good enough to skip a sound recordist?
faqs.a: No. Clean-up tools rescue recordings that went wrong, but they work best on audio that was decent to begin with. Push them hard on a poor recording and voices start to sound processed. A good microphone in the right place, and someone listening while it's recorded, still gives you far better sound than any repair afterwards.

faqs.q: Are automatic subtitles accurate enough to publish?
faqs.a: As a first draft, usually yes. As a finished file, no. They regularly get names, places, technical terms and accents wrong, and the line breaks often split phrases awkwardly. Every subtitle file should be read through against the film by a person before it goes out, especially for anything people will act on, like an explainer about a grant or a price.

faqs.q: Can we translate our brand film with AI dubbing?
faqs.a: You can, and the results can be impressive, but treat it carefully. Have a fluent speaker check the translation, get the consent of anyone whose voice is being recreated, and be open with viewers that it's a dubbed version. For many businesses, translated subtitles over the original voices are the simpler, more trustworthy option, and they keep the real person's delivery intact.

stat.takeaway: Most marketers now use AI somewhere in making video, so the useful question is which jobs it's doing and who checks them.

items.title: How to brief your team before a film shoot
items.excerpt: How to brief staff before a brand film shoot: who to film, release forms, UK consent, what to tidy, scheduling, customers and the running order.
items.coverAlt: Cast and crew together on a field above a fjord at the end of a shoot
items.body:
To brief your team before a film shoot, tell them a week ahead who's being filmed and when, make being on camera genuinely optional, and get a release form signed by everyone who appears. Tidy anything private or messy, leave the real work exactly as it is, and protect the interviewees' diaries so their jobs are covered while they're in the chair. Send everyone a simple running order for the day, with one named person to ask.

If you're the marketer or office manager who's just booked a film, this one's for you. The crew handles the filming. You handle the people, the building and the calendar, and that part decides how smoothly the day goes.

Who should be filmed?

The people with the best stories, which isn't always the most senior people. Start with the film's purpose. If it's about how a product gets made, you want the people who make it. If it's for recruitment, you want people who joined recently and can remember what it was like. A managing director can open the film, but the person who's been on the shop floor for fifteen years is often the one viewers believe.

Ask for volunteers before you pick anyone, and mean it. Someone who's been told to do it will sound exactly like someone who's been told to do it. Quiet people are worth a gentle ask, though. Some of the best interviews come from people who'd never put themselves forward.

Keep the list short. Every person interviewed needs time in the chair and time in the edit, and three good voices make a stronger film than eight rushed ones. Everyone else can still appear in the background, doing their jobs.

Do staff need to sign a release form?

Yes, anyone identifiable should, and it's simple to do. What follows is general UK guidance, not legal advice, so if your situation is unusual, check with someone qualified.

Footage of a recognisable person counts as personal data under UK data protection law, so you need a proper basis for using it. The obvious answer seems to be consent, but there's a catch with employees. The Information Commissioner's Office says in its guidance on consent that consent won't usually be appropriate where there's a clear imbalance of power, and it uses employees as the example: people who rely on you for their job may feel they can't say no. Employers can still use consent if they can show it's truly voluntary, with no consequences for refusing.

In practice that means three things:

  • Make it optional, and visibly so. Saying no should cost nothing, and people should know that before they're asked.
  • Get a written release anyway. It records what they agreed to: that they'll appear, where the film will be used (website, social, events, paid advertising) and for how long.
  • Decide now what happens when someone leaves. People change jobs. Agree up front whether the film stays up, and write it down.

Release forms also cover the words people say, which matters more than most people realise. I've gone into that in who owns the footage when you commission a film. Anyone under 18 needs a parent or guardian's consent, and if the film involves vulnerable people, there's more to think about, covered in brand films for charities.

What should we tidy, and what should we leave real?

The crew will tidy a frame as they shoot, but some things are better sorted before anyone arrives, because they're private rather than messy:

  • Screens. Emails, customer records, pipelines, anything with a name or a number on it. Close it or lock it.
  • Whiteboards and walls. Client names, sales targets, rotas with phone numbers, the post-it with the Wi-Fi password.
  • Paperwork on desks. Invoices and delivery notes carry addresses.
  • Other brands. Posters, branded mugs, a competitor's catalogue on the shelf.

Then stop. Don't repaint, don't clear the benches and don't stage anything. Tools, work in progress and a bit of wear are what make a place look real on camera, and they're a big part of why a viewer believes a documentary. If a corner genuinely can't be shown, tell the crew and they'll frame around it.

Someone who's been told to do it will sound exactly like someone who's been told to do it.

That can go a long way. Our Car Planet film was shot during a live installation at a working car supermarket, and the client didn't want the site itself on display. So the customer story was filmed almost entirely in close-up, and the edit was filled out with b-roll from previous installs and Car Planet's own image bank. Knowing that in advance is what made it possible.

How do we schedule filming around work?

Pick a normal working day with real work happening, but not your busiest. You want the place to look alive without the crew being in the way of something that can't wait.

  • Block out the interviewees properly. An interview can run well over an hour once you include getting the mic on. Book at least ninety minutes each and cover their work, so they're not checking their phone between answers.
  • Find a quiet room. Away from the kitchen, the loading bay and the printer. Air con, fridges and radios usually get switched off for the interview, so let people know.
  • Plan around noise. If machinery runs on a schedule, tell the crew. They may want the interview between runs and the machines running for the b-roll.
  • Warn the people who aren't being filmed. They'll walk past a camera at some point. Tell them roughly where the crew will be and that they're welcome to stay out of shot.

And sort lunch. A crew and an interviewee who haven't eaten by three o'clock is nobody's best work.

The most important person on any shoot day is whoever knows where the fridge switch is. And remembers to turn it back on.

Can customers appear in the film?

Yes, and they're often the most convincing people in it, but never by surprise. If you want a customer interviewed, ask them well before the day, explain where the film will go, and get their own release signed. Our piece on testimonial videos covers how to choose and approach them.

Customers who just happen to be around are different. If the shoot happens while you're open, put a clear notice at the entrance saying filming is taking place, and tell staff what to say if someone asks. Anyone who doesn't want to be filmed should be kept out of shot, and anyone identifiable who ends up prominent in a shot should be asked and given a release, or left out of the edit. Crews can work around customers with angles and framing far more than people expect.

What should the running order for the day look like?

Send a one-page running order to everyone involved, a week ahead and again the day before. It doesn't have to be fancy. Something like:

  1. Arrival and setup. Where the crew should park and unload, and who meets them.
  2. Walk round. Ten minutes with the crew and the point of contact, no cameras.
  3. Interviews. Names and times, with gaps between them.
  4. Filming the work. Which areas, roughly when, and what should be happening there.
  5. Stills. Portraits or team photos, if they're part of the job.
  6. Wrap. What time the crew expects to leave, and who signs off.

Put one name at the top as the person to ask on the day, with a mobile number. Attach the release form, and link the people being interviewed to what to wear on camera and how to prepare for being filmed, so nobody turns up in a pinstripe shirt wondering what they're meant to say.

If you want the whole planning stage in one place, our free playbook, Before the camera comes out, goes through it in more depth. And if you haven't booked the film yet, here's how we make them.
items.author: Earl Duncan

faqs.q: How much notice should staff get before a film shoot?
faqs.a: At least a week for anyone being interviewed, and a few days for everyone else in the building. That gives interviewees time to think about stories, sort their clothes and get their work covered. A reminder with the running order the day before helps, especially for people who'll only appear in the background.

faqs.q: What if someone changes their mind after filming?
faqs.a: Talk to them early and take it seriously. If they're identifiable and genuinely don't want to appear, it's usually better to cut them than to lean on the form, especially with staff. That's far easier at rough cut stage than after launch, so tell the production company as soon as it comes up.

faqs.q: Do people in the background need to sign a release?
faqs.a: Not always. Someone passing through in the distance is treated differently from someone featured prominently. Notices that filming is happening help, and anyone who asks not to be filmed should be kept out of shot. If a background person ends up clearly identifiable and prominent, ask them for a release or leave that shot out.

faqs.q: Should we pay staff extra to appear in the film?
faqs.a: Usually not, as long as it happens in working hours and it's genuinely optional. If filming runs outside someone's normal hours, treat it like any other overtime. What matters more is that nobody feels pressured, because a reluctant interviewee rarely gives a usable interview and pressure undermines the consent you're relying on.
