items.title: Playing the long game as a small studio
items.excerpt: What the long game means for a small creative studio: saying no to the wrong work, staying consistent, and why one good film quietly leads to the next.
items.coverAlt: A referee raising a fighter’s hand after a match
items.body:
Playing the long game as a small studio means making decisions for where you want to be in five years rather than this month. You turn down work that would pull you off course, you treat every film as the first thing your next client will see, you stay consistent when nothing seems to be happening, and you let your reputation do the compounding. For a small studio it's the one strategy that doesn't depend on outspending anybody.

I find this easy to believe and hard to practise. The short game is always louder. There's always a job that would pay this month's bills, a trend you could chase, a shortcut that would get something out the door faster. Most of the time the long game is just saying no to those, politely, and getting on with the work.

What does the long game actually mean for a small studio?

For us it comes down to a few habits. Choose the work carefully. Make every film as well as we can, whatever the budget. Treat people properly at every stage, including the ones who don't hire us. Keep showing up, even when it feels like nobody's watching.

None of that is clever, and that's partly the point. A small studio can't win on scale or on price. What it can do is build the kind of reputation that means, a few years in, people arrive already half convinced because someone they trust told them about you.

Why say no to work that pays?

Because every job you take is a sample of what you'll be asked for next. Make a lot of one kind of video and you'll be offered more of that kind. Your portfolio steers your future whether you mean it to or not.

So if a job pulls you away from the work you want to be known for, it costs more than the time it takes. It fills the slot where the right job could have gone, and it adds a film to your showreel that sends people the wrong signal.

That doesn't mean only taking dream projects. Bills are real, and I'm not going to pretend otherwise. It means knowing which jobs move you forward, which ones simply pay, and which ones you'd be better off without. The third group is the one to get comfortable turning down.

How does one good film lead to the next?

A good film keeps working long after shoot day. It sits on the client's website, gets shared by their staff, turns up in their sales conversations and gets watched by people in the same sector who then ask who made it. It carries your name into rooms you'll never be in.

It works the other way too. A rushed film made to hit a deadline also keeps working, just against you. That's why the budget doesn't decide how much care goes in. The next client won't know what this one paid.

Why does consistency matter more than one big moment?

Because trust builds through repetition. One great launch gets attention for a week. Turning up every month, doing what you said you'd do, gets you remembered.

Some of the businesses we've filmed show this better than any studio could. Carreducker documented all 210 steps of making a bespoke shoe publicly, one post at a time, years before anyone called that content. La Fromagerie started with a market stall at Camden Lock and a shop in Highbury at eighty pounds a week. Thirty three years later it's three shops with walk-in cheese rooms and a wholesale business supplying restaurants across London.

Watch that film and you're watching what the long game looks like when it's worked. Nobody in it describes a shortcut. They describe years of doing the same thing properly, and being known for it.

A rushed film keeps working too, just against you.

How do you stay patient when work is slow?

Honestly, it's uncomfortable. Quiet months happen to every small business, and they bring the doubt with them. Is this working? Should I just take whatever comes in? I don't think there's a trick that makes that feeling go away.

Patience is far easier to recommend than to practise. I'm still working on mine.

What helps me is keeping busy with the right things. Activity is king. Make something, even if nobody's paying for it yet. Reach out to the people you'd genuinely like to work with. Finish the thing you've been putting off. Then judge progress over a year rather than a week. Look back twelve months and you'll usually see more movement than any single week suggested.

It also helps to stop comparing yourself to whoever's loudest online. Comparison is the thief of joy. The studio posting every day might be booked solid, or might be doing exactly what you're doing, just louder.

What does a studio's reputation actually rest on?

Mostly on small things done reliably. Turning up on time. Replying to emails. Delivering what you said, when you said. Being straight about what something will cost, and not changing the number because someone pushed. How you behave when something goes wrong on a shoot, because eventually something always does.

And how you treat people who don't hire you. The conversation that went quiet, the quote that wasn't accepted, the project that went to someone else. If you've handled those kindly, as I've written about in closing the file kindly, they become part of your reputation too, and some of them become clients later.

If you're thinking about a film that you'd want to still be working for you in a few years, have a look at our films or read our free guide, then tell us what you've got in mind.
items.author: Earl Duncan

faqs.q: How long does it take a small creative studio to build a reputation?
faqs.a: Longer than most people hope, usually a few years of steady work before referrals do much of the heavy lifting. It speeds up when every film is good enough to share and when you treat people well at every stage. There isn't a reliable shortcut, but each good project makes the next conversation a little easier.

faqs.q: How do you decide which jobs to turn down?
faqs.a: Ask whether the job moves you towards the work you want to be known for, simply pays the bills, or pulls you away from both. Take the first gladly, take the second when you need to, and get comfortable declining the third. A job that's underpriced, keeps growing in scope or sends the wrong signal in your portfolio usually belongs in that last group.

faqs.q: Should a small studio specialise or stay broad?
faqs.a: Specialising helps people remember you and refer you, because they can describe what you do in one sentence. That doesn't mean only one sector. It can be a way of working, like documentary-style films built on real people, applied across different kinds of business. Stay broad enough to pay the bills, but be known for one clear thing.

faqs.q: How often should a small studio share its own work?
faqs.a: Regularly enough that people see you're active, which for most small studios is a few times a month. Consistency matters more than volume. Sharing finished films, short clips and what you learned on a shoot keeps you in mind without needing to post daily. Pick a pace you can actually keep up through busy months as well as quiet ones.

items.title: Light stands, C-stands and grip, explained
items.excerpt: What grip is and why it matters: light stands versus C-stands, sandbags and safety, boom arms, clamps, flags, and what a small documentary crew carries.
items.coverAlt: A lit stage with a panel at a live event
items.body:
Light stands hold lights up. C-stands hold almost anything up, more steadily, at awkward angles, and with an arm that can reach out over a subject. Grip is the name for all the gear that supports, shapes and secures things on a shoot: stands, arms, clamps, sandbags and flags. It doesn't show up in the finished film, which is exactly why it gets underestimated.

If you've ever wondered why a small crew turns up to film one interview with a car full of metal poles and bags of sand, this is what they're for.

Why do stands matter so much?

Because a light is only as good as where it can be put. The best light in the world is useless if it can't sit high enough, close enough or at the right angle. Stands also decide whether things stay put. A light that droops slowly over a forty minute interview changes the picture halfway through an answer, and the edit can't hide that.

And they're a safety issue. A stand holding a heavy light with a big softbox on it is a tall, top-heavy object in a room full of people, usually somebody's office or shop. If it goes over, it lands on someone, or their stock, or their kit. Good grip is boring, and boring is what you want.

What's the difference between a light stand and a C-stand?

A light stand is a lightweight, collapsible stand with three legs folding out from the bottom and sections that slide out to raise it. Most are aluminium, quick to set up and easy to carry several at once. They're designed to hold a light straight up on top, and they do that well. The small spigot on top that the light fits onto is usually called a baby pin. Bigger lights use a wider fitting called a junior.

A C-stand, short for century stand, is heavier, mostly steel, and much more versatile. A few things set it apart:

  • Staggered legs. The three legs sit at different heights, so stands nest together and one leg can stand on a step or a kerb.
  • A low footprint. The legs sit flat to the floor, which makes it more stable than its size suggests.
  • The grip head and arm. A clamp with several slots at the top holds an arm that can reach out sideways at almost any angle. That arm is what lets a C-stand hold a flag, a reflector, a small light or a mic in places a light stand can't.

Light stands are for getting a light up quickly and moving on. C-stands are for anything that needs to be precise, reach over something, or stay exactly where it was put. Most crews carry both.

A C-stand weighs about the same as a small child and is roughly as cooperative when you're carrying three of them up a flight of stairs.

Why does every stand need a sandbag?

Because the weight of the light, the arm and any modifier sits high up, and a stand on its own is only as stable as its feet. A sandbag draped over the base lowers the centre of gravity and pins the stand down. The usual rule is one sandbag per stand, more for anything heavy or reaching out on an arm.

Where it goes matters. On a C-stand with an arm reaching out, the bag goes on the leg underneath the load, which is usually the highest leg, so the weight is fighting the direction the stand would tip. On a light stand, it goes over the base so it rests on the legs, not swinging off a single one.

Outdoors, sandbags go from sensible to essential. A softbox or a reflector is basically a sail. A gust that feels mild on your face will lift an unweighted stand and drop it on whatever's nearby.

How do you set up a stand safely?

A few habits cover most of it.

  • Raise the lowest, thickest section first. It's the strongest. The thin top section should go up last, and only if it has to.
  • Load on the right. Grip heads are built so that the weight of an arm tightens the knob rather than loosening it. Set the arm so the load sits on the side that turns the knob clockwise, and gravity works for you. Crews call it righty-tighty.
  • Keep the long end over a leg. An arm should reach out over one of the stand's legs, not between them.
  • Tape or cover the cables. A cable across a walkway is a trip waiting to happen. Gaffer tape it down, run it along the wall, or use a cable mat.
  • Mind the head height. An arm sticking out at eye level is easy to walk into. Put a bit of tape or a tennis ball on the end if people are moving around.

None of this is complicated. It's just the stuff that gets skipped when everyone's in a hurry, and in somebody else's working business, that's when it matters most.

What is a boom arm for lights?

A boom arm is a long pole mounted on a stand that holds a light out and over a subject, with a counterweight on the other end to balance it. It lets a light sit directly above someone, or come in from high and to the side, without the stand appearing in shot.

Booms are where the safety habits matter most, because the weight is far from the base. Heavy-duty stand, the boom balanced properly, the stand's leg under the load, and sandbags on the base. A light hanging over somebody's head is not where you cut a corner.

What do clamps do?

Clamps let you mount things where there's no room for a stand. A small documentary crew leans on them heavily, because most of the places we film are tight. A few common types:

  • Super clamps. Small, very strong clamps that grip a pipe, a shelf edge or a door frame and take a light or a small arm.
  • Spring clamps. Big versions of the clamps in a hardware shop, used for clipping fabric, diffusion and reflectors to things.
  • Wooden pegs. Plain clothes pegs. They don't conduct heat, so they're used to clip gels and diffusion onto hot lights.

A clamp on a shelf can replace a stand that wouldn't have fitted in the room at all. That's often the difference between filming in someone's actual workspace and dragging them somewhere bigger and less interesting.

What are flags, and why use them?

Lighting is as much about taking light away as adding it. Flags are frames of black fabric that block light, held on a C-stand arm. They stop a light spilling onto a background, keep it off the lens to avoid flare, or cut a hard edge so light falls exactly where it's wanted.

There are a few relatives. Nets are fine mesh that reduce light without blocking it. Silks are white fabric that soften it. And black fabric on the opposite side of a face from the light, called negative fill, deepens the shadow and gives the face more shape. I've gone into why that matters in interview lighting explained simply.

Lighting is as much about taking light away as adding it.

Our exhibition film for a portrait artist was shot in a gallery lit for paintings rather than faces, with reflections everywhere. Spaces like that are where control matters, because the job is to make the work read on camera without flare, and that's as much about what you block as what you add.

What does a small documentary crew actually carry?

Less than a commercial crew, but more grip than most people expect. Every crew packs differently, but a typical small documentary kit for an interview and some coverage of the work tends to include:

  • Two or three lightweight light stands, plus one or two C-stands with arms
  • A sandbag for every stand
  • A handful of super clamps and spring clamps
  • A couple of flags or a collapsible black and white reflector that does both jobs
  • Gaffer tape, cable mats or covers, and an extension lead or two

The trade-off is always weight against options. In London especially, where you might be carrying everything from a loading bay or on public transport, every stand has to justify itself. The rest of the kit bag is a whole other conversation, which I've gone through in what's in a documentary shooter's kit bag. If you're planning a shoot and wondering what you need to arrange your end, the free guide covers it.
items.author: Earl Duncan

faqs.q: Can you use a C-stand for a light?
faqs.a: Yes, and many crews do. A C-stand will hold a small or medium light on its top spigot or out on the arm, and it's more stable than a light stand of a similar height. It's heavier to carry and slower to set up, so crews often use light stands for lights that just need to go up, and keep C-stands for anything that needs reach or precision.

faqs.q: What should you fill a sandbag with?
faqs.a: Film sandbags are usually filled with sand or small gravel, sealed in an inner bag so nothing leaks onto the floor. Gravel is less messy if a bag splits. For travel, some crews carry empty bags and fill them on location, or use water bags, though these are less dense and can leak. A full standard bag usually weighs somewhere between about five and fifteen kilograms.

faqs.q: Do you need grip for a shoot in a small office?
faqs.a: Usually yes, just less of it. Small rooms are where clamps, compact stands and flags earn their place, because there's no space to put lights where they'd normally go. A couple of stands with sandbags, some clamps and a flag can turn an awkward office into a decent interview space. The tighter the room, the more the grip has to do.

faqs.q: Who looks after the grip on a small shoot?
faqs.a: On a big production there's a whole grip department, led by a key grip. On a small documentary shoot, the camera operator or a camera assistant usually handles it alongside everything else. That's one reason setup takes as long as it does: the same few people are building the lighting, rigging the stands, running the cables and checking it's all safe before anyone sits down.

items.title: Phone video for business: when it's enough
items.excerpt: What a modern phone can really do for business video, the settings that matter, why sound is the weak spot, simple light and stability fixes, and a routine.
items.coverAlt: A man on his phone on a sofa during a shoot
items.body:
A modern phone can shoot video good enough for most of a business's weekly content: behind the scenes, quick updates, short talking-to-camera pieces, the job in progress. The picture is rarely the weak spot. Sound is, followed by light and wobble. A phone stops being enough when the content has to carry trust over several minutes, when interviews need to sound properly good, or when you need several angles and a proper grade.

I'm all for businesses filming more of their own stuff. Most of the companies we talk to would get more from twenty decent phone clips a month than from waiting for the perfect moment to make something polished.

What can a modern phone genuinely do?

More than most people use it for. Recent phones shoot sharp 4K, handle low light far better than they used to, stabilise handheld shots well and let you choose frame rates. In the right hands, with the right kit around them, they can shoot something that looks expensive.

Apple's behind the scenes film of its Scary Fast event is a good example, and a revealing one. According to Apple's own newsroom, all of the presenters, locations and drone footage were filmed on iPhone 15 Pro Max. Watch what's around the phone, though: cranes, dollies, drones, rigs, a professional camera app recording in a log format for grading, and a top colourist finishing it. The phone was the least of it. That's the useful lesson for a business. Better results come from everything around the phone far more than from a newer one.

When isn't a phone enough?

  • Interviews that need to hold attention for minutes. Small sensors and fixed lenses make it hard to separate a person from a busy background, and the sound needs proper microphones anyway.
  • Multi-camera work. Two angles on an interview, matched and synced, is where dedicated cameras earn their keep.
  • Difficult light. Dark workshops, mixed lighting and bright windows behind people are much more forgiving on a bigger sensor.
  • Anything that has to carry a big decision. A film you send to someone deciding whether to trust you with a large job needs to look like you took it seriously.

That's the split we work to. Phone for the steady weekly flow, a proper shoot for the pieces that do the heavy lifting. The films are the second kind.

Which phone camera settings actually matter?

Frame rate

In the UK, 25 frames per second is a sensible default. Our mains electricity runs at 50Hz, and some indoor lights can flicker or band on camera at 30fps. Apple's iPhone guide lists 25fps and PAL formats as options on supported models, and most Android phones offer something similar. Pick one and stick to it so clips cut together cleanly. On iPhone, also check the Auto FPS setting, which can drop the frame rate to 24 in low light.

Locking exposure and focus

Left on auto, a phone keeps adjusting brightness and focus as you move, which shows up as pulsing and hunting. On iPhone you can touch and hold on your subject until AE/AF Lock appears, and many Android camera apps have an equivalent. Lock it once the shot looks right, then record.

Locking white balance and the lens

iPhone's video settings include Lock White Balance, so the colour doesn't drift mid-shot, and Lock Camera, which stops the phone switching between its lenses while you record. Both are worth turning on.

Cleaning the lens

Phones live in pockets, and a greasy lens gives you a soft, hazy picture with smeared highlights. Wipe it with something clean before you start. It's free, and it makes more difference than most settings.

Wiping the lens on your T-shirt is the single best free upgrade in video. Do it before every take, not after the shoot.

Orientation

Decide before you press record. Vertical for Reels, Shorts and TikTok, horizontal for YouTube and your website. If you need both from one clip, shoot horizontal with plenty of room around the subject, then crop. Our free video resizer does that in the browser.

Why is sound the real weak spot?

Because the phone's microphone is designed to pick up everything around it, from wherever the phone happens to be. Hold it at arm's length in a busy room and the voice ends up small, echoey and competing with the extractor fan.

Nobody scrolls past a video because it was shot on a phone. They scroll past because they can't hear it.

The fix is to get a microphone close to the mouth. A small clip-on lav mic that plugs into the phone, or a compact wireless kit, changes the result more than any phone upgrade will. We explain the options in lav mics explained and how wireless audio works. Then pick the quietest spot available, ideally one with soft furnishings, and record a few seconds and play it back on headphones before you do the real take.

How do you sort light and stability?

For light, face a window. Soft daylight from the side or front flatters almost everyone. Avoid standing with a window behind you, which turns you into a silhouette, and avoid overhead lights directly above, which put shadows in your eyes. Our post on interview lighting goes deeper if you want it.

For stability, a small tripod or a clamp is cheap and makes talking-to-camera clips look far more considered. Handheld, tuck your elbows in, move with your feet rather than your wrists, and avoid digital zoom, which just enlarges the pixels. Get closer instead.

What does a simple weekly phone routine look like?

  1. Monday, ten minutes: note three things worth filming this week. A job, a question customers keep asking, someone on the team.
  2. During the week: capture as you work. Clean the lens, lock exposure, get the mic on for anything with talking.
  3. Once a week: record one short talking-to-camera piece answering a real customer question.
  4. Friday, an hour: trim, add captions, resize for each platform and schedule.
  5. Keep everything: a simple folder of the week's clips becomes a library you'll reuse for months.

If you want help working out what's worth filming in the first place, our free playbook, Before the camera comes out, covers the planning side. And when there's a story that deserves more than a phone, tell us about it.
items.author: Earl Duncan

faqs.q: Do I need the newest phone to make good business videos?
faqs.a: No. Any phone from the last few years shoots video that's sharp enough for social media and your website. A cheap clip-on microphone, a small tripod and sensible light will improve your results far more than upgrading the phone. Spend on those first, and only think about a new handset once the sound, light and steadiness are sorted.

faqs.q: Should I shoot in 4K or 1080p on my phone?
faqs.a: 4K gives you room to crop and reframe later, which is handy if you need vertical and horizontal versions from one clip. It also uses a lot more storage and can make older phones run hot. For quick social clips you'll post as they are, 1080p is fine. Whichever you choose, keep it consistent across a shoot.

faqs.q: What's the best free app for editing phone videos?
faqs.a: The editor already on your phone, or the one built into the platform you're posting to, is enough for trimming, captions and simple cuts. Learn one tool well rather than hopping between several. When you need resizing between formats, a browser tool does the job without installing anything, and you can move to a desktop editor once your edits get more ambitious.

faqs.q: Can phone footage be mixed with professional footage in one film?
faqs.a: Yes, and it happens more than people think, especially for moments a crew wasn't there for. It works best when the phone footage is clearly a different kind of moment, like a customer's own clip, rather than pretending to match. Shoot at the same frame rate as the main film, keep it steady and well lit, and let the grade bring the two closer together.

items.title: How to give a good answer in a film interview
items.excerpt: What documentary interviewers ask and why, how to turn an answer into a short story, why specifics beat claims, and what to do when you go blank on camera.
items.coverAlt: Two people mid-conversation in an office interview
items.body:
A good interview answer is a short story with a turn in it. Where things stood, what changed, and where it landed, told with real names, real numbers and the words you'd use with a friend. Documentary interviewers ask about moments rather than opinions because moments produce those stories. If you go blank, say so and take a breath. You can always answer again.

I've written separately about how to speak on camera, which is about delivery. This one's about content: what you're actually being asked, and what makes an answer the one that ends up in the film.

What questions do documentary interviewers ask?

Every interviewer has their own way in, but the questions in a brand film interview tend to fall into a few groups, and each one is there for a reason.

  • The easy start. Your name, your role, how long you've been there. Partly for the editor's notes, mostly to get you talking about something you can't get wrong.
  • The beginning. How did this start? What were you doing before? Origins give a film its first act.
  • The ordinary day. Walk me through a normal Tuesday. It sounds dull, and it's where the details live that nobody outside the business knows.
  • The hard moment. When did it nearly go wrong? What was the worst week? This is where the stakes come from, and stakes are what keep a stranger watching.
  • Other people. A customer you remember. Someone who taught you. Films are about people, and talking about someone else is often when you sound most like yourself.
  • Now. What's different? What would you tell someone in the position you were in? These are the endings.
  • The open door. Is there anything I haven't asked that I should have? Some of the best material in any interview comes from this one, so don't wave it away.

Notice how few of those ask what you think of your own business. That's deliberate. Ask someone to describe their company and you get the brochure. Ask them about a particular Tuesday and you get the film.

Why do interviewers ask about moments and not opinions?

Because opinions sound the same from everyone, and moments are unique. "Quality is really important to us" could be said by any business in the country. Something like "in our first year we turned down the biggest order we'd ever been offered, because we couldn't do it properly in the time, and we really needed the money" could only be said by one.

A good interviewer will keep nudging you from the general to the particular. "Can you think of a time when that happened?" "What did that actually look like?" They aren't doubting you. They're asking for the version of your answer that a viewer will believe.

What makes an answer a story?

A beginning, a turn and somewhere to land. You don't need a dramatic arc. You need a situation, something that changed it, and what it meant.

  1. Where things stood. "We'd been running the shop for about two years, just the two of us."
  2. The turn. "Then a restaurant rang and asked if we could supply them every week."
  3. Where it landed. "That one phone call is basically why we've got a wholesale side now."

Three sentences, and the editor has something they can use almost anywhere. The turn is the part people leave out. They describe the before and the after and skip the moment between, which is the bit a viewer actually leans in for.

Our Barry Road film is built on that shape. The homeowner gives their own account of a full renovation: what they wanted, what it was like to live through, and what they ended up with. Nobody narrates over the top. The structure is in the way the story is told.

Why do specifics and numbers matter so much?

Because they're proof you were there. A number is hard to make up and easy to picture. Some of the details that carry our films are exactly that kind of thing. At Carreducker, every pair of shoes goes through 210 steps and takes six months. La Fromagerie started with a market stall at Camden Lock and a shop in Highbury at eighty pounds a week. On Nimrod Road, the work finished in eight weeks, two weeks inside the estimate, with a baby due.

Ask someone to describe their company and you get the brochure. Ask them about a particular Tuesday and you get the film.

You don't need impressive figures. Small, odd, exact ones are often better. The van you bought for £900. The forty-minute drive you did every morning. The customer who rang at quarter to seven. Before your interview, jot down a handful of numbers and names from your own story, so they're near the surface when you need them.

How do I avoid jargon and sales-speak?

Talk the way you would to a friend in the pub who doesn't work in your industry. If they'd ask "what does that mean?", the viewer will too, and the viewer can't ask.

Jargon creeps in two ways. The first is industry language: acronyms, product codes, technical terms you've used so long you've forgotten they're technical. Drop down one level. Say what the thing does instead of what it's called. The second is marketing language: solutions, passionate, customer-centric, end-to-end, best-in-class. These words are on every website, which is exactly why nobody hears them any more.

A quick test for any sentence you're about to say: could a competitor say it word for word? If so, it isn't doing anything. Swap it for something that happened.

If a phrase would fit on the side of any company's van, it probably doesn't belong in your interview.

What should I do if I go blank?

Say so. "Sorry, I've lost it, can you ask me that again?" is completely normal, and the interviewer will have heard it hundreds of times. They'll often rephrase the question, which can be easier to answer than the original.

A few other things that help:

  • Stop and breathe. The silence costs nothing. It comes out in the edit.
  • Go to an example. If you can't answer the big question, answer a small one. "I'm not sure how to sum it up, but I remember one job..." usually gets you moving again.
  • Park it. "Can we come back to that one?" is a perfectly good answer. Often it comes to you ten minutes later in the middle of something else.

Don't fill the gap with filler. "That's a really good question" while you think gives the editor nothing and makes you sound like a politician.

Can I answer a question again?

Yes, as many times as you like. Just tell the interviewer you want another go and start from the beginning of the answer, in a full sentence, so the editor has a clean version to use. Second attempts are often better, because you know where you're heading.

There's a limit, though. By the third or fourth go, an answer usually starts to sound rehearsed, and the life drains out of it. If you've had a couple of tries and it still feels wrong, move on. The interviewer may come back to the same idea later from a different angle, and you'll find you say it better without trying.

And sometimes the interviewer will ask you the same thing twice on purpose. Usually they heard something good the first time and want a cleaner version, or they think there's more to come. Answer it fresh rather than trying to repeat yourself.

If your business has a story that deserves telling properly, see how we make films, or tell us about the people in it.
items.author: Earl Duncan

faqs.q: Will I get the questions before the interview?
faqs.a: Usually you'll get the topics rather than a word-for-word list, and that's on purpose. Knowing the areas helps you think of stories in advance. Having exact questions tends to make people write answers and memorise them, which sounds rehearsed on camera. The best material often comes from follow-up questions nobody could have planned.

faqs.q: Can I say no to a question?
faqs.a: Yes. If a question touches something you don't want to talk about, just say so and the interviewer will move on. A documentary brand film relies on people being comfortable, and nothing good comes from pushing someone. You'll also see a rough cut before the film is finished, so you can flag anything you're unhappy with.

faqs.q: How long should each answer be?
faqs.a: Most strong answers run somewhere between twenty seconds and a couple of minutes. Long enough to tell one story properly, short enough to stay on one idea. If you notice you've drifted onto a second topic, finish your sentence and stop. The interviewer can always ask a follow-up, which is easier to edit than one answer covering three things.

faqs.q: What if I say something wrong or inaccurate?
faqs.a: Say so straight away and give the right version, starting the sentence again. The editor will use the corrected take. If you only realise afterwards, tell the crew or flag it when you see the rough cut. Facts, figures and names should be checked before a film goes out, so a slip in the interview doesn't have to end up on screen.

items.title: Why we don't undercut on price
items.excerpt: Why a creative studio shouldn't compete on price: what undercutting does to the work, how to hold your number kindly, and when it's right to walk away.
items.coverAlt: A smiling competitor among her team at a jiu-jitsu event
items.body:
We don't undercut on price because competing on price in creative work tends to make everything worse. The client ends up with a film made by someone cutting corners to hit a number, the studio quietly resents the job, and the low price becomes the thing you're known for. We'd rather quote what the work actually costs, explain it plainly, and be at peace if it isn't right for someone this time.

That's easy to say and harder to live by, especially in a quiet month. So here's how I think about it.

What happens when creative businesses compete on price?

Something has to give, and in film it's usually the parts the client won't notice until it's too late. The recce gets skipped. The shoot gets squeezed into half a day. There's no time to wait for the moment that would have made the film, so you get the version that was available at 2pm. The edit gets one pass instead of three. Music comes from whatever's cheapest.

None of those cuts are visible in a quote. They're all visible in the finished film. A viewer can't tell you why a video feels flat, but they feel it, and they scroll on.

There's a longer-term cost too. Once you've won work on price, that's what the client expects next time, and it's what they tell their friends you're good for. You've attracted exactly the clients who'll leave the moment someone's cheaper.

Why does a cheaper film often cost the client more?

Because the real cost of a film is more than the invoice. It's the hours your team gives up on shoot day, the weeks of back and forth, and the years the film then sits on your website representing you. A film that doesn't do its job wastes all of that, and often ends up being made again properly anyway.

The cheapest quote can also be a sign that someone hasn't understood the brief. If three studios quote in the same range and one comes in at a fraction, it's worth asking what they think they're making. Often it's a different, smaller film. We wrote about how to compare quotes fairly in how much a brand film costs in the UK.

How do you hold your number without sounding defensive?

Kindly, and without apologising for it. If the price is right for the work, there's nothing to apologise for.

Explain what's in it at the top level, so they can see where the money goes, and stop there. You don't need to justify every line. A client wants to know they're getting a proper film and what that involves, not a lecture on day rates.

It helps a lot to understand their real budget before you quote. A big number that scares off a small client is a lost conversation, and it's avoidable. Ask what they've set aside, or point them to our film budget calculator first. There's more on that in how to set a video budget. Once you both know the number, the conversation moves from whether to what.

And if it's still too much, say so with grace. "That's completely fair" goes a long way. It tells them there's no hard feelings, and it keeps the door open for later.

Change the scope and the price can honestly follow. Drop the price for the same work and you've told them the first number was made up.

Is it ever right to change the price?

Yes, if you change the work. Fewer locations, a shorter film, one interview instead of three, a single shoot day with photography from the same visit rather than a full production. Those are real differences, and the price can honestly reflect them. We keep a smaller option on our services page for exactly that reason, so a business that isn't ready for a full documentary still has a proper way in.

What we won't do is the same film for less because someone pushed. That's unfair on every client who paid the real price, and it teaches the person pushing that pushing works.

Occasionally we'll make something on our own terms, a film for a cause we care about, chosen by us. That's a decision we make with our eyes open, and it's very different from being talked down in a meeting.

When should you walk away from a job?

When the budget can't fund the film they want and they won't change what they want. When price is the only thing they ask about, and the haggling starts before anyone's talked about the story. When saying yes would mean making something you wouldn't put your name to.

The client who haggles hardest before the shoot rarely relaxes once the camera's out. Funny, that.

Walking away doesn't have to be dramatic. Thank them, say it's not the right fit at this moment, and wish them well. If you've handled it kindly, there's every chance they come back when the budget's grown or the project's changed. I've written about how to do that in closing the file kindly.

Doesn't refusing to discount lose you work?

Some, yes. I won't pretend otherwise. There are months when a discount looks very tempting, and I've had the same doubts any small business owner has when the diary's emptier than you'd like.

But when I look at the work we'd lose on price, it's mostly work we'd have struggled to do well. A squeezed budget usually comes with a squeezed timeline and a client who's nervous about every pound, and that's a hard place to make anything good. The films that turn out best are almost always the ones where both sides felt the deal was fair.

So we put the generosity somewhere else. An extra cut for social, a vertical version, stills from the shoot day, a bit more time on the edit when the story needs it. That way a client feels they've had real value, and the number stays honest.

If you'd like a straight conversation about what your film would cost and what it'd need to include, tell us what you're thinking. We'll give you a real number, and if it's not right for you, that's completely fine.
items.author: Earl Duncan

faqs.q: Should you match a competitor's lower quote?
faqs.a: Usually not. First check whether the two quotes are for the same film, because a much lower one often means fewer shoot hours, less editing or a different deliverable. If they really are like for like and the client prefers the cheaper option, it's fine to let them go. Matching on the spot tells them your original price was negotiable.

faqs.q: How do you respond when a client says your price is too high?
faqs.a: Thank them for being straight, ask what budget they have in mind, and see whether a smaller scope would work. Sometimes a shorter film or a single shoot day fits their number properly. If nothing fits, say that's completely fair and leave the door open. There's no need to defend the price or explain it line by line.

faqs.q: Is it worth doing a cheap first job to win a new client?
faqs.a: Rarely. A cheap first job sets the price the client expects for every job after it, and it's very hard to raise later without it feeling like a bait and switch. If you want to make it easier for a new client to try you, offer a smaller piece of work at your normal rate instead of the full project at a discount.

faqs.q: Should creative businesses publish their prices?
faqs.a: Publishing a starting price or a range helps, because it saves both sides from conversations that were never going to work. It doesn't need to be a full price list, since every film is different. A clear 'from' figure lets a client check their budget before getting in touch, and the detail can be worked out once you know what they need.

items.title: VFX for brand video: what's worth paying for
items.excerpt: What visual effects and motion graphics really are in a brand film, which ones are cheap or costly, and when effects help a documentary or make it look fake.
items.coverAlt: An animated floorplan graphic from a renovation film
items.body:
Visual effects in a brand film are mostly invisible repair work: removing something that shouldn't be in shot, putting the right picture on a phone or laptop screen, fixing a blown-out sky, steadying a shaky shot. Motion graphics are the designed bits that move, like titles, name captions, maps and simple diagrams. Titles and small fixes on a still camera are cheap. Anything where the camera moves and things pass in front of the area you're changing gets expensive fast. In a documentary-style film, effects help when they repair or explain, and they hurt the moment they change what actually happened.

I get asked about effects more than you'd think, usually by someone who's seen a slick advert and wants a bit of that. Fair enough. It's worth knowing what you're actually asking for first.

What's the difference between VFX and motion graphics?

VFX, or visual effects, means changing the footage itself. Something is added to the picture, taken out of it or swapped for something else, and the aim is usually that nobody notices. Motion graphics are designed elements laid over or between the footage: the opening title, the name and job title that appears under someone in an interview, an animated map showing where your sites are, a number counting up.

The two get lumped together because the same people and software often do both. They're priced and judged differently though. Good VFX disappears. Good motion graphics are seen, and should look like they belong to your brand rather than a template library.

What does visual effects work actually involve?

For a business film, nearly all of it falls into a handful of jobs.

Clean-up

Painting out things that distract: a fire exit sign over someone's shoulder, a stray cable, a competitor's van parked in the background, a boom mic dipping into the top of frame. On a locked-off shot this can be quick. On a moving shot it's a different job entirely.

Screen replacement

Phones, laptops and monitors rarely look good on camera. They flicker, reflect the lights and show whatever was on them at the time. Screen replacement puts a clean recording of your app or website onto the screen afterwards. It's common in product films, and it's usually easier if the screen was filmed showing a plain colour with a few tracking marks on it.

Tracking

Tracking follows a point in the picture so that something added later moves with it. A title that sits on a wall as the camera pans past, a label that stays attached to a machine, a replaced screen that stays put when someone tilts their phone. Most other effects rely on it.

Sky replacement

Swapping a white, overexposed sky for a properly exposed one. It's tempting on exteriors shot on grey days, and it's also where effects most easily cross into fiction, which I'll come back to.

Compositing

Layering separate elements into one picture. That covers green screen, putting a product shot into a different background, or combining two takes so that everyone in a group shot looks their best.

Which effects are cheap, and which get expensive?

The cost of an effect has less to do with how impressive it looks and more to do with how much the picture moves and how many frames need touching. A few things push the price up every time:

  • A moving camera. A tripod shot can sometimes be fixed with one corrected frame held for the whole shot. A handheld or gimbal shot needs tracking, and the fix has to survive every frame of the move.
  • Things crossing in front. If a hand, a person or a car passes over the area you're changing, someone has to cut that object out, often frame by frame. That process is called rotoscoping, and it eats hours.
  • Hair, glass and reflections. Fine detail and see-through surfaces are the hardest edges to separate cleanly.
  • Length and volume. One three second shot is a small job. Forty shots of the same fix is a project.

Titles, name captions and a well designed end card are cheap by comparison, especially once they've been designed once and can be reused across every cut-down.

The cheapest visual effect I know is a roll of gaffer tape over a logo before anyone presses record.

That's the real lesson. Almost every clean-up job is cheaper to avoid on the day than to fix afterwards. Move the bin, turn the monitor off, take the sign down, put the van round the corner. It's one of the reasons a recce matters, and it's why our free playbook spends so long on the time before the camera comes out.

When do effects help a documentary-style film?

When they repair the picture without changing the story, or when they explain something the camera can't. A name caption so viewers know who's talking. A simple diagram of a process that happens inside a pipe or a machine. A map of where a business operates. A distraction removed so the eye goes to the person speaking. None of those change what happened, and all of them make the film easier to follow.

A lot of the most useful finishing work isn't strictly VFX at all. It's matching material from different places so it reads as one film.

The Car Planet film for Plug In Stations was made on a live site the client didn't want shown, so it was filmed almost entirely in close up and the edit was filled out from three sources: the day itself, b-roll from previous installs and Car Planet's own image bank. It had to be cut so the joins don't show and it still reads as one day in one place. Nobody watching would call that an effect, and that's the point.

When do effects make a film feel fake?

When they change what happened, or when they're so polished that the viewer starts wondering what else has been changed. Documentary-style films work because they're evidence. The minute an effect makes something look better than it was, the evidence is weaker, and viewers are getting quicker at spotting it. We wrote about that shift in why real people on camera matter more now.

If an effect changes what happened, it's stopped being a repair.

Some places I'd hold back:

  • Replacing the sky on a real event. If it rained on the day, it rained. A dramatic sunset over a commemoration that happened under cloud is a small lie, and small lies are the ones people remember.
  • Showing a product doing something it can't. A screen replacement showing a feature that doesn't exist yet is a misleading advert, whatever tool made it.
  • Heavy retouching on people. Smoothing skin, reshaping faces or tidying a workshop until it looks like a showroom. People are buying the real thing.
  • Motion graphics that wiggle for the sake of it. Animated titles bouncing in on every line pull attention away from the person talking, which is usually the best thing in the film.

Effects can also date a film. A look that was fashionable two years ago screams two years ago. Plain, well set type and honest pictures tend to last.

How should you plan effects into a brand film?

Talk about them before the shoot, not in the edit. If you'll need app screens, a map or a diagram, say so in the brief so the shots are framed with room for them and the graphics are designed alongside the film rather than bolted on. If there's something on site you'd rather not show, say that too, so it can be framed out or moved on the day. Our guide to writing a video brief covers what to include.

Then decide what's worth paying for. A clean title sequence and good name captions are worth it on almost every film. Big compositing jobs belong in campaigns where the idea depends on them. If you're weighing that up, our film budget calculator and how to set a video budget are a sensible place to start.

For most of the films we make, the effects budget is small because the story is carried by real people and real places, shot carefully. If that's the kind of film you're after, here's how we make them, or tell us what you're planning.
items.author: Earl Duncan

faqs.q: Do we need a separate VFX company for a brand film?
faqs.a: Usually not. Clean-up, screen replacement, simple tracking and titles are within reach of a good editor or a motion designer working alongside the edit. A specialist VFX house makes sense when the idea depends on heavy compositing, 3D or a lot of shots needing the same complex fix. If that's the case, it should be planned and budgeted from the start, not discovered in the edit.

faqs.q: Can you remove a logo or brand name from footage after filming?
faqs.a: Often, yes, but it can be fiddly and it costs time, especially if the camera moves or people walk in front of it. It's far cheaper to cover, turn or move the item on the day. If a third-party brand is clearly visible, think about whether you need it removed at all, or whether it's simply background in a real place.

faqs.q: Should a brand film use motion graphics templates?
faqs.a: Templates are fine as a starting point, but they're easy to spot and they make a film look like many others. At minimum, the type, colours and timing should be set to match your brand. A small set of designed titles and captions, used consistently across every cut-down, does more for a film than a lot of borrowed animation.

faqs.q: Is colour grading a visual effect?
faqs.a: Not usually. Grading adjusts the colour and contrast of the whole picture so shots match and the film has a consistent look. It sits in finishing alongside the sound mix. It can overlap with effects when a grade targets one part of the frame, like darkening a bright window, but most people treat it as its own discipline with its own specialists.

items.title: UGC for businesses: what it is and how to use it
items.excerpt: What user-generated content is, how real customer posts differ from paid UGC creators, UK permissions for reusing them, and how UGC sits with a brand film.
items.coverAlt: Three teammates arm in arm at a jiu-jitsu competition
items.body:
User-generated content, or UGC, is content your customers make about you: the photo of the finished kitchen, the clip of a kid collecting a medal, the post tagging your shop. The term is now also used for paid creators who make ads in a casual, customer-style way, which is a different thing entirely, because that's advertising. Both have a place. The rule that matters is never passing one off as the other, and getting permission before you reuse anything a customer made, because in the UK they own the copyright in it.

I like real UGC a lot. It's proof that the thing you do keeps happening, made by people with no reason to flatter you. The paid version I'm more careful with, for reasons I'll get to.

What's the difference between real UGC and paid UGC creators?

Real UGC is made by actual customers, unprompted or with a light nudge, because they wanted to share something. It's often rough, badly lit and completely believable.

Paid UGC is made by creators who are hired to film themselves using a product, usually in a phone-shot, talk-to-camera style designed to look like a customer's post. It's become a big part of social advertising because it's cheap to produce in volume and it fits naturally in a feed. Some of those creators genuinely use the product. Plenty don't, and many are working through a script.

There's nothing wrong with paid creator content as an ad format. The problem starts when it's presented as an independent customer's opinion. It's an advert, so it needs to be clearly identifiable as one. A real customer and an actor in a customer's clothes aren't the same evidence, and viewers are getting better at telling which is which.

If your "customer" has a ring light, a script and an invoice, they're a creator. Lovely people. Different thing.

Where does UGC work best for a business?

Anywhere the question in someone's head is "do people like me actually use this?"

  • Product and service pages. A handful of real customer photos near the price does more than another line of copy.
  • Your social feed. Reposted customer content, credited properly, keeps your channels active between bigger pieces and shows the work is ongoing.
  • Events and community businesses. Gyms, venues, schools and clubs generate content every time something happens, because people want to share their own moment.
  • Paid social. Creator-style ads often perform well in feeds, as long as they're clearly ads.

It's weaker for anything that needs explaining, anything high-value where the buyer wants depth, and anything where the quality of the work is what's on trial. A blurry phone photo of a beautiful renovation can make it look worse than it is.

Can you repost a customer's photo or video?

With their permission, yes. Without it, you're on shaky ground. This is general UK guidance rather than legal advice, so check anything important with a solicitor.

Copyright in the UK is automatic. The government's own guidance is clear that photography and film are protected from the moment they're created, without registering anything, and that copyright stops other people copying the work or putting it on the internet without permission. A customer who posts a photo of your work owns that photo. Posting it publicly gives the platform the rights it needs to show it. It doesn't give you the right to download it and use it on your website or in an ad.

In practice:

  • Ask in writing. A direct message is fine. Say exactly where you'd like to use it, such as your feed, your website or paid ads, and for how long.
  • Credit them the way they'd like, or not at all if they'd rather.
  • Think about who's in it. Permission from the person who took the photo doesn't automatically cover other people in the shot. Be especially careful with children.
  • Keep a record of the permission alongside the file.

There's an advertising side too. The ASA's guidance on user-generated content explains that once a business adopts a customer's post into its own marketing, by reposting it for instance, it becomes the business's responsibility under the advertising code. Claims in it need to be true. It also warns against curating so that only the positive posts survive. And if you've given someone a discount, a freebie or payment for a review or post, the CMA's fake reviews guidance is clear that concealing an incentive is now a banned practice.

A real customer and an actor in a customer's clothes aren't the same evidence.

How does UGC sit alongside a brand film?

They do different jobs. A brand film is the considered version: the full story, filmed properly, with the people who matter, which you can send to someone making a big decision. UGC is volume and recency. It shows that what the film describes is still happening, this week, to people like the viewer.

The closest a brand film gets to UGC is letting the customer tell the story.

The Nimrod Road film is a renovation told entirely by the couple who paid for it, filmed once they'd moved back in. It has the credibility of a customer's own account, with proper sound, proper pictures and consent agreed up front. That's the version I'd put in a sales conversation. Their own photos on social would be the version that keeps the story going.

Done right, the two feed each other. At the grappling competitions we covered, the deliverables included vertical reels the competitors share themselves. The organiser gets professional content, and the athletes spread it to people the organiser would never have reached. Make content people want to share and the sharing takes care of itself. There's more on the trust side in why real people on camera matter more now.

How do you get more genuine customer content?

  • Ask at the right moment. Right after the result, while they're pleased, not three weeks later with the invoice.
  • Make it easy. Tell them what you'd love to see and how to tag you. One clear handle beats a hashtag nobody remembers.
  • Give them something worth sharing. A good photo of the finished job, a clip of their moment. People share what makes them look good.
  • Feature them properly. Credit, thank and celebrate the people who post. Others notice.
  • Don't buy it quietly. If there's an incentive, it has to be disclosed.

If you'd like a brand film that gives your customers something worth sharing, see how we make them or tell us about your business.
items.author: Earl Duncan

faqs.q: Is paid UGC legal in the UK?
faqs.a: Yes, as long as it's honest about what it is. Paid creator content is advertising, so it has to be obviously identifiable as an ad, and any claims in it must be true and backed up. Where it goes wrong is presenting paid content as an independent customer's opinion, or creators posting it on their own channels without labelling it as an ad.

faqs.q: Do we need permission to share a post we've been tagged in?
faqs.a: Using a platform's own share or repost feature, which keeps the original post and credit intact, is generally within the platform's terms. Downloading the photo or video and uploading it yourself, or using it on your website or in ads, needs the creator's permission. Either way, once you've reposted it, it counts as your marketing, so the claims in it become your responsibility.

faqs.q: Can we edit a customer's video before posting it?
faqs.a: Only if they've agreed to that as well. Light trims and adding captions are usually fine to ask for. Cutting their words so they say something different, or reusing their clip in an ad they didn't expect, isn't. Tell them what you plan to do with it, show them the edit if it changes much, and keep their agreement in writing.

faqs.q: Is UGC better than professional video?
faqs.a: It's better at some things. Customer content is quick, cheap and believable, so it's great for showing that people keep buying and enjoying what you do. Professional video is better at telling the full story, explaining something complicated and carrying a high-value decision. Most businesses that use video well do both, with the film as the anchor and UGC keeping it current.

items.title: How to speak on camera when you're not a presenter
items.excerpt: How to speak on camera in a brand film interview: pace, stand-alone answers, energy, stories, pauses, eyeline, hands, nerves and how editors cut you.
items.coverAlt: A speaker talking to camera beside a wartime map
items.body:
To speak well on camera, talk a little slower than you normally would, answer in full sentences that make sense without the question, and tell stories instead of making claims. Look at the person asking, not the lens, let your hands do what they'd normally do, and leave a pause before you start each answer. That pause is a gift to whoever edits it.

None of this needs practice in front of a mirror. It's mostly about understanding what happens to your words after you've said them, because once you know how an editor works, the habits make sense on their own. If you're still at the stage of worrying about the day itself, start with how to prepare for being filmed, then come back here.

How fast should I talk on camera?

A touch slower than feels natural. Nerves speed everyone up, and what feels like a calm pace in the chair often plays back as a rush. Slowing down also gives your brain time to find the next sentence, so you say fewer ums and lose your thread less often.

Don't overdo it, though. Talking deliberately slowly sounds like a hostage video. Aim for the pace you'd use explaining something to a colleague who's genuinely interested and taking notes. If the interviewer thinks you're racing, they'll tell you.

Why do my answers need to stand on their own?

Because the question won't be in the film. In a documentary brand film, the interviewer's voice is almost always cut out, and your answer has to carry the meaning by itself. The well-known tip is folding the question into the answer. "When did you start?" becomes "I started the business in 2011". There's more to it than that, though.

  • Name things. "They were brilliant" means nothing out of context. "The installers were brilliant" works anywhere in the film.
  • Avoid pointing backwards. "Like I said earlier", "as you mentioned" and "going back to that" tie the sentence to a moment the viewer never saw.
  • Don't start with "yeah, so" or "I mean". It's how people naturally start talking, and the editor has to trim it every time.
  • Finish the sentence. Let your voice come down at the end instead of trailing off into "and so, yeah". A clean ending is a clean place to cut.

How does an editor use what I say?

An hour of interview might become three minutes of film. The editor reads a transcript, marks the strongest lines, and builds the story from those, often in a different order from the one you said them in. A sentence from minute forty can open the film. A great answer might be split in two and used in different places.

That's why the stand-alone habit matters so much. Every sentence you say is a possible building block, and the more of them that work in isolation, the more the editor can do with you.

Your words also end up in places you might not expect. The best lines get pulled out as short vertical clips for social, where they play with captions and often without sound. A clear sentence reads as well as it sounds. A rambling one doesn't survive being typed out on screen.

How much energy should I bring?

A bit more than you'd use across a desk. A camera flattens people slightly, so someone who's relaxed in the room can come across as flat on screen. Sitting forward a little, away from the back of the chair, helps more than anything else. It lifts your voice and it makes you look interested, because you are.

What you don't want is presenter energy. Forced enthusiasm is easy to spot and hard to believe. The energy that works on camera is the energy you've already got when you talk about the part of your work you love. A good interviewer will spend time finding that subject, and you'll feel the difference when they do.

Why do stories work better than claims?

Because a viewer can check a story against their own experience, and they can't check a claim at all. "We really care about our customers" is something every business says. "A customer rang at nine on a Saturday because her heating had gone, and our engineer was there by eleven" is something only you can say, and it proves the first sentence without you saying it.

A claim asks the viewer to trust you. A story lets them decide for themselves.

When you feel a claim coming, ask yourself for the example. What happened, when, to whom. There's a whole piece on building those answers in how to give a good interview answer.

Should I pause before answering?

Yes. Take a breath, think, then start. Silence feels enormous in the chair and invisible in the edit, because the editor simply cuts it out. A pause before you start also keeps your first word clear of the end of the question, which matters when the two voices are on separate microphones.

Pauses in the middle are fine too. If you need a moment to find the right word, take it. A searched-for word often lands better than a fluent one, because the viewer can see you meant it.

Where should I look during an interview?

At the interviewer, not the lens. In most documentary interviews the person asking sits just beside the camera, so your eyeline goes slightly off to one side. It reads as you talking to someone in the room, and the viewer watches a conversation. Keep looking at them even when you're thinking. Glancing at the camera mid-answer, or at someone else in the room, is one of the few things that's hard to cut around.

There are exceptions. A piece to camera, where you're talking directly to the viewer, needs you to look straight down the lens. And some directors set things up so the interview happens straight to camera. Errol Morris built a device he called the Interrotron, which projects his face onto glass in front of the lens, so the person can look him in the eye and look straight down the barrel at the same time. You can see the effect in his film The Fog of War, where Robert McNamara looks straight out at you.

It's intense, and it's a deliberate choice for a particular kind of film. For a brand film, the off-axis conversation is usually kinder and more natural. If the crew wants you to look into the lens, they'll tell you.

What do I do with my hands?

Whatever you'd normally do. People who talk with their hands should keep doing it, because pinning them down makes the rest of you stiff. Rest them loosely in your lap between answers and let them come up when they want to.

There are a few things to avoid. Don't tap your chest, where the mic lives. Don't fiddle with a pen, a ring or the arm of the chair, because the mic hears it. And keep big gestures roughly at chest height, so they stay in the frame on a closer shot rather than flashing in and out of the bottom edge.

Nobody has ever watched a brand film and thought, lovely answer, shame about the hands.

How do I stop nerves showing?

Mostly you don't have to. The first ten or fifteen minutes of any interview are a warm-up, and a good interviewer will spend them on easy questions while you settle. The nervous answers from the start rarely make the cut, and you'll be past them before the questions that matter.

A few physical things help. Breathe out for longer than you breathe in, a couple of times, before you sit down. Go easy on the coffee. Keep water nearby and take a sip between answers. And don't learn lines. People who memorise answers spend the interview trying to remember them, which looks far more nervous than someone simply thinking.

If someone on your team is dreading their turn, the most useful thing you can tell them is that the edit is on their side. Every stumble, restart and long pause comes out. What's left is them at their clearest. And if you'd like to see what that looks like in a finished film, have a look at our films or get in touch.
items.author: Earl Duncan

faqs.q: Should I watch myself back after the interview?
faqs.a: You can, but there's not much to gain from watching raw footage. Everyone dislikes hearing their own voice, and the rushes include every stumble that the edit will remove. It's far more useful to see the rough cut, where you're shown at your clearest and can comment on whether the story is right.

faqs.q: Is it fine to swear in a brand film interview?
faqs.a: It's fine to swear in the room if that's how you talk, and it can help you relax. Whether it stays in the film is a decision for you and the business, and most brand films cut it or bleep it. If a great answer has a swear in the middle, the interviewer may ask you to say it again without.

faqs.q: What if English isn't my first language?
faqs.a: Speak in whichever way feels most natural and don't worry about the odd mistake. Accents and imperfect grammar don't stop an answer working, and sincerity matters far more than polish. If you'd find it easier to answer some questions in your first language, say so, because subtitles are a normal part of documentary films.

faqs.q: Can I have notes with me during the interview?
faqs.a: A few prompts are fine, like names, dates or numbers you're worried about forgetting. Keep them off camera and glance at them between answers rather than reading from them. Full written answers are a bad idea, because reading changes your voice and your eyeline, and the viewer can tell straight away.

stat.takeaway: Your words are likely to be read as well as heard, so clear, complete sentences carry further than rambling ones.
