items.title: Why the best work comes from people who trust you
items.excerpt: Why the best creative work comes from people who already trust you, and how to stay in touch without pestering: no-agenda check-ins and small useful things.
items.coverAlt: A man laughing with a colleague on an exhibition stand
items.body:
The best work tends to come from people who already trust you, because trust makes everything easier. They tell you the real budget and the real worry. They give you proper access. They make decisions quickly and back your judgement on the day. You earn that by staying in touch without asking for anything, doing small useful things, and treating every project as one chapter in a longer conversation.

I'd go further and say that for a documentary studio, trust is most of the job. We're asking people to let us into their workplace, put a microphone on them and talk honestly about something they care about. That's a lot to ask of a stranger.

Why does the best work come from people who already know you?

Because the first project with anyone spends a lot of energy on working each other out. Will they deliver? Do they get what we do? Can I say what I actually think in this meeting? All reasonable questions, and all time not spent on the film.

Once that's settled, the brief gets honest. A client who trusts you will tell you the thing they'd normally keep back, like the part of the business they're nervous about showing, or the person who'll freeze on camera, or the budget they really have. Those details are what a good film gets built on. You can't plan around a worry nobody's mentioned.

And it shows on screen. People talk differently to someone they've met before. Interviews loosen up faster, staff stop performing sooner, and the moments that make a documentary feel true turn up earlier in the day.

What's the difference between a relationship and a transaction?

In a transaction, the conversation ends when the invoice is paid. In a relationship, delivery is somewhere in the middle.

The difference is mostly in what happens after the film goes out. Do you ask how it's landing? Do you notice they've posted it in the wrong shape for a platform and send them the right cut? Do you remember that the launch was this week and drop them a line? None of that takes long, and almost none of it is billable. It's also exactly what people mention when they recommend you.

I want any deal we do to feel fair to both sides, and a relationship is what makes that possible over time. When you know you'll be working together again, nobody's trying to squeeze the last drop out of one job.

How do you stay in touch without pestering?

Only get in touch when there's a reason that's about them. A good test is whether they'd be glad to get the message even if they never bought anything from you again. If the honest answer is no, don't send it.

"Just checking in to see if you've got any projects coming up" fails that test every time. It's a sales email dressed up as a hello, and people can tell. They start reading everything you send as a pitch, which is a hard habit to undo.

If you only write to someone when you want something, they'll learn to read every email you send that way.

Spacing matters too. There's no fixed rule, but every few months is plenty for most people unless you're actually working together. Silence in between is fine. Silence isn't rude, and nobody's sitting there wondering why you haven't emailed.

What does a check-in with no agenda look like?

Short, and it says outright that there's no agenda. Then it means it. It asks how they are, or how something they mentioned turned out, and it ends there. No link, no "while I've got you", no call to action tucked into the last line.

This matters most when someone's going through something hard. Illness, a bereavement, a rough year for the business. Work can wait, and it should. If there was a project on the table, the kindest thing to say is that nothing has changed or expired at your end and there's genuinely no rush. Then leave them to it. People remember who checked on them when they had nothing to offer back.

The most underrated business tool I know is remembering what someone told you last time. No subscription required.

What small, useful things actually build trust?

Most of them take five minutes. A few that tend to go down well:

  • Sending a cut they'll need before they ask for it, like a vertical version for a campaign you know is coming.
  • Pointing out a broken video link or an old film still sitting on their homepage.
  • Introducing them to someone who can genuinely help them, with no angle for you.
  • Tagging and crediting them properly when you share the work, so they get the attention as well.
  • Passing on something you read that's relevant to their sector.
  • Remembering the detail, whether that's the launch date, the new hire or the event they were dreading.

None of these are tactics if you do them because they're useful. They only become tactics when you do them while counting.

Doesn't this take too long for a small business?

Honestly, yes, it's slower. Relationship work doesn't show up in this month's numbers, and there are weeks when it feels like a luxury. I'd be lying if I said I never wondered whether the time would be better spent sending more cold emails.

But cold outreach is hard work for a small studio, and most of it goes nowhere. Work that comes back from people who already know you takes less convincing, starts from a better brief, and usually ends in a better film. Over a few years, that adds up to most of what keeps a studio going. It's also a much nicer way to spend your days.

How does this show up in the films themselves?

In the access. On a second or third shoot with the same people you know where the light's good at that time of day, who'll talk for an hour and who needs a quiet word first, and which corner of the building nobody wants on camera. All of that time goes back into the film.

It's also why we like ongoing work as much as one-off films. When you film the same business regularly, you start to see the stories they're too close to notice. Our post on turning one film into a year of content goes into how that works in practice.

If you'd like to see the kind of work that comes out of that trust, have a look at our films. And if you've a story in mind, even a vague one, drop us a line. No pitch, just a conversation.
items.author: Earl Duncan

faqs.q: How often should a small business contact past clients?
faqs.a: Every few months is plenty for most past clients, as long as each message has a reason that's about them. A film relevant to their sector, a note on something they launched, or a simple hello all count. If you're working together on an ongoing basis you'll naturally talk more, but for everyone else, less often and more useful beats a regular newsletter they don't read.

faqs.q: Is a newsletter a good way to stay in touch with clients?
faqs.a: It can be, if it's genuinely useful and people chose to get it. But it doesn't replace a personal message. A newsletter goes to everyone, so it can't remember that someone's launch was this week or that they mentioned a new hire. Use one for broad updates if you like, and keep the personal notes personal.

faqs.q: How do you ask a happy client for a referral without it feeling awkward?
faqs.a: Ask once, specifically, at a natural moment such as just after they've told you they're pleased with the work. Name the kind of person you'd love to meet rather than asking if they know anyone at all. Then make it easy to say no. Most people are glad to help someone who's looked after them, and a light ask respects that.

faqs.q: Should you send clients gifts to build the relationship?
faqs.a: Small, thoughtful gestures are fine, but they're no substitute for being useful. A handwritten note or something connected to a conversation you had will mean more than a branded hamper. Be careful with public sector and larger organisations, as many have rules on accepting gifts. When in doubt, a useful introduction or an extra cut of their film is the better present.

items.title: Shotgun microphones explained for interviews
items.excerpt: What a shotgun mic is, how polar patterns work, boom versus on-camera, indoors versus outdoors, wind protection, and why interviews pair it with a lav.
items.coverAlt: A panel talk in a marquee at the Southwick D-Day 80 event
items.body:
A shotgun microphone is a long, thin mic that mostly hears what it's pointed at and turns down sound coming from the sides. It's the mic you see on the end of a boom pole on a film set, held just above the frame and aimed at the speaker's mouth. It works best close to the voice, outdoors or in rooms that aren't too echoey, and it struggles when it's sat on top of a camera several metres away.

I've written about lav mics and wireless systems already. This is the other half of interview sound: what a shotgun actually does, where it goes, and why it's so often paired with a lav.

How does a shotgun microphone work?

Inside the long tube is a fairly normal directional capsule. The tube is what makes it a shotgun. It's called an interference tube, and it's covered in slots or holes along its length.

Sound arriving from straight ahead travels down the tube cleanly and reaches the capsule in one go. Sound arriving from the side comes in through the slots at lots of slightly different points, so the pieces arrive at the capsule out of step with each other and partly cancel out. The result is a mic that's noticeably more sensitive in front than at the sides.

Two things follow from that. First, the trick works better at higher frequencies than lower ones, so a shotgun is less directional for low rumble like traffic and air con than it is for voices. Second, sound from off to the side gets quieter and also coloured, sounding thin, hollow and a bit phasey. That colouring matters a lot indoors, which I'll get to.

Length changes things too. A short shotgun is the everyday film and TV mic, easy to boom and forgiving. A long shotgun reaches further and rejects more from the sides, which suits outdoor work and documentaries where you can't get close, but it's heavier, harder to aim and less forgiving when the speaker moves.

What are polar patterns?

A polar pattern is a map of which directions a mic hears best. They're drawn as a shape around the mic, and the ones you'll hear about most are:

  • Omnidirectional. Hears equally in every direction. Most lavs are omni, which works because they're so close to the mouth.
  • Cardioid. A heart shape. Hears the front well, the sides less, and the back hardly at all. Common on vocal mics.
  • Supercardioid and hypercardioid. Tighter at the front than a cardioid, with a small sensitive patch at the back. Good indoors on a boom.
  • Lobar. The narrow, stretched shape of a shotgun, very tight at the front with smaller lobes elsewhere, including at the back.

That little patch at the back catches people out. A shotgun pointed down at someone from above is also listening, faintly, to whatever's above it. A shotgun on a camera pointed at a speaker is also listening to the camera operator breathing behind it.

A shotgun hears the sides a bit less. Distance still decides how it sounds.

Does a shotgun mic pick up sound from far away?

Not in the way most people think. It doesn't zoom. It hears a distant voice no louder than any other mic would, it just hears less of the room around it. Distance still wins.

Every time you double the distance between a mic and a mouth, the voice drops by around six decibels, while the room noise stays where it was. So a shotgun at three metres sounds roomier and thinner than the same mic at half a metre, however good it is. On a sit-down interview, the boom wants to be as close as the frame allows, usually somewhere between a forearm and an arm's length from the mouth.

Boom or on-camera: which is better?

For an interview, the boom, by a long way. A boom pole lets the mic sit just out of shot, close to the voice, aimed exactly where it needs to be. The camera can be wherever the picture needs it to be.

The usual position is overhead, angled down at the mouth or upper chest, just above the top of the frame. From there the mic hears the voice, and its less sensitive sides face the walls. Booming from below, pointing up from under the frame, is sometimes used to get away from noise above, like a ceiling full of air con, though it tends to pick up more of the body and the floor.

A good boom operator is doing a real job. They watch the frame edge so the mic never dips in, follow the speaker as they lean and turn, and keep the pole steady for an hour. It's more tiring than it looks.

An on-camera shotgun is fine for what it's for: picking up sound you'll use to line up audio in the edit, recording atmosphere, and grabbing quick moments when you're right next to someone. For a proper interview it's usually too far away, pointed wherever the camera's pointed rather than at the mouth, and it hears the operator's every move. It's better than the camera's built-in mic. It's still the wrong tool for the job.

The camera-top shotgun is the mic equivalent of shouting your order from the back of the queue. Technically it gets there.

Should you use a shotgun indoors or outdoors?

Outdoors is where a shotgun is happiest. There are no walls to bounce sound back, so the tight front pattern works exactly as intended. Point it so the noise you don't want, a road or a building site, is off to the side or behind, and angle it down so the background is the ground rather than the street.

Indoors is trickier. In a small room with hard walls, your voice bounces around and arrives at the mic from every direction. The shotgun hears those reflections through its sides and colours them, so the voice can come out hollow and boxy. That's why many sound recordists switch to a hypercardioid mic for interiors. It's shorter, handles reflections more gracefully and is easier to swing in a cramped space. Soft furnishings, rugs and curtains help either way, and picking the least echoey room for the interview is one of the easiest wins there is.

Why do interviews often use a boom and a lav together?

Because they fail in different ways. The boom sounds open and natural, like you're sat across from the person, but it can be caught out by a bus going past or the speaker leaning out of its sweet spot. The lav is right on the chest so it holds up in noise, but it can rustle and sometimes sounds a bit close and boxed in.

Recording both to separate tracks means the editor can pick the better one moment by moment, or blend them. When they're blended, the two need lining up carefully, because the boom is further away and its sound arrives a fraction later, which can make the mix sound thin if it's ignored.

Our coverage of the D-Day eightieth anniversary in Southwick is a good reminder of why sound gets planned in layers. It included a full panel talk recorded end to end in front of a packed marquee, at an event that couldn't be asked for twice. When nothing can be repeated, two sources for every voice is the sensible default.

How do you stop wind noise on a shotgun mic?

With layers of protection, and the more wind there is, the more layers you need.

  • Foam. The grey sleeve most shotguns come with. Fine indoors, and for the small rush of air when a boom is swung. Close to useless in a real breeze.
  • Slip-on fur. A furry sleeve that fits straight over the mic. Good for on-camera mics and light wind.
  • Basket windshield. A cage, sometimes called a blimp or zeppelin, that surrounds the mic with a pocket of still air. Wind hits the cage, not the capsule.
  • Fur over the basket. The fluffy grey thing on a pole you see at outdoor shoots. The fur slows the air before it reaches the cage, and together they deal with strong wind.

A low-cut filter, on the mic or the recorder, trims the very low rumble that wind and traffic produce without touching much of the voice. A shock mount, the cradle of elastic the mic sits in, stops knocks on the pole travelling into the recording. Neither replaces proper wind protection, but both help.

The lav needs protecting outdoors as well. I use URSA Fur Circles on lav mics, small furry discs that sit over the capsule under or on the clothing, because a lav catches wind just as easily as a shotgun does. If you want to see how sound fits into everything else on a shoot, what a shoot day looks like walks through it, and our free guide covers the planning before it.
items.author: Earl Duncan

faqs.q: Can you use a shotgun mic for a podcast or voiceover?
faqs.a: You can, but it's rarely the best choice. A voiceover is usually recorded close up in a treated space, where a large diaphragm cardioid studio mic sounds fuller and warmer. Shotguns are built for film sets, where the mic has to stay out of shot. If a shotgun is all you have, get it close, point it at the mouth and record in a room with plenty of soft furnishings.

faqs.q: Do shotgun mics need phantom power?
faqs.a: Most professional shotguns are condenser mics and need 48 volt phantom power, supplied by the recorder, mixer or camera through the XLR cable. Some can also run on an internal battery. Small on-camera shotguns often take power from the camera's mic socket or have their own battery. Check before the shoot, because a mic with no power records nothing at all.

faqs.q: How far should a boom mic be from the speaker?
faqs.a: As close as the frame allows, which for a sit-down interview usually means roughly half a metre to a metre from the mouth, just above the top edge of the shot. Closer means more voice and less room. A wide shot pushes the mic further away, which is one reason many crews frame interviews in mid shots or close-ups and rely on the lav for wider angles.

faqs.q: Is an expensive shotgun mic worth it?
faqs.a: Up to a point. Better shotguns tend to have lower self-noise, smoother off-axis sound and better handling of humidity, which matters on long outdoor days. But placement and wind protection make a bigger difference than price. A mid-range mic on a boom half a metre from the mouth will beat an expensive one sat on a camera across the room every time.

items.title: How video actually makes a business money
items.excerpt: The real routes from a brand film to revenue, from trust before the first call to faster sales and hiring, how to measure it simply, and what video can't do.
items.coverAlt: Visitors talking on a busy exhibition stand
items.body:
Video mostly makes a business money indirectly. It builds trust before the first call, shortens the time between someone finding you and deciding, lifts conversion on the pages where people make up their minds, helps you hire, gives the press and partners something to run, and keeps feeding your channels for months. It's rare for someone to watch a film and buy on the spot. The way to know it's working is to pick one of those routes before you make the film, and measure one number against it.

I'd rather be straight about this than sell you on magic. A film is a tool for a sales process you already have. Used well, it makes that process quicker and easier. Left on a homepage on its own, it mostly makes you feel good.

How does a film actually turn into revenue?

Through a handful of routes, and most good films work on two or three at once.

Trust before the first call

If a prospect has already watched your founder talk, seen your team at work and heard a customer describe the job, the first call starts further along. You spend less time proving you're real and more time talking about their problem. For higher priced services, where people research before they ever get in touch, that's where a film does its heaviest lifting.

Shorter sales cycles

Most business decisions involve more than one person, and some of them never meet you. A film you can send after a meeting goes to the finance director, the partner, the board member who'll make the call without ever speaking to you. Fewer meetings to get everyone comfortable means a quicker yes or a quicker no, and both save you money.

Higher conversion on the pages that matter

The pages that make you money are usually a few service pages and the contact page. A short, relevant film on those pages gives someone who's nearly convinced the last bit of reassurance. That works far better than a general film on the homepage that's trying to talk to everyone.

Recruitment

Good people check you out the same way buyers do. A film that shows the real work and the real people helps the right candidates apply and the wrong ones rule themselves out, which saves money on every hire.

PR and partnerships

Journalists, event organisers and partners need something to show. A well made film gives a partner something to post on their own channels and gives a story a visual to run with.

Repurposing

One shoot becomes a main film, a short cut, vertical clips and stills. That's months of content that would otherwise cost time or money to produce. We cover how in turning one brand film into a year of content.

Super Efficient are a good example of the trust route. Almost all of their work came from recommendation, which is a good problem and a fragile one. The brief was to turn the work they already do into something a stranger can watch, judge them on and call them about, without adding a single day to their diary. One day on one job became a longform film, shorts and carousels aimed at two different buyers.

How do you measure whether a video is making money?

Simply. Fancy attribution models tend to give confident answers to questions they can't really answer. A few honest measures beat a dashboard nobody trusts.

  1. Decide the route first. Is this film meant to help sales calls, a specific service page or hiring? That's the whole argument of why a brand film needs a business goal.
  2. Take a baseline. Enquiries per month from that page, how long deals take to close, how many applicants a typical job ad gets. Write it down before the film goes live.
  3. Ask people. Add "did you watch our film?" to your enquiry form or first call. It's crude, and it's also the most reliable signal a small business has.
  4. Track the sends. If the film's for sales, count how often it's sent and how those deals go compared with the ones where it wasn't.
  5. Check the watching. YouTube and most hosting tools show how much of a film people watch. If everyone leaves at thirty seconds, the film's job is being done by the first thirty seconds.

Then give it time, which is the hard part.

How long before a video pays for itself?

About as long as your sales cycle, and usually a bit longer. If customers take a week to decide, you'll get a feel within a couple of months. If deals take six months and involve a committee, the first film sent in a sales conversation might not show up in revenue for half a year.

That's why I'm wary of anyone who promises a return figure up front. The honest answer depends on your prices, your margins and how many people are already looking at you. Our film budget calculator can help with the cost side, and how to set a video budget works backwards from what a new customer is worth.

Which film should you make first if money's the goal?

The one closest to the sale. For most businesses that's a customer story about the service you most want to sell, told by a customer whose situation looks like the people you want more of. It goes straight into sales conversations and onto the page where that service is sold. A founder story or a broader brand film earns its place too, but it usually works further from the moment someone decides. There's more on making the customer version land in testimonial videos that don't sound like testimonials.

What can't video do for a business?

Quite a lot, and it's better to know before you spend.

  • It can't fix an offer people don't want or a price that's wrong for the market.
  • It can't make up for slow replies. If enquiries sit for three days, a better film just means more people waiting.
  • It can't reach people on its own. A film nobody's sent, posted or put behind ads does nothing. See where to put your brand film.
  • It won't usually produce a sale you can trace neatly from one view to one invoice. Most of its value shows up as things going a bit easier.

A film can get someone to pick up the phone. It can't make you answer it.

A film is a tool for a sales process you already have. On its own, it mostly makes you feel good.

If you've got a process that works and you'd like it to work faster, that's exactly when a film is worth making. See how we make them, or tell us where your sales get stuck and we'll tell you honestly whether a film would help.
items.author: Earl Duncan

faqs.q: Can a single video really increase sales?
faqs.a: It can, but usually by helping a sale that was already possible go more smoothly, rather than creating one from nothing. A film that answers the questions buyers ask, sent at the right moment, tends to shorten decisions and reduce drop-off. It works best alongside a decent offer, quick replies and a sales process people can actually follow.

faqs.q: What metrics should we report on a brand film?
faqs.a: Pick the ones linked to the film's job. For sales, track how often it's sent and how those deals close. For a service page, track enquiries from that page against a baseline. For hiring, track applicant numbers and quality. Views and likes are worth glancing at, but they rarely tell you whether the film is earning its keep.

faqs.q: Is a cheaper video a better return than an expensive film?
faqs.a: Sometimes. A modest video that answers one common question can pay back quickly. A bigger film earns its cost when trust is what's being bought, prices are high and people research hard before committing. The right spend depends on what a new customer is worth to you, so work out that number before deciding how much to put into the film.

faqs.q: Should we put ad spend behind our film to get a return?
faqs.a: Often behind the short cuts, yes, especially shown to people who've already visited your site. A full length film rarely works as a cold ad to strangers. Before spending, make sure your licence and the music licence cover paid advertising on every platform you'll use, and set a clear goal for the campaign so you can tell if it worked.

items.title: What to wear on camera for an interview
items.excerpt: What to wear on camera: colours that film well, why stripes shimmer, logos, fit, mic-friendly layers, glasses, jewellery, make-up and what to pack as a backup.
items.coverAlt: A man in a plain green jumper being interviewed in a living room
items.body:
For a filmed interview, wear solid, mid-tone clothes that fit you sitting down, in fabrics that don't rustle, with a collar or a proper waistband so the mic has somewhere to go. Skip fine patterns, other brands' logos and anything that jangles. Bring a second top in a different colour, some blotting paper or powder for shine, and the glasses you always wear.

I've covered the basics in how to prepare for being filmed. This is the longer version, for people who want to know why the rules exist and what to do when their wardrobe doesn't fit them neatly.

What colours look best on camera?

Mid tones. Navy, slate, olive, rust, mustard, a dusty blue or a soft green. They hold their detail, they sit well against most backgrounds, and they don't fight with the face for attention.

The colours that cause trouble are the extremes. Bright white sits at the very top of what a camera can record, so the person exposing the shot has a choice: keep detail in the shirt and let the face go a bit dark, or expose for the face and let the shirt glow. That gets harder the darker your skin is, because the gap between shirt and face is bigger. Solid black has the opposite problem, and it can turn into a flat shape with no folds in it. Neither is banned. They just make the job harder, and an off-white or a charcoal does nearly everything the extremes do without the fuss.

The thing people forget is the background. If you're being filmed against a navy wall and you turn up in navy, you'll disappear into it. You don't need to know the exact set, so just ask the crew what's behind you. A quick message the week before saves a change of shirt on the day.

Why do stripes and checks shimmer on camera?

The effect is called moiré. A camera sensor is a grid of tiny pixels, and a fine, regular pattern is also a grid. When the two grids nearly line up, they interfere with each other and you get rippling bands of colour that crawl across the fabric every time you move. Your eyes see a perfectly nice shirt. The camera sees a television that's lost its signal.

The usual offenders are pinstripes, narrow stripes, small checks, herringbone, houndstooth, fine corduroy and some knitted textures. The problem is that it depends on the camera, the lens and how wide the shot is, so the same shirt can be fine in a close-up and wobble in a wide.

Every office has one person whose favourite shirt is a fine check. Ask them, gently, to bring a second one.

A quick test at home: film yourself on your phone from a few feet away and zoom in slightly. If the pattern starts dancing, it'll probably dance on the day. Moiré is very hard to remove in the edit, so it's one to settle before you leave the house.

Can I wear a logo or branded clothing?

Your own company's branding is usually fine, and sometimes it's exactly right. Check with whoever's making the film, because some brand films deliberately keep logos out so the people feel less like a corporate video.

Other brands' logos are a different matter. A big sportswear logo on your chest pulls focus, and if the film ends up in paid advertising, a visible third-party brand can cause headaches nobody wants.

How should clothes fit when you're sitting down?

Most interviews are filmed seated, and clothes behave differently in a chair. Jackets ride up at the back and bunch at the collar. Shirts pull and gape between the buttons. Trousers rise, and suddenly the wide shot is all shin and sock.

Do the sit test. Put the outfit on, sit in a chair in front of a mirror, lean forward a little the way people do when they're talking, and look. If anything pulls, gapes or bunches, change it.

For the filmed work, the bits of you doing your job, wear what you'd actually wear to do it. If you're up a ladder or at a bench, your normal work clothes look right, and anything else looks like a costume.

Our film about Signwriting Jack is shot in the workshop and out on the shopfronts. In a film like that the clothes are part of the place, and anything smarter than the work would look odd up a ladder.

What should I wear so the mic is easy to fit?

This is where layers help. The interview mic is usually a small lavalier clipped to the chest, with a cable running down to a transmitter pack on the waistband or belt. I've explained how it all works in lav mics explained, but from a wardrobe point of view, you want three things:

  • Somewhere to clip it. A shirt placket, a collar, the edge of a jacket. A plain crew-neck t-shirt works too, though the mic sits a bit more exposed.
  • A route for the cable. A buttoned shirt or a jacket lets the cable run inside out of sight.
  • Somewhere for the pack. A belt or a firm waistband. A dress with no waistband means the pack goes on a thigh strap or clipped somewhere at the back, which is fine but worth knowing about in advance.

Fabric matters as much as the cut. Cotton and wool are quiet. Silk, stiff new shirts, synthetics and waterproofs rustle against the mic every time you breathe. A chunky knit muffles the voice if the mic has to go underneath it. If you're torn between two outfits, wear the cotton one.

Will my glasses reflect on camera?

They can, but wear them anyway if you normally wear them. You'll look like yourself, and squinting is worse than any reflection.

Reflections come from lights and windows bouncing off the lenses. Moving a light higher or wider usually fixes it, and I've explained where those lights sit in interview lighting explained. Lifting the arms of the glasses very slightly off the ears angles the lenses down, which is an old trick that works more often than it should. An anti-reflective coating helps a lot.

The one pair to leave at home is lenses that darken in daylight. Near a window or outside, they'll slowly turn to sunglasses mid-interview, and the edit can't fix that.

What jewellery should I avoid on camera?

Anything that moves and makes a noise. Bangles and chunky bracelets clink against the table and the chair. Long necklaces swing into the mic. Big hoop earrings can tap a collar mic. Lanyards and ID badges knock against everything, and they often carry a name and a photo you might not want in a film. A watch is fine until you rest your wrist on a hard table, then every gesture becomes a tap.

Your eyes see a perfectly nice shirt. The camera sees a television that's lost its signal.

Rings, studs and a simple necklace that sits close to the neck are usually fine. If a piece matters to you, keep it on and tell the sound person, and they'll work around it.

Do I need make-up for a filmed interview?

Most people don't need much, men included. The main enemy is shine. Interview lighting picks up oil on the forehead, the nose and the top of the head, and a shiny patch reads as sweat even when you're calm.

  • For everyone: a translucent powder or blotting papers for shine, lip balm, and moisturiser that's had time to sink in.
  • If you don't usually wear make-up: powder is enough. If you shave, do it a few hours before rather than right before, so any redness settles. Bald heads shine more than you'd think, so powder there too.
  • If you do usually wear make-up: wear your everyday look, slightly more defined if anything. Go easy on shimmer and highlighter, which turn into hot spots under lights, and match foundation carefully at the jaw so there's no line.

What should I bring as a backup?

A small bag that saves a lot of trouble:

  • A second top in a different colour, in case the first clashes with the background or shimmers.
  • A plain t-shirt or vest to wear under a shirt, which helps the mic and hides it.
  • Blotting papers or powder, lip balm, a comb or brush.
  • Your glasses case, and contact lens kit if you use one.
  • A lint roller, because dark fabric shows every hair under good light.

If you're organising the shoot for other people, forward them this a week before rather than the night before. And if you want the whole planning side in one place, our free playbook, Before the camera comes out, covers it. When you're ready to talk about a film, tell us about the business.
items.author: Earl Duncan

faqs.q: Can I wear a white shirt on camera?
faqs.a: Yes, but an off-white or pale blue is easier. Bright white sits at the top of what a camera can record, so the crew has to choose between detail in the shirt and a well-exposed face. Under a jacket or jumper it's much less of a problem, because there's less of it in the frame.

faqs.q: Should I wear the same outfit on both days of a shoot?
faqs.a: Usually yes, if the interview might carry on into the second day or the editor might cut between the two. Changing clothes mid-story breaks continuity and makes the edit harder. If the days are clearly separate, say an interview one day and filming the work the next, check with the crew first and they'll tell you what matters.

faqs.q: Is it fine to wear a hat or cap in an interview?
faqs.a: If it's what you always wear for work, often yes, though a peak can throw a shadow across your eyes under interview lighting. The crew can usually light around it or ask you to tip it back slightly. Avoid caps with large logos, and bear in mind a hat you take off halfway through can cause continuity problems in the edit.

faqs.q: Do I need to bring my own make-up to a shoot?
faqs.a: Bring whatever you'd use on a normal day, plus blotting papers or translucent powder for shine. Plenty of brand film shoots don't have a make-up artist, so check in advance whether it's down to you. Keep it simple and close to how you usually look, because the aim is for you to look like yourself on a good day.

items.title: Never burn a bridge: how to close the file kindly
items.excerpt: How to end a sales conversation that's gone quiet so the door stays open: the close-the-file email, why people come back later, and how to take a no.
items.coverAlt: People chatting with drinks at an outdoor work event
items.body:
If a conversation with a prospect has gone quiet, the kindest thing you can do is close it yourself. Send one short, warm email saying you've not heard back, that you're taking it as the timing not being right, and that you'll stop there. Leave one door open, tied to something real in their world. People remember being let go gracefully, and a good number of them come back when things change.

Most advice on follow-up is about squeezing a reply out of someone. Chase on day three, day seven, day fourteen, then a "breakup email" written to guilt them into answering. I understand why it exists. I just don't think it suits a business where the work depends on people liking you enough to let you into their building with a camera.

Why does it matter how a conversation ends?

Because the ending is the part people remember. Someone might forget the details of your proposal within a week. They won't forget whether you made them feel hassled.

In creative work especially, a no is rarely a verdict on you. It's usually timing. A budget that hasn't been signed off, a board that hasn't met, a person who's left, a launch that's slipped to next year. None of that's permanent. If the last thing they had from you was polite and easy, you're still a name they'd be glad to see when those things change. If the last thing was the fifth "just bumping this up", you've turned a not yet into a never.

There's a practical side too. The people we'd most like to work with tend to know each other. Marketing leads move jobs, founders sit on the same panels, charity directors compare notes. A heavy-handed chase doesn't stay between you and one inbox.

How many times should you follow up before stopping?

For us it's usually twice, then a close. One email to start, one follow-up a week or so later with something genuinely useful in it, and then a short note saying we'll leave it there. Three touches, spread out, each one easy to ignore without feeling guilty.

The number matters less than the reason behind each email. A follow-up has to earn its place. If you've nothing new to say, saying it again won't help. "Did you get my last email?" is the clearest example. They did. They're busy, or it isn't right for them, and either answer is fine.

And if they've actually told you no, you don't follow up at all. You say thanks, you mean it, and you wish them well with whatever's on their plate.

What does a good "close the file" email say?

Not much, which is the point. It does four things:

  • Says what's happened, plainly. You've written twice and not heard back, or the quote went out and it's gone quiet.
  • Gives them the generous reading. You're assuming it's timing rather than anything else, and that's completely fair.
  • Says you'll stop, so they don't have to manage you.
  • Leaves one specific door open, linked to something they're actually doing, rather than a vague "let me know if anything changes".

Something like: "I've not heard back, which usually means the timing isn't right, and that's completely fair. I'll stop there rather than keep turning up in your inbox. If the new site goes ahead and a film would help, I'd be glad to pick it up then. Shall I close the file?"

That last question does a lot of work. It can be answered in one word, it hands them the decision, and it's the easiest email in the whole sequence to reply to. Some people will say yes, close it, thanks for asking. Some will say sorry, it's been chaos here, can we talk in the spring. Both are better than silence, and both leave you on good terms.

Nobody has ever read a fifth chaser and felt warmer about the sender. They've just got quicker at the delete key.

Why do people come back months later?

Because their situation changes and yours hasn't. The budget lands in a new financial year. The person who was blocking it moves on. A launch finally gets a date. When that happens they think of whoever left the cleanest impression, and that's rarely the person who chased hardest.

A closed file also takes the awkwardness away. There's no pile of unanswered emails for them to apologise for before they can say hello again. You've cleared the slate for them, which makes getting back in touch easy.

A no is usually about timing, and timing changes. How you took it doesn't.

How do you take a no without it stinging?

It does sting a bit, especially when you've put time into a proposal or a treatment you were proud of. I don't think pretending otherwise helps anyone. What helps is having a way of handling it that you don't have to think about.

Reply the same day if you can. Thank them for letting you know, because plenty of people never do, and a clear no is a courtesy. If they've gone with someone else, wish the project well and mean it. If it turns out to be a good film, that's good for everyone who makes this kind of work.

Then, if it feels right, ask one useful question. Not "why didn't you pick us", which puts them on the spot. Something that helps you next time, like who usually holds the budget for this kind of work, or whether there's a better time of year to talk. Most people are happy to answer one small question from someone who's taken the news well.

What you don't do is argue, knock the price down on the spot, or send a revised proposal nobody asked for. That tells them your first number wasn't real. There's more on that in why we don't undercut on price.

Isn't closing the file just giving up?

I see it as choosing where your energy goes. Every hour spent chasing someone who's gone quiet is an hour taken from the people who do want to talk, or from the work itself. A small studio can't keep twenty half-open conversations alive on hope.

It's also more honest. Keeping someone in a follow-up sequence they never asked to join is a way of avoiding their answer. Closing the file means accepting it, and it makes the rest of your week a lot lighter.

How do you keep the door open without pestering?

Leave it alone for a good while, then only come back with a reason that's about them. A film you've made that's close to what they do. Some news in their world you genuinely noticed. A check in that asks for nothing. If you've nothing to say, don't write. I've gone into this more in why the best work comes from people who already trust you.

Keep a note of the closed files somewhere you'll actually see it. Not to chase anyone, just so that when their name turns up again you remember the context and can pick it up properly, without asking them to repeat everything.

And if you're on the other side of this, with a film in mind and no rush at all, that's completely fine by us. Get in touch whenever it suits, or read our free guide first so you know what to expect before the camera comes out.
items.author: Earl Duncan

faqs.q: How long should I wait before sending a closing email?
faqs.a: Two to three weeks after your last follow-up is about right. That's long enough that they've clearly seen your earlier emails and chosen not to reply yet, and short enough that the conversation is still fresh. Waiting months and then closing it can read oddly, as if you'd forgotten about them and suddenly remembered.

faqs.q: Should I send a closing email if they've already said no?
faqs.a: No. If someone has given you a clear answer, the closing email is the thank you you send in reply. Thank them for letting you know, wish the project well, and leave it there. Sending a separate close-the-file note after a no just makes them deal with you twice, which is the opposite of what you're trying to do.

faqs.q: Is it pushy to ask who holds the budget after a no?
faqs.a: Not if you ask once, politely, and make it easy to ignore. It's a reasonable question that helps you approach the right person next time, and most people don't mind answering it. What makes it pushy is asking it straight after a hard sell, or following it up when they don't reply. One question, then you're done.

faqs.q: What if they reply to the closing email saying they're still interested?
faqs.a: Then you pick it up as if nothing happened, with no hint of 'finally'. Ask what's changed and what timing would suit them, and let them set the pace. People often reply to a closing email because it took the pressure off, so carrying that same easy tone forward is what keeps the conversation going.

items.title: Colour grading explained: how films get their mood
items.excerpt: What colour grading is, how it differs from correction, what LUTs do, and how The Matrix, O Brother and Fury Road use colour to tell the story.
items.coverAlt: A black and white frame of boxers training on the bags
items.body:
Colour grading is the stage at the end of the edit where the colour, contrast and brightness of every shot are set, so the film looks the way it's meant to feel. It's how a director makes one world feel sickly and another feel cold, or makes a summer field look like an old postcard. Done well, you never notice it. You just feel it.

I covered the basics briefly in what cinematography means. This goes further: what a grade is actually doing, why it isn't the same as fixing the colour, and a few famous films where the colour was doing a lot more of the storytelling than most people realise.

What's the difference between colour correction and colour grading?

Correction is technical. Grading is creative. They happen in that order, and people mix the two words up all the time.

Correction makes the footage accurate and consistent. White balance so a white wall reads white. Exposure evened out so one shot isn't a stop darker than the next. Two cameras matched so a cut between them doesn't jump. The aim is a neutral, honest starting point where every shot in a scene looks like it was filmed in the same place at the same time.

Grading is what you do with that neutral image. Pushing the shadows cooler, warming the highlights, pulling saturation out of everything except one colour, crushing the blacks or lifting them so the image goes soft and milky.

On a documentary shoot you can't control most of what's in front of you, so correction does a lot of heavy lifting. A morning interview by a window and an afternoon shot under strip lights need to sit next to each other without the viewer feeling the join. There's more on why mixed light causes so much trouble in interview lighting explained simply.

How does colour create mood?

Mostly through association. We've spent our whole lives seeing warm light at sunset, by a fire, in a kitchen at night. Cool, blue light is overcast mornings, hospitals and the hour before dawn. A grade borrows those associations and points them at a scene.

A few of the levers a colourist actually pulls:

  • Temperature. Warmer reads as comfortable, nostalgic or intimate. Cooler reads as detached, clinical or lonely.
  • Saturation. Rich colour feels alive and heightened. Muted colour feels serious, tired or documentary-real.
  • Contrast. Deep blacks and bright highlights feel punchy and dramatic. Lower contrast feels gentle and soft.
  • Separation. Different colours in the shadows and the highlights, which is where most stylised looks live.

None of these mean anything on their own. Cool and desaturated can feel calm in one film and grim in another. The grade only works when it agrees with what the story's already saying.

Why is The Matrix green?

Because the computers made it. The Matrix is probably the best-known example of colour being used as a map. Scenes inside the simulation carry a green tint. Scenes in the real world, aboard the ship and in the ruins, are cool and blue, with almost no green in them at all.

The film's cinematographer, Bill Pope, explained the thinking in an interview for the film's official website. The Matrix is a decaying world created by machines, so it got a green hue, and it was meant to make you feel slightly sick. The real world got a colder, bluer look, because in that future the sun's been blotted out and there's no natural warmth left.

Once you've noticed it, you always know where you are.

What is the teal and orange look?

It's the look of a huge number of action films from the 2000s onwards: skin pushed warm towards orange, and shadows, skies and backgrounds pushed cool towards teal. Watch almost any big blockbuster trailer and you'll see it.

It caught on for a sound reason. Orange and teal sit roughly opposite each other on the colour wheel, so they contrast strongly, and most skin tones fall in the orange range. As Adobe's guide to the look puts it, pushing blues into the shadows helps those skin tones stand out. It also mimics golden hour, warm sun on a face against a blue sky, which people already find beautiful.

The trouble is that it got used everywhere, whether the story asked for it or not. When every film has the same look, the look stops meaning anything, and it starts to feel like a preset rather than a decision.

Which other films use colour to tell the story?

O Brother, Where Art Thou?

The Coen brothers wanted a dry, dusty, faded postcard look. The problem was that they were shooting in Mississippi in summer, where everything was lush and green. Roger Deakins, the cinematographer, told Filmmaker Magazine that they didn't want anything to be green, and couldn't find a way to turn the greens into browns and yellows with traditional film processing. So they scanned the film and graded it digitally. It's widely credited as the first Hollywood feature to be colour graded digitally from start to finish, which makes it a quiet turning point.

Mad Max: Fury Road

Fury Road went the opposite way to most post-apocalyptic films. Its colourist, Eric Whipp, told FilmLight that George Miller had noticed thirty years of the genre using the same desaturated, bleached look, and was adamant this one should be saturated, sharp and graphic. Whipp built rich skies against warm sand and characters, and the night scenes were shot in bright sun, then darkened and pushed blue in the grade. He worked on it for about a year.

The official trailer above shows that saturated orange and blue at full volume. Miller has since said he thinks the black and white version, released as the Black & Chrome edition, is the best version of the film, as /Film reported. Same footage, completely different grade, and the director's favourite.

Same footage, completely different grade, and a different film.

What is a LUT, and is it the same as a grade?

A LUT, short for look-up table, is a file that maps one set of colours to another. Feed it a pixel of one colour and it hands back a different one. That's all it is.

There are two kinds worth knowing about. A technical LUT converts footage from one colour space to another, most often turning the flat, grey log footage a cinema camera records into a normal-looking image. A creative LUT applies a look, like a filter on your phone.

Treat a LUT as a starting point. It treats every shot exactly the same way, and no two shots are exactly the same. A look built for a bright exterior can turn a dim interior muddy and push skin somewhere strange. A proper grade still goes shot by shot, adjusting each one so the look holds across the whole film.

Half the LUT packs online promise a Hollywood look. The other half promise a vintage film look. Very few of them promise your skin will still look like skin.

Why do skin tones matter so much in a grade?

Because people notice faces before anything else, and they're very good at knowing when one looks wrong. A wall can go teal and nobody minds. A face goes grey, green or orange and the viewer feels something's off straight away, even if they can't say what.

Colourists usually protect skin first, isolating it so it stays natural while the rest of the image is pushed around it. There's a scope for this called a vectorscope, which has a line marking roughly where healthy skin of every complexion tends to sit. The real skill is lighting and grading darker and lighter skin in the same frame so both look right, which was handled badly for a long time and still is on plenty of corporate video.

What does grading mean for a brand film?

Most brand films don't need a dramatic look. They need to look like the place on a good day and to feel consistent from start to finish. A workshop should feel warm and lived in, a shop should look like the shop, and the founder should look like themselves. If the grade gets noticed, it's probably gone too far.

Where it does earn its keep is in mood and in continuity. A documentary is shot over different days, rooms and weather, and the grade is what makes it feel like one film. It can also carry a story, the way The Matrix does.

On our films the grade is done by a specialist colourist, after the edit is locked, because it's one of the clearest differences between a film that looks expensive and one that looks like a video. You can see how that fits into the rest of the process on the films page, and if you're working out what a film should cost, the film budget calculator is a decent place to start.
items.author: Earl Duncan

faqs.q: How long does colour grading take?
faqs.a: It depends on the length of the film and how stylised the look is. A short brand film might take a day or two of a colourist's time, while a feature can take weeks. Most of the time goes on matching shots and adjusting skin, not on building the look itself. Documentary footage shot across different rooms and days usually needs more matching than something filmed in one controlled space.

faqs.q: Can grading fix footage that was badly shot?
faqs.a: Only partly. A grade can rescue white balance, lift a slightly dark shot and match cameras, but it can't add detail that was never recorded. Blown out windows stay blown out, and heavily underexposed shots get noisy when they're brightened. Log footage gives the colourist more room to work, but the best grades start from footage that was lit and exposed properly on the day.

faqs.q: What software do colourists use?
faqs.a: DaVinci Resolve is the most widely used grading software, from freelancers up to feature films, and it has a capable free version. Baselight, made by FilmLight, is common on high-end features and television. Most editing software, including Premiere Pro and Final Cut, has colour tools too, which are fine for correction and simple looks but less suited to detailed shot by shot work.

faqs.q: Should our brand film have a distinctive colour look?
faqs.a: Only if the story calls for it. Most brand films are better served by a natural, consistent grade that makes your place and people look their best on a good day. A strong stylised look can date quickly and can make real people look less real. If there's a reason for it, like a change in time or mood across the film, a deliberate look can help tell the story.

items.title: Testimonial videos that don't sound like testimonials
items.excerpt: How to make a customer testimonial video people believe: let the customer tell their own story, film once the result is real, and ask about them, not you.
items.coverAlt: The homeowner in the finished front room at Nimrod Road
items.body:
A testimonial video stops sounding like a testimonial when the customer tells the story of what happened to them, in their own words, instead of praising the business. You film them once the result is real, ask about their situation rather than about you, and cut it as their account. The praise is then implied by the story, and the viewer believes it because they've worked it out for themselves.

Most testimonial videos are a customer on a sofa saying they were really professional and they'd definitely recommend them. It's sincere, and it doesn't land, because every business has one and they all sound the same.

Why do most testimonial videos sound the same?

Because the questions are about the business. Ask someone what it was like working with you and you get adjectives. Professional, friendly, on time, tidy. Lovely to hear and almost impossible to believe, because the viewer knows the business picked its happiest customer and pointed a camera at them.

There's a scripting problem too. When a customer's been handed lines, or asked to say that again but mention the price this time, it shows. People can hear the difference between someone remembering and someone performing.

And trust in second hand praise is wearing thin. BrightLocal's annual consumer survey tracks how many people trust online reviews as much as a personal recommendation, and that figure has dropped a long way in five years. Generic praise gets discounted in any format. Specific stories still get through.

What makes a customer story believable?

Specifics, stakes and a bit of friction. What the person needed, what was at risk, what was hard, and what they've got now. A story with a worry in it is more convincing than one that's all praise, because real projects have worries.

The Nimrod Road film works because of its stakes. A Victorian house in Tooting that had sat empty after the previous owners died. A couple who wanted the period features kept and the ground floor opened up. A project that started in September, with a baby due at the end of November. The work was finished in eight weeks, two weeks inside the estimate. Both homeowners tell it as their account, and anyone weighing up the same decision hears it from people in their own position.

The praise is implied by the story, and the viewer believes it because they've worked it out for themselves.

Who should tell the story, the customer or the business?

The customer, almost always. A business talking about its own quality is the one voice a prospective customer discounts straight away, because it's the voice being paid.

That was the thinking behind Barry Road, a full house renovation in East Dulwich. Every contractor says the same things about themselves: quality, on time, on budget. So the film is the homeowner giving their own account of the job, what they wanted, what it was like to live through, and what they ended up with. We handed the film to them and let them say whatever they were going to say.

The business can still appear, briefly and doing the work. Just don't let it narrate its own reputation.

Which customer should you film?

Not automatically the happiest one. Pick the customer whose situation looks most like the people you want more of. If your best jobs are period houses with tight deadlines, film the family with the period house and the tight deadline. Someone weighing you up should watch it and recognise their own situation.

Look for someone who had something at stake and can talk about it naturally. A worry, a deadline, a previous bad experience with someone else. They don't need to be polished, and the ones who are a bit unsure on camera often come across as the most honest. Most of all, they need to want to do it. A customer doing you a reluctant favour sounds exactly like one.

When should you film a testimonial?

Once the result is real, and ideally while it's still fresh. Both of those renovation films were made after the family had moved back in, so the customer is talking about a home they live in rather than a promise.

The downside of waiting is that the before has gone. At Nimrod Road the before only exists in the original listing photos, so those were cut against the finished rooms. At Barry Road, before and after floorplans were cut in so the scale of the work reads on screen. If there's any chance you'll want a customer film, photograph the start of the job properly. It costs almost nothing, and you can't get it back later.

The best time to plan a testimonial is before the customer has anything to testify about. Annoying, but true.

What should you ask in a testimonial interview?

Ask about them, not you. Questions that tend to open people up:

  • What was going on before you got in touch?
  • What were you most worried about?
  • What was it like day to day while the work was happening?
  • Was there a moment you weren't sure it would work out?
  • What's different now?
  • What would you tell someone in the position you were in?

Then listen, and follow whatever's interesting rather than ticking through the list. Never feed them the answer. If a customer says something in a way that's a bit clunky but true, keep it. The odd stumble is part of why it sounds real. There's more on this in how to make a brand video people actually watch.

How do you get the most from a customer story film?

Use it in the sales conversation, which is where it earns its money. Both renovation films were made as edits a contractor can send to someone deciding whether to trust them with a house. That's a precise job, and it decided how they were cut.

Beyond that, put the full film on the relevant service page, cut a short version for the top of the site, and pull vertical clips for social, where one honest line can carry a post. Ask the customer's permission for every use up front, paid ads included, so you're not chasing them six months later.

If you've got customers whose stories would sell your work better than you can, see the films we've made or tell us about them.
items.author: Earl Duncan

faqs.q: Should customers be paid to appear in a testimonial video?
faqs.a: Generally no, and it's worth avoiding anything that looks like payment for praise. A small thank you for their time is fine, but the value of a testimonial comes from it being freely given. If a customer is paid or given something significant, viewers would reasonably want to know, so be open about it. Choosing customers who genuinely had a good experience makes the question mostly irrelevant.

faqs.q: How long should a customer testimonial video be?
faqs.a: Long enough to tell one story properly, which is usually two to five minutes for the main film. That's what you send in a sales conversation or put on a service page. From the same interview you can cut a sixty to ninety second version for the top of your site and short vertical clips for social, where a single honest line from the customer can work on its own.

faqs.q: What if a customer gets nervous on camera?
faqs.a: Most people do at first, and it usually passes within ten minutes. Run it as a conversation, with no lines to learn and no autocue, and start with easy questions about their situation before anything that matters. Film them somewhere familiar, ideally the place the work was done. If they stumble, carry on rather than restarting, because those natural moments are often what makes it believable.

faqs.q: Do we need a customer's written permission to use their video?
faqs.a: Yes. Get written consent that covers where the film will appear and for how long, including your website, social media and any paid advertising. It protects you and it's fair to them. Agree up front what happens if they later want it taken down, and keep their personal details, like a full address, out of the film unless they're happy for them to be shown.

stat.title: People who trust online reviews as much as a personal recommendation
stat.takeaway: Generic praise is being discounted, so a specific customer story told on camera carries more weight than another five star line.

source.name: BrightLocal, Local Consumer Review Survey 2025 (1,026 US adults)

items.title: Why real people on camera matter more now
items.excerpt: As AI content floods feeds, real people on camera become proof. What the 2026 trust research says, and why documentary films built on real voices land.
items.coverAlt: A competitor with his hand raised after a match, surrounded by his team
items.body:
Real people on camera matter more as AI content floods feeds because they're proof. A generated face can say anything, so it carries no weight. A real founder, a real member of staff or a real customer, filmed where the work actually happens, is evidence that the business exists and stands behind what it says. Research from The Harris Poll UK, published in April 2026, found seven in ten consumers trust adverts made entirely by humans, and that drops to two in ten when an advert is generated by AI alone.

I've believed this for a long time, but the gap is getting wider. The cheaper it gets to make something that looks real, the more a viewer's first question becomes whether it is.

Why do people trust a brand more when they see real people?

Because a person on camera is putting their face to it. They can be recognised, called, held to what they said. That's a risk a business takes on deliberately, and viewers read it as confidence. A stock presenter or a generated spokesperson costs the business nothing to put in front of you, so it proves nothing.

It's also about who's speaking. People have always believed customers and staff more than the company talking about itself. We wrote about why in brand documentary vs corporate video, and it's the same instinct here. Someone in your position, describing what happened to them, is the version people believe.

What happens to trust when AI is involved?

It falls, and it falls further the more of the work AI does. The Harris Poll UK found trust in an advert drops from seven in ten when it's made entirely by humans, to four in ten when AI tools are used, to two in ten when it's generated by AI alone. Six in ten said a person should always be involved in making advertising that uses AI.

The same research picked out what makes people suspicious. Images that look too perfect, scenes that feel unrealistic and small inconsistencies were the most common giveaways. That's an interesting turn. For years, polish was how a brand showed it had spent money. Now flawless can read as fake.

The cheaper it gets to make something that looks real, the more people want to know whether it is.

Does it have to be the founder on camera?

No, and often it's better when it isn't only the founder. The most convincing person in a film is usually the one with the least reason to flatter the business.

On Barry Road it's the homeowner describing a full renovation in their own words, once the family had moved back in. On the Car Planet film for Plug In Stations, the whole thing is the customer talking. The installer never makes the claim about themselves, which is exactly what makes it usable in a sales conversation.

And La Fromagerie carries four people's accounts of the same business. The founder tells how it started, with a wheel of Beaufort in a garden shed, and the cheesemongers and the wholesale side fill in what it is now. Four voices that don't sound rehearsed are harder to doubt than one polished one.

What if you or your team hate being on camera?

Most people do, at first. The good news is that documentary filming doesn't ask anyone to perform. Nothing's read off an autocue, and nobody's asked to do it again with more energy. The interviews are conversations, and the people who are most nervous at the start often give the best answers an hour in, once they've stopped noticing the camera.

Nobody has ever been more relaxed because someone said “just act natural”. A decent conversation does the job far better.

We've written a practical guide to preparing to be filmed for a brand film, and the short version is that you don't need to be good on camera. You need to know your subject, which you already do.

How do documentary films use real people differently?

They let the story come from the people instead of handing them a script. We spend time with a business before filming, work out what the story actually is, and then go and film conversations in the places the business really lives. La Fromagerie was filmed during trading hours, around customers, in cheese rooms that are cold and dark. That's harder work. It also looks exactly like the shop you'd walk into, and no prompt can give you that.

The other difference is time. A documentary leaves room for the pause before someone answers and the work happening at the speed it really happens. Those are the moments that make a viewer feel they're seeing something true, and they're the hardest thing to fake.

Isn't AI content just cheaper to make?

Per piece, yes, and that's exactly the problem with it. When anyone can produce a polished video in an afternoon, polish stops telling the viewer anything about you. Feeds fill up with it, and it all starts to look the same. What can't be produced in an afternoon is access: the people in your business, the place they work and the things they've been through.

A smaller business usually has more of that than it thinks. The owner answers the phone. The person on camera is the person who'll turn up. That's something a big brand with a generated spokesperson can't buy, and it's worth putting on screen while it still stands out.

Is polished production a bad thing now?

No. Craft still matters. A badly lit, badly recorded film of real people tells the viewer you didn't care enough to do it properly. The point of a proper grade, proper sound and a patient edit is to show real people clearly. Smooth them into something that looks generated and you've thrown away the reason they were there.

Where I'd draw the line is anything that makes the person look less like themselves. Heavy retouching, a script they'd never say in real life, a set that looks nothing like where they work. Keep the people real and spend the budget on showing them well. If there's someone in your business people should hear from, tell us about them, or see more of the films we've made on our films page.
items.author: Earl Duncan

faqs.q: Do we need professional actors for a brand film?
faqs.a: No, and for a documentary-style film you'd usually avoid them. The people who actually run the business, work in it or buy from it carry far more weight than anyone hired to play them, because viewers can tell. Actors make sense for scripted adverts and dramatised scenes. For a film meant to build trust, real people with real stories are the stronger choice.

faqs.q: Can we use customers in our brand film?
faqs.a: Yes, and they're often the most convincing people in it. Ask customers who had a genuinely good experience and are happy to talk about it, and film once the result is real. Keep it a conversation rather than a script, and get their written consent to appear and to the footage being used. A customer's own account is the version prospective buyers believe.

faqs.q: How many people should appear in a brand film?
faqs.a: As many as the story needs, which is usually fewer than people expect. One strong voice can carry a short film. A longer documentary often works best with two to four, each adding something the others can't, like the founder's history alongside the people doing the work now. Every extra person needs time on screen, so more voices usually means a longer film.

faqs.q: Is AI ever fine to use in a film about real people?
faqs.a: Yes, behind the scenes. Transcribing interviews, cleaning up audio, drafting captions and reframing clips for social don't change what anyone said or did. The line is making a real person appear to say or do something they didn't, or generating scenes presented as real. That undermines the whole point of filming real people, and platforms like YouTube ask you to label it.

stat.title: How many consumers trust an advert, by who made it
stat.takeaway: Trust drops sharply as AI takes over the work, so a film that shows real people doing real things has more to offer than ever.

source.name: The Harris Poll UK, The Authenticity Trade-Off: How AI is reshaping trust in advertising, 2026 (reported as seven, four and two in ten)

items.title: What we keep hearing from businesses about video
items.excerpt: No faces on the website, stock passed off as content, a decision maker who isn't in the room, missed timing and camera nerves. What we hear, and how to fix it.
items.coverAlt: An engineer in hi-vis smiling on camera on site
items.body:
When businesses talk to us about video, the same handful of things come up again and again, whatever the sector. The work's excellent but there isn't one real face on the website. The content they've got turns out to be stock. The person keen on a film isn't the person who signs it off. The moment that would have made the story has already gone. And nobody wants to be on camera. Every one of these is fixable, usually without spending more.

I'm keeping this general and anonymised. These are patterns, and if you recognise your own business in one, you're in very good company.

Why does great work end up with no faces on the website?

Because the people doing the best work are usually too busy doing it to think about how it looks. You get a site with brilliant project photos, a logo, a phone number and nobody. Or a team page with a row of grey silhouettes.

The trouble is that buyers choose people. For anything expensive or personal, someone wants to know who's turning up, who they'll be dealing with and whether they seem trustworthy. A business with no faces on its site is asking a stranger to trust it blind, and a competitor with a slightly weaker portfolio and a friendly face on the homepage will often win that one.

The fix is smaller than people expect. Proper photos of the team at work, a short film of the founder explaining why they started, and one or two customers talking about the result. That's often a single day. Our Spotlight shoot exists for exactly this.

What's wrong with "we've already got content"?

Often, nothing. But sometimes, when you look properly, the content is stock footage, AI images and a few phone clips from years ago. Stock fills space, but it can't prove anything about you, because the same handshake and the same smiling team in the same glass office appear on hundreds of other sites. People have learned to scroll straight past it.

The test I use is simple. If you swapped your logo for a competitor's, would the content still make sense? If it would, it's doing no work for you. Footage of your actual people, premises and jobs can only belong to you, and that's why people believe it.

The Super Efficient drainage film shows real content made without much fuss. One day on a live job in Enfield, filmed start to finish with no reshoots, became an eight minute YouTube film, a run of vertical shorts and two carousels. Nothing staged, and nothing that could belong to any other company.

Why do video projects stall when someone else decides?

Because the person who gets in touch is often a marketing lead, an office manager or a founder's right hand, and the decision sits with a director, a board or a partner who wasn't on the call. The enthusiasm doesn't travel up the chain. What reaches the decision maker is a line on a spreadsheet with a number next to it.

It's common enough that Wyzowl's annual survey lists being unable to convince key decision makers as one of the reasons marketers give for not using video at all. If that's where you are, give the person deciding something to react to besides a price: the job the film will do, everything that comes out of one shoot, and an example from a similar business. Our free 44-page guide, Before the camera comes out, was written partly for this. Send it upwards.

Better still, get the person who signs it off into a conversation early. Twenty minutes with them saves weeks of relaying questions back and forth.

Somewhere in the UK right now, a brilliant video idea is sitting in the inbox of someone who's on holiday until the 14th.

What happens when the timing window closes?

Lots of stories have a moment, and once it's gone you can't film it again. A building going up. A project finishing. An anniversary. A team that's about to change. A customer in the first weeks after the work's done, while they're still delighted with it.

We see it with renovation films. On Nimrod Road, the family had already moved back in by the time we filmed, so the before only exists in the original listing photos. It still works, because the couple tell it well and the listing photos are cut against the finished rooms. But it shows how easily the most visual part of a story disappears while a business is still deciding.

So when someone says "let's do it next year", I'd ask what will have changed by then. Sometimes nothing, and waiting's fine. Often the scaffolding's down, the event's over or the people involved have moved on. A film takes six to ten weeks from the first conversation, so if there's a date that matters, count backwards from it.

What if nobody wants to be on camera?

Almost nobody does at first. It's the thing we hear most, and it's completely normal. People worry about how they'll look, what they'll say and whether colleagues will take the mickey afterwards.

Almost nobody wants to be on camera at first. It's the thing we hear most, and it's completely normal.

A few things make a real difference. Interviews run as conversations, with nothing to learn. No autocue. Filming people doing the job they're good at, which relaxes them because they're on their own ground. And time. The good material tends to arrive once people stop noticing the camera, which is one reason our films take two to three shoot days rather than an hour.

It doesn't have to be the boss, either. Sometimes the best person in the film is the engineer who explains things clearly, a long serving member of the team, or a customer. If you're the one going on camera and you're dreading it, read how to prepare for being filmed. It's less painful than you're expecting.

Is any of this a reason not to make a film?

Not really. Each of these comes down to planning and permission. The businesses that end up with a film they're proud of tend to decide early what it's for, get the decision maker involved, pick their moment and let real people speak. Budget matters, but less than any of that.

If one of these sounds like your business, tell us where you're stuck. If a film isn't the right spend yet, we'll say so.
items.author: Earl Duncan

faqs.q: Can we make a brand film if the boss won't appear in it?
faqs.a: Yes. The founder or MD doesn't have to be the face of the film, and sometimes someone else tells the story better. An engineer who explains the work clearly, a long serving member of staff or a customer talking about the result can carry a film well. It's worth the boss appearing briefly if they can, because buyers like to know who's in charge, but it isn't essential.

faqs.q: Is stock footage ever fine to use in a business video?
faqs.a: It's fine for small jobs like filling a gap in an explainer or illustrating something you genuinely can't film, such as a general street scene. It shouldn't carry the story. Anything meant to build trust, like who you are, what your work looks like and what customers say, needs real footage of your own people and jobs, because stock can't prove anything about your business specifically.

faqs.q: How do I pitch a video budget to a director or board?
faqs.a: Lead with the job the film will do and the business problem it's tied to, then the price. Show everything that comes from one shoot, such as the main film, short cuts, vertical clips and photography, so the cost reads per use rather than as one video.
